10071-by-ways-of-bombay:
S. M. Edwardes, a government official in Bombay, first published these sketches in the Times of India under the pen name Etonensis. They claim no critical study, only a brief record of persons he met and things he saw during several years of service in the city.

Chapters visit the spirit of Chandrabai, Bombay scenes, shadows of night, the birthplace of Shivaji, and the Ganesh caves, with pictures of mill-hands, Marwari sweet sellers, Koli women, and opium clubs. Edwardes writes as an observant insider. Readers get Bombay's inner life, street by street, in short, vivid sketches.
10111-boys-and-girls-from-thackeray:
Kate Dickinson Sweetser's 1907 book, with pictures by George Alfred Williams, retells Thackeray's boys and girls for young readers. Its chapters visit Henry Esmond, the Virginians, Becky Sharp at school, and Cuff's fight with Figs.

Further chapters meet George Osborne and Rawdon Crawley, Clive and Ethel Newcome, Arthur Pendennis, and Caroline, chosen from Thackeray's great novels. Sweetser softens the satire for children without losing the characters. Young readers get a friendly doorway into Vanity Fair, Esmond, and the Newcomes, with Thackeray's humor kept gentle for children. It is a kind first meeting with a great novelist.
10320-dotty-dimple-at-play:
Sophie May, author of the Little Prudy stories, published this children's book in 1868, dedicating it to blind children in Indianapolis. Dotty Dimple, a lively little girl, visits those children, then plays at home with friends and family. The book treats kindness to others as part of play itself, and moral lessons grow from fun.

Chapters cover playing ship, playing truant, playing prisoner and thief, a spoiled dinner, and Thanksgiving Day. Grandma's old times and a crystal wedding close the fun, with Emily's trials along the way. Readers get a sweet, old-fashioned story of childhood games, mischief, and gentle morals.
10508-the-sorrows-of-a-show-girl-a-story:
Kenneth McGaffey published this show-girl storybook in 1908, gathering pieces first printed in New York's Morning Telegraph. Its heroine is Sabrina, a chorus girl on Broadway's Great White Way, who discourses on theatrical conditions, fortunes, and love with sharp, comic wit. The tone is slangy, knowing, and kind.

Sabrina gets money from an unexpected source, visits Emporia and shocks that staid town, joins a chorus girls' union ball, and falls for a press agent. An automobile, a beefsteak party, and a mangled doughnut add farce. Readers get a lively, period portrait of Broadway life behind the footlights.
10629-britain-at-bay:
Spenser Wilkinson published Britain at Bay in 1909, a warning that Britain was unready for modern war. Writing before the First World War, he argues that the British constitution, built for peace and party politics, worked poorly as an instrument of war. Chapters weigh force and right, arbitration, the balance of power, and the rise of Germany.

Wilkinson turns from argument to remedy, urging a national army, a stronger navy, and clear principles for raising troops. Several chapters first ran in the Morning Post. Readers get a sharp pre-war debate about defense, and a measure of how Britain saw the German threat five years before 1914.
10716-the-epic-an-essay:
Lascelles Abercrombie, poet and critic, published The Epic: An Essay in 1914 to explain why epic poetry appears when it does. He argues that epic is invented again and again, in many lands, whenever a people passes through a "heroic age," before its warring elements cool into settled civilization. The needs that prompt the invention are broadly the same, so the poems resemble each other.

Abercrombie tests this view against the great epics and their societies, in clear, thoughtful prose. His essay suits readers who want to know what an epic is, not just which epics exist. It remains a respected piece of criticism on poetry's largest form.
11098-happy-and-gay-marching-away:
This small illustrated picture book for very young children pairs short verses with pictures of Tot, Tom, and Toby, dogs, cats, horses, and goats, all as happy as they can be. The introduction warns children to turn the leaves gently, since dogs, cats, and little children too will be hurt if torn. The book teaches kindness through its own handling.

Verses follow a little girl who frees her caged bird, watches it fly away, weeps that she will never get it again, then finds it hopping back into its cage. Other pieces celebrate May Day, Jack and Jill, a doll going to school, and a birthday present. Words are broken into syllables, lit-tle, joy-ous, heav-ens, to help early readers sound them out, making the book both story and reading lesson.
11124-northumberland-yesterday-and-to-da:
Jean F. Terry wrote this 1913 guide to Northumberland, past and present, dedicated to Sir Francis Douglas Blake. Terry disclaims deep research, aiming instead to help county dwellers spend a pleasant hour learning what happened in their own fields, streets, and riversides. Chapters cover the coast, the North and South Tyne, Newcastle, Elswick and its founder, the Cheviots, and the Roman Wall.

Later chapters follow streams, drums and trumpets, tales and legends, and ballads and poems, with photographs of Bamburgh Castle, Hexham Abbey, Tynemouth Priory, and the Tyne swing bridge. Terry listens to burns running to the Till, hearing children's laughter and manhood's deeper notes in the water. The book suits visitors and locals who want Northumberland's story in readable, local form.
11172-abraham-lincoln-a-play:
John Drinkwater's 1919 play stages Abraham Lincoln's presidency as drama rather than biography, compressing events and inventing one cabinet figure, Burnet Hook, to voice opposition to the president. Arnold Bennett supplies an introduction, and Drinkwater explains in a note that he shaped history freely where the stage required it. Scenes move through the White House, the cabinet, and the war years.

The play's interest lies in character more than chronology: Lincoln appears as a man handling war with patience, humor, and moral weight. Drinkwater, writing as an Englishman, avoids imitation dialect and local color he did not know firsthand. For readers, it offers a compact way to see how Lincoln's image traveled abroad soon after his death.
11213-brotherly-love-shewing-that-as-mer:
Mrs. Sherwood and her daughter Mrs. Streeten published this 1851 moral tale to show that merely human brotherly love cannot always be depended upon. When Mr. and Mrs. Mortimer must rush to Portsmouth on a brother's urgent letter, they leave thirteen-year-old Marten in charge of his little brother Reuben. Marten's confidence in his own maturity is tested by the week that follows.

The story's lesson is religious as well as domestic: family affection needs duty and faith to hold under strain. Sherwood, a prolific writer of children's moral fiction, keeps the prose plain and the episodes homely. The book gives modern readers a clear sample of Victorian instruction for children, earnest and unembarrassed.
11257-little-folks-astray:
Sophie May's 1872 children's book brings back the Parlin and Clifford children, who refuse to stay tucked in bed and instead join the company downstairs. Chapters follow Dotty having her own way and being rebuked, a lost fly, a freckled dog. hen-houses, and a pumpkin hood, with Grandma Read's Quaker speech and Aunt Madge's childhood story woven in. The author addresses parents directly, promising lectures on self-will.

May's method is gentle moral comedy: children misbehave, elders correct them, and the story, not a sermon, does the teaching. The book belongs to a popular series of domestic tales for young readers. Its charm lies in the children's voices and the cozy, crowded household around them.
11731-virginia-the-old-dominion-as-seen-:
Frank and Cortelle Hutchins wrote Virginia: The Old Dominion as a new edition of their earlier Houseboating on a Colonial Waterway, retitled for the See America First series. A map and fifty-four plates, six in colour, from the authors' photographs, illustrate a journey up the historic James River.

Chapters open with Gadabout, their floating home, a first run, a cozy harbour, and a run around the country's birthplace. One scene clears a forgotten grave, reading the name Elizabeth on a granite slab slowly buried by earth. The book follows Captain John Smith's river to the present day, turn by turn.
12000-a-walk-from-london-to-john-o-groat:
Elihu Burritt's Walk from London to John o' Groats, with notes by the way, recounts a long walk across Britain at a time when railways were changing travel. Burritt opens with motives to the walk, the iron horse and his rider, and the losses and gains by speed, comparing railway track and turnpike road scenery.

The second chapter records first days' observations and enjoyment, rural footpaths, and a visit to Tiptree Farm and Alderman Mechi's operations. Burritt, a learned blacksmith turned lecturer, walks to see the country slowly. He argues that speed costs a traveller the very things a journey should give: people, fields, and unhurried thought.
12334-a-bicycle-of-cathay:
Frank R. Stockton published A Bicycle of Cathay in 1900, a novel illustrated by Orson Lowell. Stockton, known for fanciful tales, here sends his hero on a bicycle journey that turns into a romance and a puzzle.

Chapters open with the doctor daughter, a bad twist, and a hero who must convince himself that nothing dreadful lurks in a certain spot. The doctor daughter tells him what she would like better than anything in the world, and the plot follows misunderstandings, rides, and revelations in the manner of Stockton comedy. Cathay in the title is a joke on a distant, dreamlike place reached by wheel. The novel is light, inventive, and typical of Stockton late romances.
12415-byways-around-san-francisco-bay:
W. E. Hutchinson's 1915 book, illustrated by the author, wanders the byways around San Francisco Bay in essays and poems. Contents run from Sunset in the Golden Gate and Brook and Waterfall to Muir Woods, Chinatown, a glass-bottom boat, fog on the bay, Meiggs' Wharf and moonlight on Mount Tamalpais.

Hutchinson walks, fishes for trout in the Berkeley hills, camps, and watches the bay change with light and weather. Poems punctuate the prose, and his own drawings give the scenes a personal stamp. Dedicated to his wife, called his dearest yet severest critic, the book reads as an affectionate local guide, a walker's record of a bay region before it grew crowded.
1245-night-and-day:
Virginia Woolf's second novel follows Katharine Hilbery, a young woman of a literary London family, torn between a safe marriage to a poet and her love for Ralph Denham, a struggling solicitor. The tale moves through drawing rooms, offices, and walks along the Thames.

Woolf writes London life with care and wit, and the novel's question is modern: can a woman have both love and a life of her own? The book, more traditional than her later work, still shows her eye for the inner life. It draws readers who like Woolf before the experiments.
12658-shapes-of-clay:
Ambrose Bierce's Shapes of Clay, published in 1903, gathers verses, some personally censorious, with names of real persons used without assent. Bierce, author of In the Midst of Life, Can Such Things Be, Black Beetles in Amber and Fantastic Fables, dedicates the book with pride, faith and affection. His young friends and pupils George Sterling and Herman Scheffauer receive it.

A preface explains the censorious part in sober prose. It quotes his earlier preface to Black Beetles in Amber, where verses republished from newspapers appear with considerable alterations. Shapes of Clay mixes satire, epigram and lyric, sharp and bitter in Bierce's manner. The book offers a late Bierce collection, fond of pupils, harsh toward enemies, and unmistakably his own.
1336-shelley-an-essay:
Written from a Catholic point of view, this short essay takes up the poet Percy Bysshe Shelley and asks why the Church had let poetry slip from its care. It argues that song and faith once grew side by side, in Dante and in Francis of Assisi, and that casting poetry out harmed both faith and art.

The writer then reads Shelley as a poet of beauty who reached toward light through nature and love, even while standing outside the Church. The essay pleads for poets to be welcomed back as helpers of the mind. It is less a life of Shelley than a case for poetry as a spiritual art.
13574-keeping-fit-all-the-way:
Walter Camp writes Keeping Fit All the Way in 1919 on how to obtain and maintain health, strength, and efficiency, with photographs taken under his direction. Three pioneers in senior service work, Colonel Ullman, ex-President Taft, and Camp himself, front the book, and the Daily Dozen exercises run through its middle chapters.

Camp promises men over military age that three or four hours a week, with a score of companions, in a scientifically tested system, can renew youth. Draft boards seeking two hundred men, and a Cleveland sanitary police examination where thirty-seven of forty-two women passed but only twenty-two of seventy-two men, show why he worries. Camp's system is group exercise, discipline, and daily habit for a nation at war's end.
14490-a-daughter-of-to-day:
Sara Jeannette Duncan's novel follows Elfrida Bell, a young Canadian woman of artistic ambition, as she navigates London and Paris society in the 1890s. Miss Kimpsey, a tired visitor, opens the story in Mrs. Bell's drawing room.

Elfrida writes, paints, and argues with friends such as Kendal, weighing a career against marriage and convention. Duncan, herself a journalist and novelist, writes with wit about the new woman, the press, and the art world. The novel is a thoughtful study of independence, neither preaching nor scolding, and it holds up well as a portrait of its era.
14491-the-twenty-fourth-of-june-midsumme:
Grace S. Richmond's 1914 novel Midsummer's Day opens with Richard Kendrick arriving at the Gray house by the wrong door, a small mistake that sets the whole story moving. The chapters follow a summer household through rain, roses, and theater.

Richard changes plans, pricks fingers, stages The Taming of the Shrew, and joins intrigues over flags, blankets, and lavender linen, while Roberta and other young people sort out affection and duty. Richmond writes warmly about home life. The novel is a light, good-natured romance of a June house party, full of small domestic comedy.
14813-the-life-and-death-of-richard-yea-:
Maurice Hewlett's 1901 chronicle retells the life of Richard the Lionheart, called here Richard Yea-and-Nay for his swift yes and no. The Book of Yea opens with Abbot Milo on the nature of the leopard, Count Richard, fires by night and the fair Jehane bestowing herself.

Anjou, a noble lady and the old lion king shape a tale of crusade, love and kingship, told in rich, archaic prose with an Italian epigraph from Dante. Hewlett dedicates the chronicle to Edmund Gosse, always benevolent to his invention. Readers who like historical romance in high style will find battles, courts and passion, all coloured by the legend of a king more lion than statesman.
14854-martha-by-the-day:
Julie M. Lippmann's 1912 novel opens on Broadway in a late November storm, during the evening rush hour. Claire Lang stands ten minutes in drenching wet at a crossing, pushed by crowds, bewildered and small, until she darts into traffic with every chance of being trampled.

Martha by the day, the working woman of the title, enters a city where getting across the street can feel like a battle. Lippmann writes New York as a place of chaises for the favoured few and public conveyances for the rest, often at a price barely afforded. The novel follows women who work, wait and keep going, with humour and a keen eye for street life.
14884-famous-violinists-of-to-day-and-ye:
Henry C. Lahee follows the plan of his Famous Singers in this bird's-eye view of celebrated violinists from earliest times to the present day, illustrated and published in Boston in 1899. Period chapters run from 1650 to 1750, 1750 to 1800, 1800 to 1830 and 1830 to 1850.

Paganini, Ole Bull and Joachim each earn a chapter, with violinists of today, women as violinists and famous quartets to close. Lahee writes for music lovers, not only players, giving careers, styles and anecdotes in short compass. The book remains a lively survey of violin playing before recordings made every great player audible.
15082-the-life-of-the-spirit-and-the-lif:
Evelyn Underhill's 1922 book asks how the life of the spirit can survive in a modern world of science, schools, and social change. Chapters take up the marks of spiritual life, its history, and what psychology says about mind, contemplation, and suggestion. Institutional religion, education, and the social order each get a chapter.

Underhill writes as a learned guide, not a preacher, drawing on mystics and modern thinkers alike. She argues that prayer and inner life still matter when outward life grows busy and mechanical. Readers interested in faith, mysticism, or the history of religion will find the book clear, serious, and humane.
15140-washington-s-birthday:
Robert Haven Schauffler edited this holiday anthology on George Washington's birthday, gathering prose and verse on its history, observance, spirit, and meaning. Poems by Oliver Wendell Holmes and Margaret Sangster open the book, followed by pieces on Washington's boyhood, his looks, and his training. Selections from his speeches close the set.

Sections move from the day itself to his early years, his generalship, and his place in schools and colleges. The tone is warm and patriotic, in the style of early twentieth-century holiday books. Readers who want Washington as Americans once celebrated him will find the collection both useful and nostalgic.
15214-sevenoaks-a-story-of-today:
J. G. Holland's 1875 novel Sevenoaks opens with Miss Butterworth passing an evening in a New England village, then follows town meeting politics and the poor knocked down to Thomas Buffum. Jim Fenton, a rough, kind hero, seeks lodgings, adopts violent ways of gaining boarders, and faces trial with Mike Conlin.

Mr. Belcher's rise, Palgrave's Folly in New York, and Mrs. Talbot's dinner parties widen the satire of money, power, and village life. Holland writes with moral earnestness and Yankee humor. Readers of nineteenth-century American fiction will find Sevenoaks lively, didactic, and full of local color.
15538-hetty-gray:
Rosa Mulholland, Lady Gilbert, wrote this children's novel, Hetty Gray, or Nobody's Bairn, in twenty chapters. It opens in Wavertree, called the prettiest village in all England, where cottages stand in twos and threes with red-tiled roofs, little gardens, and hedges overrun with flowering weeds. A forge under a great sycamore, a cave of fire in shadow, draws children on their way to school.

Chapters follow Hetty from four years old, under horses' feet, adopted, lonely, and desolate, through a new home, rebellion, and a cottage childhood again. A trick on the governess, a children's dance, a trial of patience, and a question about a drowning close the tale: if she was drowned, how can she be Hetty? Mulholland writes a warm Victorian story of an orphan finding her place, with village life drawn in loving detail.
15542-a-daughter-of-the-dons-a-story-of-:
William MacLeod Raine, author of Wyoming and Bucky O'Connor, published this New Mexico novel in New York in 1914, with Grosset and Dunlap, illustrated by D. C. Hutchison. A frontispiece shows little hands catching hold of a man and fighting with the current. Twenty-five chapters carry the tale from Don Manuel introducing himself through two grants and fisherman's luck.

Later chapters bring Juanita, two messages, taming an outlaw, Don Manuel and moonlight, and the sixteenth century meeting the twentieth. An ambush, a thousand-dollar reward, Valencia's promise and ring, cut wires, and an attack drive the plot toward a prince consort. Raine writes a western romance of old Spanish grants, new American law, and love across that divide, in his popular, fast-moving style.
15755-english-dialects-from-the-eighth-c:
A scholarly survey of English dialects by Walter W. Skeat, Elrington and Bosworth Professor of Anglo-Saxon at Cambridge. First issued in 1911 and reprinted in 1912, it traces local speech from the eighth century to Skeat's own day. Skeat founded the English Dialect Society, and his book sums up a life of work on old texts. Cambridge University Press issued it as a compact history with specimens.

Early chapters treat the four old dialects and the meaning of Anglo-Saxon itself. Northumbrian speech gets long treatment, from Bede and Caedmon through the Metrical Psalter and Barbour's Bruce. Later pages follow southern and midland forms, with extracts that let readers hear each stage. The book still serves students who want to see how English varied by place before print smoothed it out.
15893-the-lighted-way:
A mystery romance by E. Phillips Oppenheim, author of Havoc and Peter Ruff, issued by Little, Brown, and Company in Boston in 1912. A. B. Wenzell supplied the pictures. A frontispiece shows a woman's head sinking on a man's shoulder, hands clasped, at page three hundred and fifty-four. Oppenheim, a master of popular intrigue, opens with an invitation to dinner.

Ruth enters, Arnold scents mystery, and the lighted way leads through love and danger. Spies, secrets, and high society tangle around the hero. Oppenheim keeps the pace swift and the ending fair. The novel delights as Edwardian thriller romance: a dinner, a mystery, and a love that finds its way through darkness.
16198-her-own-way:
Clyde Fitch's Her Own Way, a play in four acts published by Macmillan in 1907, bears a stern copyright notice on its title page. All acting rights, professional and amateur, were reserved, and any public performance without consent risked damages under the United States statutes, with section 4966 quoted in full. Applications to perform had to go to the Macmillan Company.

The play itself belongs to Fitch's popular stage world of society, marriage, and strong-willed heroines, in the years when he ruled Broadway. Readers can study its dialogue, scenes, and stage business as a printed play, even without a production. Theater lovers will find a lively specimen of Edwardian American drama.
16416-an-essay-toward-a-history-of-shake:
Martin Brown Ruud traces Shakespeare in Norway in this 1917 Chicago dissertation, reprinted from Scandinavian Studies and Notes. He follows translations of the plays, Norwegian criticism, and stage performances, while leaving Shakespeare's influence on Norwegian literature for another study. Fellowships from Chicago and the American-Scandinavian Foundation made the research possible.

Ruud writes as a careful scholar, with dates, names, and sources in order. The essay serves students of Shakespeare's reception abroad. Short as it is, it maps a whole national story: how Norway read, staged, and argued over England's greatest playwright.
16467-musicians-of-to-day:
Romain Rolland surveys the musicians of his day in this volume, translated by Mary Blaiklock in 1915. Berlioz opens the set, followed by Wagner, Saint-Saens, Vincent d'Indy, Richard Strauss, Hugo Wolf, Perosi, and Debussy's Pelleas et Melisande. A long closing sketch traces the musical movement in Paris since 1870.

Rolland writes as a critic with strong views and wide sympathy, praising and scolding in turn. The Berlioz chapter notes the paradox that the world thinks it knows a composer it barely knows. Music lovers will find a passionate, learned guide to the age of Strauss and Debussy.
17091-oliver-cromwell-a-play:
John Drinkwater's play on Oliver Cromwell, dedicated to Bernard Shaw, opens at Cromwell's house at Ely about 1639. Elizabeth sews at the table, his eighty-year-old mother reads by the window, and talk turns to Oliver's restless persuading. The cast runs from his mother, wife, and daughter Bridget to Hampden, Ireton, Fairfax, and Charles I himself.

Drinkwater follows Cromwell from Ely home life to Parliament, war, and rule, in blank, stage-ready scenes. The play keeps its focus on character and choice rather than battle noise. Theatre readers and history fans will find a clear, humane portrait of a ruler who troubled his own kin as much as his foes.
17133-mildred-s-inheritance-just-her-way:
Annie Fellows Johnston's Cosy Corner volume joins three short tales: Mildred's Inheritance, Just Her Way, and Ann's Own Way. A picture of three pretty college girls leaning over a steamer rail opens the set, promising travel, friendship, and small trials. The tales belong to Johnston's world of kind girls, home duties, and gentle morals, sold at fifty cents in cloth.

Each story is brief, warm, and made for young readers, with character shown in choices rather than lectures. The set suits fans of the Little Colonel books who want more of Johnston's cozy, old-style charm. It is a light, pleasant trio for a quiet afternoon's reading.
17481-the-parts-men-play:
Arthur Beverley Baxter, author of The Blower of Bubbles, published this novel in Toronto in 1920, with a foreword by Lord Beaverbrook, who commends it as a Canadian book of literary vitality. The story opens with Lady Durwent deciding on a dinner, and moves through her family, a town house, a dinner party, and a house party at Roselawn. Gathering shadows and a rending of the veil mark a turn toward darker matter.

Later chapters follow Malcolm Durwent, a man of solitude, Dick Durwent, Elise, smugglers, a challenge, and a fight for a bridge. Readers get a Canadian novel that mixes society life with adventure, ending on a light upon the water. Baxter's range, from drawing rooms to open conflict, gives the book its energy.
1755-ivanoff-a-play:
Nicholas Ivanoff is a landowner worn down by debt, a dying wife, and his own loss of purpose, and he cannot explain his coldness even to himself. Anna, born Sarah Abramson, loves him still, while his uncle Count Shabelski and his neighbor Lebedieff press him toward a new match with Lebedieff's daughter.

The play's tension is inward: Ivanoff cannot explain his own coldness, and his honesty makes him crueller than a villain would be. Chekhov wrote it as a study of a man out of step with his age. It remains a sharp portrait of depression before the word was common, played out in drawing rooms and country houses.
1759-the-black-bearded-barbarian-the-lif:
Mary Esther Miller MacGregor, writing as Marion Keith, tells the life of George Leslie Mackay, the Canadian missionary whom the Chinese of north Formosa called the Black-Bearded Barbarian. The book opens with Mackay as a boy splitting rocks in a stony pasture behind the barn. It follows him to Formosa, where he preached nearly every day in houses by the river and in open squares.

Mackay also treated disease wherever he found it, and the biography stresses his plain manner and his stamina. Written for young readers, it presents a missionary life as adventure and service together, and it keeps its focus on the man himself rather than on doctrine.
17732-tales-of-hearsay:
Joseph Conrad published this set of tales with copyrights from 1911, 1917, and 1918, held by the Metropolitan Magazine Company of Garden City, New York. The contents list four stories: The Warrior's Soul, Prince Roman, The Tale, and The Black Mate. The first, dated 1917, opens with an old officer with long white moustaches giving rein to his indignation at young judges.

He scolds youngsters who pass judgment on the few poor stragglers of a generation that has done and suffered not a little in its time. Readers get Conrad's late short fiction, sombre, ironic, and concerned with honour under pressure. The book suits readers of Conrad's tales beyond his famous novels.
17750-laugh-and-play:
This collection of original stories, with pictures by E. Stuart Hardy, was published in London and New York by Ernest Nister and E. P. Dutton and Company, and printed in Bavaria. Its opening verse invites readers to laugh and play all day, arguing that song keeps days from seeming long. Maid and lad, faces bright, and tears kept at bay set the tone.

Readers get a children's story book of the gift-book kind, cheerful, moral, and richly pictured. The stories suit young children and family reading aloud. The volume's Bavarian printing marks the fine colour work of its era.
17802-myth-and-science-an-essay:
Tito Vignoli wrote this essay on myth and science for the International Scientific Series, volume thirty-eight, in a third edition published in London in 1885 by Kegan Paul, Trench and Company. Contents open with ideas and sources of myth, then turn to animal sensation and perception and human sensation and perception. A statement of the problem follows.

Later chapters cover the animal and human exercise of the intellect, perception of things, and the intrinsic law of apprehension, closing with the historical evolution of myth and science. Readers get a late Victorian attempt to ground myth in the science of mind. The book suits readers of anthropology and of the history of psychology.
17841-the-old-flute-player-a-romance-of-:
Edward Marshall and Charles T. Dazey wrote The Old Flute-Player in 1910, published in New York by G. W. Dillingham with pictures by Clarence Rowe. The tale opens in a small London orchestra, where Herr Kreutzer plays the flute and keeps his daughter Anna in strict seclusion near Soho Square.

Kreutzer is a mystery to his mates, and the landlady swears the Dutchman in the attic is something in disguise. A bully, a young hero named Vanderlyn, and Anna's own cry of guilt soon drive the plot. It is a melodramatic romance of music, secrets, and love, in the full, old style of stage and novel.
17903-writing-the-photoplay:
J. Berg Esenwein and Arthur Leeds wrote this manual for the new art of the photoplay, revised in 1919 for the Home Correspondence School. Esenwein edited The Writer's Monthly, and Leeds had been script editor at the Edison Studio, so both men knew the film trade from the inside.

Chapters define what a photoplay is, who can write one, and what terms the trade uses. They then show the parts of a script, give a full sample form, and teach the plain craft of typing and laying it out. For fans of early film, it is a clear window on how silent movies were built, scene by scene.
18110-the-bridal-march-one-day:
Björnstjerne Björnson wrote The Bridal March and One Day, translated from the Norwegian and printed in London in 1896 by William Heinemann. The Bridal March was first written in Christiania in 1872, as text to four designs by the painter Tidemand, and dedicated to Hans Christian Andersen.

The tale opens last century, in a high inland valley, where a girl with a thick plait walks a bridal path. One Day, first run in a Norwegian magazine late in 1893, follows as a shorter companion. Björnson writes with Norwegian warmth and moral force. The pair gives a fine, short taste of a Nobel laureate's tales.
18153-oscar-or-the-boy-who-had-his-own-w:
Walter Aimwell wrote Oscar, or the Boy Who Had His Own Way, printed in Boston in 1861 by Gould and Lincoln, entered in 1854. Aimwell, author of Clinton and the Boy's Own Guide, here portrays a bright but willful boy whose career tests home, school, and self.

The tale opens in a kitchen, where Bridget rules her realm and Oscar's rude troop demands pie, shoots peas, and stirs squabbles. School brings fresh trials, as Oscar plays schoolmaster and carries jokes too far. Aimwell writes with moral warmth and humor. It is a classic boys' book on will, temper, and the slow art of doing right.
1820-a-wasted-day:
Richard Harding Davis opens with a private secretary laying a letter in front of the Wisest Man in Wall Street, a note from Mrs. Austin, probation officer of the Court of General Sessions, asking for a letter about a young man named Spear. The wise man, Mr. Thorndike, must decide whether a word from him can save a boy from prison.

The story follows Thorndike through a day of meetings, with Mr. Andrews explaining from the depth of his wisdom that mothers are all alike when a son goes to jail. Davis uses the day to ask what wisdom is worth if it cannot act. The tale ends as a quiet rebuke to men who are wise about markets and helpless about mercy.
18324-the-third-great-plague-a-discussio:
John H. Stokes, chief of dermatology and syphilology at the Mayo Clinic, wrote this book for everyday people in 1917. Stokes treats syphilis as a social problem as well as a medical one, and he writes in plain terms for readers with no medical training. The book appeared from Saunders in Philadelphia and London, with reprints in 1918 and 1920.

Chapters trace the history of the disease, its nature and course through primary, secondary, and late stages, the blood test, and treatment, including mercury. Stokes stresses facts over fear and shame. Readers get an early public health book: honest, direct, and aimed at helping ordinary people understand, prevent, and face a disease that many would not name.
18559-the-child-s-day:
Woods Hutchinson, physician and sometime professor of anatomy at the University of Iowa, wrote this health book for children in the Woods Hutchinson Health Series, published by Houghton Mifflin in 1912. The book follows a child's day from morning to night, teaching health through daily habits.

Sections cover waking up, bathing and brushing, breakfast, going to school, and lessons in fresh air, hearing, seeing, tasting, and talking. Later pages take up keeping well and fighting foes of health, so that a child learns why clean air, clean water, and good habits matter at every hour of the day.
18645-thackeray:
Anthony Trollope wrote this study of William Makepeace Thackeray for Macmillan's English Men of Letters series in 1879, edited by John Morley. Trollope notes that no life of Thackeray existed, since Thackeray, put off by fulsome biography, asked his daughters to write none. His daughters kept that wish, so Trollope gives anecdotes and criticism rather than a full life.

Chapters cover Fraser's Magazine and Punch, Vanity Fair, Pendennis and The Newcomes, Esmond and The Virginians, burlesques, lectures, ballads, and Thackeray's style and work habits. Trollope writes as a fellow novelist with frank judgments. The book remains a classic early guide to Thackeray.
18775-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-43:
Chambers' Edinburgh Journal, number 435 of the new series, dated Saturday, May 1, 1852, was conducted by William and Robert Chambers at a penny halfpenny. Its lead essay, Forced Benefits, argues that men are often the better for things forced upon them.

Railways prove the point: landowners who petitioned against the odious thing now welcome their lines, and even Oxford is glad of one. A Scottish distillery dairy of seven hundred cows, built to eat grain refuse, shows the same pattern, turning a polluting liquid into farm manure under threat of a canal lawsuit. The essay finds progress in benefits nobody sought and many fought.
1878-a-millionaire-of-yesterday:
'Filth. ' grunts Trent at a cabin in the west of Ireland, and the novel that follows moves from such places into finance, diamonds, and South African mines. Da Souza, with beady eyes, brings news that stuns a roomful of men. The millionaire of the title must reckon with a past that will not stay buried.

Oppenheim writes the Edwardian thriller of wealth with confidence, and the novel's interest lies in its hero's rise and the price of it. Readers who like stories of fortunes made fast and lost faster will find the book brisk, worldly, and full of the author's usual polish.
18796-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-43:
Chambers' Edinburgh Journal, number 436 of the new series, dated Saturday, May 8, 1852, was conducted by William and Robert Chambers at a penny halfpenny. Its lead essay, The Musical Season, takes up the old dictum that the English are not a musical people.

Newspapers between April and August, the essay notes, overflow with concerts: symphonies and sonatas, ballads and polkas, Philharmonic societies, glee clubs, benefit concerts, and morning and evening performances. London has become the congress of nearly all the performing musical notabilities of Europe, who now come for renown as well as cash. The essay argues that lasting fervor, not hypocrisy, explains a nation that fills its halls with music.
18853-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-43:
William and Robert Chambers issued this number of Chambers' Edinburgh Journal on Saturday, May 22, 1852, priced at a penny halfpenny. The journal mixed essays, tales, and useful knowledge for a wide popular readership. Its opening piece, on the philosophy of laughter, defends laughter against the charge that it is childish and unworthy of grown men.

The number continues in the journal's usual miscellany fashion, offering short reading on varied subjects for a weekly audience. Such issues show what respectable family magazines gave readers in mid-Victorian Scotland: moral reflection, light learning, and entertainment in small doses. Readers get a snapshot of popular print culture, valuable for its tone, topics, and view of everyday taste.
18898-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-43:
William and Robert Chambers issued this number of Chambers' Edinburgh Journal on Saturday, May 15, 1852, priced at a penny halfpenny. Its opening essay defends London crossing-sweepers, the poor men who cleared a path through mud for pedestrians. No honest work, it argues, deserves contempt if it lets a man support himself without burdening others.

The essay places sweepers among the supernumeraries of the great metropolitan drama, pushed about by circumstance yet part of city life. Such pieces show the journal's humane, observant style. Readers get a short, sympathetic portrait of humble London labor, and a window into how mid-Victorian magazines asked readers to look with respect at people they passed daily.
19130-stonehenge-today-yesterday:
Frank Stevens, curator of the Salisbury Museum, wrote this guide to Stonehenge, with plans and pictures by Heywood Sumner. It asks when and by whom the stones were raised, what the monument consists of, and where its stones came from. The tone is clear and aimed at visitors.

Stevens describes the outer circle, the inner horseshoes, the five great trilithons, and the fallen Altar Stone, and compares the outer ring to the dome of St. Paul's. Fallen stones make the plan hard to read at first glance. Readers get a sound, readable account of a famous ruin and its puzzles.
19181-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-43:
This May 29, 1852, issue of Chambers' Edinburgh Journal, conducted by William and Robert Chambers, opens with Therefore and Because, on practical men who judge by instinct yet cannot state grounds. Lord Mansfield tells a general to trust native good sense but never argue his judgments, since argument will surely go wrong.

Later pieces turn on Spain's debt to Charles, a witty minister on Jacobites, and servants in Lima who blame rice for their fear of washing hands. David's Last Picture closes the number in Brussels. Readers get a Victorian weekly miscellany, learned, witty, and fond of odd reasons.
19247-dotty-dimple-s-flyaway:
Sophie May wrote this 1871 Dotty Dimple story about Flyaway, a small child with a tiny conscience folded like a leaf bud in spring. Chapters follow her running away to church, running away to heaven, meeting a railroad savage, and wheeling about in mischief. The book is dedicated to the little Lindsays.

Grandma tells stories while Ruth nurses a toothache, and Flyaway takes an orange, promises to bring it back, dons Horace's straw hat, and slips away with an old cane. Each scrape ends in gentle correction. Young readers get a sweet, old-style tale of a wilful little girl and patient family love.
1932-early-kings-of-norway:
Thomas Carlyle's Early Kings of Norway, taken from volume nineteen of the Sterling Edition of his works, tells the saga age in Carlyle's thunderous prose. Olaf, baptized but still a viking, keeps his profession, and his partnerships with Svein of the Double-beard carry him through raids and conversions.

Carlyle treats the Norse kings as heroes of a stern age, and his chapters mix saga narrative with moral commentary. The book is less a modern history than a Victorian retelling. Its value lies in Carlyle's voice: a prophet-historian who believed that great men, for good or ill, make the ages they live in.
19411-the-woman-s-way:
Charles Garvice wrote this romance novel, printed in London in the mid nineteen teens. Celia climbs the steep stone stairs of Brown's Buildings to a top-floor room, a poor girl making her way in a city that offers little ease. Milk boys and paper boys race past her, whistling as they go.

Later scenes move to grander houses, where a major-domo guards the door and a lady speaks in a voice that shakes. Garvice's plot turns on how a woman with little money keeps her pride and finds love without losing herself.
20074-the-story-of-the-cambrian-a-biogra:
C. P. Gasquoine wrote The Story of the Cambrian, a biography of a railway in Wales. Railways rarely get life stories, yet the Cambrian lines had a long, hard one. Gasquoine thanks many friends tied to the Cambrian Railways for their help. Their aid made even an attempt at the tale possible, he says.

Inside are lines, stations, firms, and the men who ran them. Welsh hills and coastal towns shaped every mile of track. The book records growth, strain, and change in one rail system. Readers who love rail history get names, dates, and local detail in depth.
20164-critical-miscellanies-vol-1-of-3-e:
John Morley wrote Critical Miscellanies, and volume one holds an essay on Macaulay. Morley was a leading critic and statesman of Victorian Britain. He praises the habit of writing down what one reads and thinks. Such notes give learning clearness, shape, and a right place, he says.

Macaulay, the famed historian and essayist, is a fit subject for Morley. Both men wrote prose of great force and wide public reach. The essay weighs Macaulay's gifts, faults, and place in English letters. Readers get two sharp Victorian minds meeting on the page at once.
20201-mary-gray:
Mary Gray is a novel of a girl raised in a poor London street. Her home was one of a squat line of mean little houses. Those houses hid behind a great church in the city's heart. The road before them led only to the church's back entrance.

From such narrow ground, Mary Gray's life and choices unfold. Poverty, work, and love test girls in tales of this kind. The church at her back stands as both shelter and shadow. Readers get a sober city novel on a poor girl's path to womanhood.
20575-my-dog-tray:
My Dog Tray is a story in verse and prose for children, about a poor girl named Nelly and her faithful dog. Tray never leaves her side. At night, while Nelly's tears are shed in hushed sorrow, the dog crouches close to keep her warm.

With pitying love, Tray licks her bitter tears away. Nelly shares her crusts with him, and he shares her hard life with a dog's steady heart. Tales like this one, of animal faithfulness to a suffering child, were nursery favorites in the Victorian years. Tray's devotion carries the whole lesson of the book.
20736-the-girl-scouts-at-home-or-rosanna:
Katherine Keene Galt wrote Rosanna's Beautiful Day for the Girl Scouts at Home set of tales. One scene shows a big garage, fit for four cars, wrapped in vines. Its one door opens into a garden, with no other door or window on that side.

Rosanna's day turns small home events into a full, happy arc for young readers. Scouting values of help, cheer, and care run through the tale. The book shows how early Scout fiction brought the movement into ordinary homes. It keeps a light touch, with family scenes and outdoor touches in equal share.
21116-the-easiest-way:
Eugene Walter's play The Easiest Way became this 1911 novel, written with Arthur Hornblow as a story of metropolitan life. Its heroine, Laura Murdock, calls herself an actress, though the foreword insists she has no talent for the stage. She has lived as a kept woman and wants to change.

Laura tries to redeem her past through an honest, unselfish love. The attempt fails badly, and she falls back toward the easy way of the title. The authors stress that working actors should not be judged by Laura's type. Broadway crowds and New York rooms frame her rise and collapse.
21228-white-lilac-or-the-queen-of-the-ma:
Amy Walton's story for girls begins with Mrs White at her cottage door. She is anxious about a promised visit from the rector's wife to see the new baby. Several of her children have died, so this one matters all the more. A branch of white lilac, brought by her husband, gives the baby her name: Lilac White.

Her father dies soon after, and her mother raises her alone. At twelve Lilac is pretty enough for a visiting artist to want her in a picture, until a cousin's new hair-do spoils the sitting. May Day brings rivalry over Queen of the May, and grief follows close behind the honour.
21267-lincoln-s-birthday:
Robert Haven Schauffler edited this anthology for the Our American Holidays series, published in New York in 1909 and reprinted through 1916. It promises a full view of Lincoln through the most noteworthy essays, orations, and poems about him, plus fiction and Lincoln's own writings. Thanksgiving and Christmas volumes stand beside it in the series.

Schools and families used such anthologies to mark February 12 with readings rather than only ceremony. Pieces from many ages and nations show Lincoln as others saw him: speaker, president, and folk hero. The editor thanks many publishers for permissions. It is a period piece of Lincoln devotion, gathered for one day a year.
2140-extracts-from-the-diary-of-william-:
William Bray, born at Shere in 1736, kept a diary from 1756 to 1800, and these extracts, printed in 1876 for his descendants, show a life of sociability, amusement, and successful industry. His brothers died unmarried, and he succeeded to the family estate in 1803. Bray's diary, kept for decades, shows a gentleman's round of visits, dinners, and business.

The diary records dinners, visits, business, and local life with steady good humour. Readers of Georgian social history will find here an ordinary gentleman's round, told without pretence and full of small, telling detail. The 1876 printing, made for family, now serves historians of Georgian sociability.
21758-hudson-bay:
In May 1841, a letter changed young R. M. Ballantyne's life: he was appointed apprentice clerk to the Hudson's Bay Company. This book is his own account of the years that followed, in the fur country of Canada. In his preface he says his chief aim is the everyday life of that world, a subject other writers had only touched in passing.

The pages follow the daily work of the trade: the outposts, the Red River Settlement, the travel, and the long winters. Later editions kept the text nearly as written, since the far posts changed so slowly. Every novel Ballantyne later wrote about the north grew from these years. As memoir, it is the seed of them all.
21782-the-yillian-way:
Jame Retief, vice-consul in Earth's Diplomatic Corps, faces the most polite danger in the galaxy in Keith Laumer's The Yillian Way. The Yill of the title are gray-skinned hosts whose ceremonial protocol is impressive, colorful, and, in the long run, deadly. Retief watches a Yill party where a raised fist and hands on a head pass for friendly custom. Every gesture means something, and a wrong one could kill.

The ambassador's staff insists that Terrestrials are a kindly, peace-loving race. Retief, junior and sharp-eyed, must work the mission in harmony while the Yill smile and sip lavender drinks. Laumer builds the tale on manners as warfare. It is a sly, funny story of diplomacy where etiquette itself is the trap.
21836-the-tale-of-jasper-jay:
Jasper Jay, the noisiest rogue in Pleasant Valley, stars in this 1917 children's tale by Arthur Scott Bailey. Some birds called old Mr. Crow the loudest in the neighborhood, but they had forgotten his knavish cousin. Jasper's shrieks ring over Farmer Green's pines on the coldest mornings, for he winters right there. He is bold and handsome in his bright blue suit, and a rogue for all that.

Chapters follow his jokes, boasts, and narrow escapes: scaring the hens, hiding from Solomon Owl, and joining the singing society. Bailey's Tuck-Me-In Tales teach nature through animal mischief. Jasper has to be got rid of more than once, and never quite is. Small readers learn the blue jay by laughing at him.
21846-crowded-out-o-crofield-or-the-boy-:
Jack Ogden, a blacksmith's boy in the village of Crofield, is crowded out into the wide world in this boys' novel by William O. Stoddard. Stoddard insists the tale is close to history: a real energetic boy was pushed from his village into a surprising career. Jack stands fifteen, sandy-haired and freckled, in the wide door of the smithy, looking toward the rickety bridge.

His road runs down the Hudson by steamboat, past the state-house, into the city and a new world. Chapters bring a runaway, a burglary charge, hunger, and work at all trades before complete success. Mary, the girl of the tale, sails her own course in the Eagle. It is a cheerful American success story of the old school.
22141-joy-in-service-forgetting-and-pres:
Joy in Service, issued by the American Tract Society in 1900, is a devotional book about the Christian life. Its full title runs Forgetting and Pressing Onward Until the Day Dawn. The writer argues that knowing Christ in history is not enough. A believer may admire Christ's power and adore him as Saviour, yet still long for a closer, personal acquaintance with him.

The chapters press readers toward active service done with joy. Forgetting what lies behind, they are to strain forward like Paul. Tract Society books were cheap, earnest, and everywhere in Protestant America. This one survives as a fair sample of the devotional reading that shaped ordinary churchgoers in 1900.
22267-a-woman-for-mayor-a-novel-of-to-da:
Helen M. Winslow, once editor of The Club Woman, wrote A Woman for Mayor as a novel of to-day in 1909. Her city, the talk runs, is going to the dogs. Municipal affairs were never so muddled, everybody agrees. Barnaby Burke is running for mayor with a ravenous pack of demagogues behind him, and honest citizens despair of the result.

Against Burke the reformers set a woman candidate. Winslow, who knew clubwomen and suffrage circles from inside, builds her plot on ward politics, newspapers, and drawing-room pressure. The question is whether a woman can clean a city hall. The novel is a suffrage argument wearing a story's clothes, lively and pointed.
22271-schwartz-a-history-from-schwartz-b:
Schwartz: A History is the title novel of David Christie Murray's linked volume Schwartz. Its narrator opens with a startling sentence: he was expatriated by a man with an axe. The man and the axe alike were visionary and unreal, he admits. Yet it took a strong effort of will to hold them at arm's length. Work on hand, and a mind broken down by overwork, explain the vision.

Murray builds the history out of that haunted start. Business, exile, and a disordered conscience drive Schwartz's story. The linked tales that follow share his world of Castle Barfield and London counting-houses. This opening piece shows Murray blending the ghostly with the commercial.
22273-bulldog-and-butterfly-from-schwart:
Bulldog and Butterfly, from David Christie Murray's Schwartz, opens with a map in words. Castle Barfield, Heydon Hey, and Beacon Hargate form three points of a triangle. Barfield has pretensions; Heydon Hey is a village; Beacon Hargate is no more than a hamlet. The house at the story's centre is crossed by great beams of black-painted oak, with diamond-paned windows sunk low in the walls.

Roses and honeysuckle cover the porch in summer, and the garden runs up to the house all round. Murray sets his contrast of bulldog and butterfly in this old place. Character against character, as the title promises, drives the slight tale. The Schwartz stories share this countryside.
22417-the-etiquette-of-to-day:
The Etiquette of To-Day, revised and enlarged in 1918, teaches the manners of its moment. It opens by naming the secret of success in society. That secret, it says, is heartiness and sympathy in company.

A man unhappy in company finds no fitting word ready. All his information sounds a little impertinent to others. A happy man finds lucky occasions at every turn. He introduces what he has to say with ease. The book builds its rules on that warm foundation. Calls, letters, dress, and table conduct follow in order. Readers get Edwardian-era social rules, useful now as a mirror of their world.
22720-the-minister-of-evil-the-secret-hi:
The Minister of Evil, subtitled The Secret History of Rasputin's Betrayal of Russia, is a 1917 insider's account of the fall of the Russian monarchy. The catalog record names no author. Its writer claims no literary renown and no pretence to fine phrases or elegant diplomacy.

The object, the author states plainly, is simply to set down the truth about Russia's crumbling and the fall of its throne. Rasputin, the Siberian holy man whose influence over the tsarina scandalized Russia, stands at the center as the minister of evil. Such books poured out in revolution's first year, mixing memoir, accusation, and grief. This one preserves the voice of a loyalist watching an empire dissolve.
2274-how-to-live-on-24-hours-a-day:
Arnold Bennett's brisk little book argues that the working day leaves everyone a hidden fortune: the hours before and after office work. How to Live on 24 Hours a Day urges clerks and office workers to claim ninety minutes each evening for reading, music, and self-improvement. That time should not slip away in tired routine. Bennett writes with cheerful bluntness.

His advice is practical rather than mystical: rise a little earlier, guard one evening, and treat the mind as a garden needing daily care. The book's fame comes from its plain arithmetic of time. Modern readers still find its message bracing and easy to try.
22758-the-new-england-magazine-volume-1-:
The New England Magazine presents its second number, volume 1, number 2, dated February 1886. The catalog record names no editor. A new regional magazine had to prove itself monthly, and this issue again mixes college history, essays, and literature for New England readers.

The sample article traces the founding impulse of Tufts College to a single sermon. Hosea Ballou the younger preached it before the General Convention of Universalists. The place was New York, in September 1847. From a sermon to a college is the kind of story the magazine loved: faith, education, and regional ambition in one thread. Poetry and fiction fill out the number. Together with its first issue, it shows the Bay State Monthly settling into the long career ahead of it.
22913-winning-his-way:
Charles Carleton Coffin's Winning His Way follows travelers into a beautiful valley. After weeks on dusty roads they reach a winding river, fair sunny hills, and groves of oak, maple, and linden. The air smells of honeysuckle and jasmine, and deer browse the tender grass on the slopes.

Coffin wrote history and adventure for boys, and this tale mixes settlement, striving, and scenery. A young hero makes his path in a new country, learning work and character along the way. The valley scene shows Coffin's method, rewarding effort with a rich land honestly described. His books taught generations of readers their American past. This one keeps the same earnest, outdoors spirit.
23024-grimm-tales-made-gay:
Guy Wetmore Carryl retells the Grimms in verse in Grimm Tales Made Gay. One tale turns on a will. Four-year-old Paul stands to take half the gold, while Beatrix, six, inherits the remainder. Uncle Ben responds with an act everyone calls splendid.

Carryl's trick is to keep the fairy-tale skeleton and swap the moral for a wink. His rhymes bounce, his endings swerve, and his morals arrive upside down on purpose. The book belonged to a brief vogue for comic retellings around 1900. Children can follow the stories, adults catch the jokes aimed over their heads. It remains a neat sample of light verse at its most professional.
23086-auction-of-to-day:
Milton C. Work calls the bids in Auction of To-Day, his 1913 guide to auction bridge. Work starts from a simple position, one spade opened and second hand passing. Case follows case from there. Dealer strength, raises to two and three spades, and minor-suit openings each get their treatment.

Work was America's bridge authority, and this book taught a generation how to bid the new auction game. Hands, conventions, and probabilities fill its pages in place of plot. Card historians prize such manuals, since they fix the exact moment when contract bridge was still unborn and auction ruled the clubs. Casual readers will find a vanished social world, conducted in spades.
23207-americans-all-stories-of-american-:
Americans All, from 1910, presents stories of American life of its own day. Its pages open by praising school days as days rich in experience. The first day at school, whether a little red schoolhouse or a big brick building holding a thousand pupils, is called the start of a new life.

As a model of school fiction, the book points to Emmy Lou, by George Madden Martin. That story follows a winsome girl from first grade through the end of high school. Readers get period stories and sketches that treat ordinary American childhood, school, and home life as worthy subjects.
23387-washed-ashore-or-the-tower-of-stor:
W. H. G. Kingston set this tale at Stormount Tower on the south coast of England, home to Jack, a young man of a good family. Foolishly tangled with smugglers who are caught, Jack faces a hanging charge, so he slips to sea aboard the Truelove, later reported lost.

At home, strange doings follow: ghostly noises, secret tunnels, smugglers' caves, and a kidnapping, while kin long to see Jack again. At last some local young men sail to the Pacific to trace the Truelove, and after misses and clues they find Jack and bring him home. Kingston keeps the mystery brisk and the sea scenes fresh, making this a fine adventure for younger teens.
23592-breakaway:
Stanley Gimble wrote this science fiction tale, first printed in Astounding Science Fiction in December nineteen fifty five. It is about Phil Conover, a test pilot in a flight suit, and his wife at home. Phil zips his suit, smiles with an alive, excited look, and asks how he looks in his monkey suit. His wife, stiff on a flowered couch not yet fully theirs, crushes a cigarette burned too far.

She says he looks fine, just right, and manages a smile, but the scene holds a wish and its price. She surely got her wish, the cover line warns, yet getting what she wanted proves another matter. Gimble writes the marriage with quiet tension, as a flight that means glory for one means dread for the other. Readers who like domestic science fiction will enjoy the tale's short, sharp look at ambition, love, and breakaway.
23603-the-music-master-novelized-from-th:
Charles Klein novelized his play The Music Master as produced by David Belasco, printed by Grosset and Dunlap in nineteen hundred nine, with scenes from the William Fox photoplay. A frontispiece shows the music master crying that his little girl had just such a doll, a clue to the tale's heart.

Anton Von Barwig, the music master, can no longer pay rent for his piano and must pawn his favourite violin. Beverly brings Helene a wedding gift, and Anton learns his newly found daughter is to be married. Helene's trousseau, a doll, and a father's long lost love drive the plot toward reunion. Klein writes the stage tale with sentiment and warmth, for readers who love theatre romance and a father's second chance.
24054-dead-giveaway:
Randall Garrett's Dead Giveaway appeared in Astounding Science Fiction in August 1959. Its motto states the method: by logic alone, one can work out the necessary reason for a highly advanced dead city on a wholly useless planet. A shipping transfer point, plainly, and necessarily so.

The story opens with Turnbull, in a blue-and-green tartan jacket, asking a clerk about Mendez. Scholar Duckworth's destination on file, six months old, is the Hotel Byron, Landing City, Mendez. The fare is seven hundred and eighty-five fifty, by regular shuttle to Luna, then by Stellar Queen or Oriona toward Sirius Six. Garrett's tale is a detective story in space, where logic itself is the giveaway.
24359-the-return-of-peter-grimm-novelise:
David Belasco's play became this novel, with pictures by John Rae, published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York, copyrighted in 1912 by Dodd, Mead and Company. Its chapters run from a man and a maid and the heir through Peter Grimm has a plan and a warning and a theory. A queer compact leads to breaking the news, the hand relaxes, and afterward.

Later chapters bring the eve of a wedding, a wasted plea, the legacies, mostly concerning gratitude, and the return. Then come I can't get it across, a half-heard message, the sensitive, Mr. Batholommey testifies, and Dr. McPherson's statement. Back to the story, the benefit of the doubt, only one thing really counts, all that happens happens again, the dawning, and the good-bye close the book. Readers get a stage ghost story in novel form.
24676-peeps-at-many-lands-norway:
Lieutenant-Colonel A. F. Mockler-Ferryman wrote this children's geography of Norway, published at London in 1911 with twelve full-page colour pictures by A. Heaton Cooper and Nico Jungman. It belongs to the Peeps at Many Lands series, which showed young readers the world country by country.

Chapters cover the land of the Vikings, modern Norway, people and industries, farms, manners, schools, fairy tales, and the Hardanger Fjord. Later chapters visit the fjelds, wild beasts and birds, waterfalls, snowfields, glaciers, Arctic days, Laplanders, and winter in Christiania. Young readers get a bright, friendly Norway.
24699-some-personal-recollections-of-dr-:
James Bayard Clark wrote these personal recollections of Dr. Janeway, published at New York and London in 1917 by G. P. Putnam's Sons. Edward Gamaliel Janeway was born at New Brunswick, New Jersey, on 31 August 1841, graduated from Rutgers College in 1860, and took his medical degree in New York in 1864.

Later honours included law degrees from Rutgers in 1898 and Columbia in 1904. Clark, who knew Janeway, recalls a great physician and teacher, his work, character, and kindness. The memoir is short and affectionate. Readers interested in American medicine will find it a warm portrait of a doctor of the old school.
25136-the-pomp-of-yesterday:
Joseph Hocking's Pomp of Yesterday, published by Hodder and Stoughton, is a First World War novel about memory, class, and quiet heroism. Its epigraph from Kipling warns that navies melt away and yesterday's pomp passes like Nineveh and Tyre, unless the living remember.

Chapters introduce a man without a past, Sir Roger Granville, George St. Mabyn, and Captain Springfield, and follow a private soldier whose rescue of an officer and capture of thirty prisoners shames a squire's prejudice. Hocking, a popular wartime novelist, writes with moral earnestness about faith, duty, and the debts owed to ordinary men.
25456-princess-polly-at-play:
Amy Brooks sends Princess Polly and Rose Atherton to Cliffmore for a summer at the shore. Polly and Rose love the salt air, though Avondale offers fine lawns and flowers at home. Chapters follow Polly, Rose, and Gwen through sea nymph games, a wedding at Cliffmore, and a call from Aunt Rose. Max, the mischievous boy of the party, turns stowaway and causes trouble wherever he goes.

A donkey ride ends in a spill on the sand, with Max turning a somersault and landing unhurt. Gwen, her temper ruffled, declares Max a little horrider than everyone else, though he did his best to stop the donkey. A. L. Burt published the book in New York in 1915, as one of Brooks' Princess Polly stories.
25659-a-week-of-instruction-and-amusemen:
Mrs. Harley's birthday present to her daughter gives this 1812 London book its frame, printed for J. Harris at St. Paul's Churchyard. A week of instruction and amusement mixes short stories with outlines of sacred and profane history, geography, and other subjects.

An advertisement explains the design: to share, in a manner agreeable to children, knowledge of subjects they often find tedious. If stories inspire a love of virtue, and lessons wake a desire for further useful knowledge, the attempt will count as success despite defects. Instruction and delight share each day.
25781-the-ghost-breaker-a-novel-based-up:
Charles Goddard and Paul Dickey write The Ghost Breaker, a novel based upon their play. Hearst's International Library published it in New York in 1915. Warren, told not to call Maria highness, fronts the book in a picture, insisting her name is Maria.

Chapters open with Jarvis of Kentucky, the blind pursuit, and the royal suite. An oath of allegiance follows, with exit Jarvis laughing. Over the sea and far away comes next, with romance of the castle and a new profession. Checkmate, a wager with the duke, and welcome to Seguro follow, as a Kentucky man breaks ghosts in a Spanish castle.
25837-the-madness-of-may:
Meredith Nicholson sets a spring mystery in Westchester County, where Billy Deering slips into his father's house near Radford Hills. A missing girl, a moonlit jest, and a studio full of clown, harlequin, and columbine sketches soon pull Billy and his friend Hood into a hunt. Proofs on the table and a half hid name in the corner, Mary B. Taylor, point to a popular illustrator with secrets.

Printed in 1917 with pictures by Frederic Dorr Steele, the novel mixes wit, romance, and mild peril. Hood feeds any comer, mocks despair with a cry of hands up, and pores over pen and ink work while Billy wonders if the painter may be Babette. May madness, the book hints, is love and folly let loose in fine weather, and the pair chase it to a bright end.
25920-the-mission-of-janice-day:
Helen Beecher Long sends Janice Day on her fourth Do Something mission in this 1917 book. Chapters open with trouble for Uncle Jason and for everybody, then Marty speaks out, Janice goes her way, and a shadow of coming events falls on Polktown. Lottie seeks a friend, Mrs. Scattergood talks, and two explosions shake the town before the mission finds its end.

A frontispiece shows Janice facing the charger ridden by a bandit chief, a bold image for a girls' book. Uncle Jason's tales add humor, as when Cale Hotchkiss, told to rhyme before Miss Blodgett strikes his hand, sings that he will dodge her blow. Marty runs into trouble, Nelson fails to grasp Janice's aim, and the black eyed woman stirs a shock. Through it all Janice acts, and action is the book's creed.
26341-on-the-structure-of-greek-tribal-s:
Hugh E. Seebohm's 1895 essay, issued by Macmillan in London and New York, rebuilds Greek tribal society from comparative clues. Its pages quote the Egyptian Book of the Dead, where the dead claim fields, corn, beer, and meat in the afterlife. Hindu rites add cake offerings to ancestors, binding kin within fixed degrees. Offerings to the manes mark who owes duty to whom.

Hair cutting as dedication offers another clue, from Achilles vowing his hair to the river Spercheios to Alexander ordering his Macedonians to shave their beards. Seebohm uses such customs to trace how Greek kin groups formed, held land, and honoured their dead. The essay is dense, learned, and comparative, built for readers of ancient social history.
26425-microcosmography-or-a-piece-of-the:
John Earle's Microcosmography, a classic of seventeenth-century character writing, appears here in a reprint of Dr. Bliss's 1811 edition, with a preface and appendix by S. T. Irwin. Earle, later Bishop of Salisbury, sketches the types of his age in short, sharp essays, each catching a figure in a few telling habits. The Bristol reprint honors the Reverend David Wright, the grave divine of its pages.

The drunkard shows Earle's method at its best. The drunkard, sighted yet unseeing and legged yet lame, drinks until his body and then the room fill, until tobacco alone airs him after a washing. Such portraits mix wit with moral judgment, and they still read as a lively gallery of Jacobean England, from courtiers to serving men.
26637-the-mystery-of-the-green-ray:
William Le Queux published this mystery with Hodder and Stoughton in a second edition in 1915. It opens on Bank Holiday, August 3, 1914, on a river annual from Richmond, where four friends in two punts hear from passing craft that war with Germany seems inevitable. Dennis Burnham, Jack Curtis, Tommy Evans, and the narrator debate what they themselves must do.

From still waters and a man going north, the tale turns to Myra, a black blow, a chemist's rock, and the mystery of Sholto. A red-haired man, a further enigma, and grave fears pile up before the truth is revealed. Le Queux wraps a wartime river holiday in a puzzle of identities, secrets, and a green ray whose meaning unfolds chapter by chapter.
26709-lord-teach-us-to-pray:
The Reverend Andrew Murray published this devotional book at Philadelphia with Henry Altemus in 1896, subtitled The Only Teacher. Murray begins with the disciples who had seen Christ pray and understood the connection between his wondrous public life and his secret life of prayer. They came with the request, Lord, teach us to pray, believing none could pray like him and none could teach like him.

Murray invites readers to enroll anew in the school Christ always keeps open for the divine art of prayer and intercession. Prayer, he says, is simple enough for a feeble child, yet the highest and holiest work of man, communion with the unseen, most holy One, and the channel of all blessings. Later sections treat worship in spirit and truth and the true worshippers, asking whether Samaria or Jerusalem is the true place, and answering that God is spirit.
26740-the-picture-of-dorian-gray:
Oscar Wilde published this novel in complete book form in 1891 with Ward, Lock and Company. This edition comes from Simpkin, Marshall, Hamilton, Kent and Company at London. It was first printed in April 1913 and reprinted through January 1916. Wilde's preface declares that there is no moral or immoral book, only books well written or badly written, and that all art is quite useless.

The preface also says the artist reveals art and conceals the artist, vice and virtue are materials for art, and art is surface and symbol at once. Chapter One opens in a studio filled with roses, lilac, and pink-flowering thorn. There Lord Henry Wotton lies on a divan of Persian saddlebags, smoking innumerable cigarettes. Dorian Gray later tells Basil Hallward he has taken his love out of poetry and found his wife in Shakespeare's plays, kissing Juliet on the mouth.
27051-the-trail-to-yesterday:
Charles Alden Seltzer's 1913 western The Trail to Yesterday opens with a woman on the trail and follows converging trails toward old scores and new trouble. Dakota evens a score, Sheila fans a flame, and Duncan adds two and two as the story moves through bogged-down wagons and river trails.

Later chapters bring a shot in the back, Langford laying off his mask, and Sheriff Allen taking a hand, before partings on the river trail and a road into the unknown. Seltzer writes a full-blooded range romance of memory, revenge, and second chances.
27285-the-foot-path-way:
Bradford Torrey's The Foot-Path Way, second edition of 1893 from Houghton, Mifflin, takes its motto from The Winter's Tale: jog on the foot-path way, and merrily hent the stile. Torrey, author of Birds in the Bush and A Rambler's Lease, walks New England on foot.

Chapters run from June in Franconia and December out-of-doors to Dyer's Hollow, five days on Mount Mansfield, a widow and twins, and the male ruby-throat. On the heights he visits a botanical resort between Mansfield and Sterling. Then he returns to robin music, chimney swifts, and the white-throat's whistle in the valley.
27392-lease-to-doomsday:
Lee Archer wrote this short science-fiction tale about a job advertisement that makes no sense at all. Kevin Muldoon, reading the New York Times over breakfast coffee in a cafeteria, finds a notice seeking a live wire real estate broker. The notice asks for no selling, and gives room 657 of the Silvers Building on a Monday morning.

Muldoon tells himself the notice is an obvious come-on, yet he walks crosstown toward the Silvers Building instead of to his own office. Behind the strange notice stand twins with a rare team of their own: they want a printing plant on a garbage dump, because, as they say, they live there. The tale turns a dull morning into a puzzle about what the twins really want.
27442-belgium-from-the-roman-invasion-to:
Emile Cammaerts wrote this history of Belgium from the Roman invasion to the present day, published by T. Fisher Unwin in London in 1921, with thirty-six illustrations and nine maps. King Albert I fronts the volume, a fitting figure for a history written just after the Great War.

The first chapter, The Coal Wood, treats Celts and Germans, the Roman conquest, roads of Roman civilization, first Christianization, Germanic invasion, and the natural obstacle of the Silva Carbonaria, the great forest. Cammaerts traces how a border country became a nation. Readers seeking a compact history of Belgium will find a clear, well-mapped guide.
2751-man-in-the-iron-mask-an-essay:
For nearly a hundred years the masked prisoner puzzled France, and this Dumas essay from Celebrated Crimes takes up the mystery. For nearly one hundred years, he notes, the masked prisoner's identity has puzzled France and tempted theorists.

Candidates parade past, twin brother, disgraced minister, royal bastard, and others, each tested against scant records. The essay is a piece of historical detective work, written with curiosity and flair. Readers get both a mystery and a lesson in how legends grow around a locked door. Dumas leaves the reader to judge which candidate fits best.
27620-mrs-hungerford-notable-women-autho:
Helen C. Black's profile of Mrs. Hungerford, from Notable Women Authors of the Day, was published by Maclaren and Company in London in 1906, with portraits. Hungerford, the well-known author of Molly Bawn, invited Black to her lovely house, St. Brenda's, at Bandon, in County Cork.

Black says it is well worth braving the perils of the sea, even in midwinter against a north-east wind, for the comfort of the journey from England to the Emerald Isle. Circumstances limit her visit to four days, not the month's holiday offered, but the Irish Mail makes it easy. She arrives at Euston in time for the 7.15 express, with a compartment reserved and an excellent meal arranged. The piece opens a visit to a popular Irish novelist.
27727-within-the-golden-gate-a-souvenir-:
Laura Young Pinney wrote this short 1893 souvenir of San Francisco Bay in verse, illustrated by Ella N. Pierce and printed in San Francisco. The poem follows a sailing party through the Golden Gate on a fair autumn morning.

Verses pause at Alcatraz, where a singer laments a lover lost at sea, and at Mount Tamalpais, where a brook is born on the slopes and runs singing to the valley. With half-tone engravings, the little book is a keepsake of the bay in the 1890s, lyrical rather than documentary. The poem also follows a brook born on Tamalpais slopes as it grows stronger on its winding way to the valley.
27951-policeman-bluejay:
Laura Bancroft, author of the Twinkle Tales, wrote Policeman Bluejay, illustrated by Maginel Wright Enright and published in Chicago by Reilly and Britton in 1907. Bancroft says the success of the Twinkle Tales encouraged her to write a new Twinkle Book about birds, a subject children especially loved.

The tale is fantastical and meant to amuse rather than instruct, though many bird traits follow natural history. Bancroft insists that in a fairy tale it makes no difference whether the two young friends were asleep or awake, and readers should accept the wonder as they would a fragrant breeze.
28365-rural-problems-of-today:
Ernest R. Groves's Rural Problems of Today, published in 1918, studies American country life through the work of the rural worker: the teacher, minister, and social helper who served farm families. Groves begins with the country home, contrasting homes that neglect children with homes that overprotect them.

Further chapters cover the family, country schools, the country church, mental hygiene in rural districts, the mind of the farmer, and the psychic causes of migration to towns. A final chapter weighs the effect of the World War on rural life. The book offers a plain, humane survey of problems that shaped farming communities a century ago.
28670-arizona-s-yesterday:
John H. Cady tells his life story in this 1916 memoir of Arizona's frontier days, rewritten and revised by Basil Dillon Woon. Cady came west as a boy soldier before the Civil War, followed the gold seekers, drove stages, ran frontier businesses, and served as deputy sheriff, cattleman, and farmer. His chapters cover rough travel by land and sea, a trip through Mexico, and years of Indian warfare on the Arizona border.

The book is dedicated to the pioneers still living and to the memory of those dead, and its tone is one of tribute to hard endurance. Cady writes as a man looking back at a territory becoming a state, and his plain account gives readers a firsthand view of forts, ranches, and mining camps. It remains a useful source for the history of the American Southwest.
29138-the-doorway:
Evelyn E. Smith wrote this short fantasy about a wish that turns ugly. A man may idly wish he had married his first love, the story warns, but an idle wish can go wrong in unknown dimensions. Professor Falabella explains his theory over cookies: no one ever really makes a decision, he says, because the self splits and carries on across two or more diverging planes.

Smith's tale, praised in its magazine introduction for a magic akin to Poe's manner, follows that split into dark, tapestried rooms. The doorway of the title leads between lives that might have been. Readers get a brief, eerie fantasy about regret, choice, and the other selves we leave behind when we choose.
2916-the-foundations-an-extravagant-play:
John Galsworthy called The Foundations an extravagant play, setting its action continuously between eight and half past ten on a summer evening some years after the Great War. Lord William Dromondy, member of Parliament, keeps a Park Lane mansion whose cellar opens the play, while old Mrs. Lemmy's room in Bethnal Green gives the other pole. Anti-sweaters, sweated workers, a duke, and a crowd fill the cast.

The play contrasts rich and poor London directly, as little Aida runs in singing and chattering about a coffin followed to Hyde Park, better than a horse-drawn hearse. Galsworthy uses farce and satire to press a serious point about sweated labor. The Foundations shows his most experimental stage manner, broad in comedy and pointed in its social aim.
29220-monday-or-tuesday:
Virginia Woolf published this collection of short pieces in New York in 1921, with Harcourt, Brace and Company. The contents run from A Haunted House and A Society through the title piece, An Unwritten Novel, and The String Quartet. Later pieces include Blue and Green, Kew Gardens, and The Mark on the Wall.
