A Haunted House opens with a ghostly couple moving from room to room, hand in hand, looking for something left behind. Woolf's method is impression and image rather than straight plot: a mark on a wall, a garden, or a quartet becomes an occasion for thought. Readers get Woolf's early experimental prose, brief and luminous, showing the style that would shape her novels.
29391-blue-grass-and-broadway:
Maria Thompson Daviess published this novel in New York in 1919 with the Century Company, after serial publication in 1918. Daviess wrote The Melting of Molly and The Tinder Box. She opens with a paradox. Needing much money fast drives many noble ambitions. In the branches of those ambitions roost strange companies of birds, pecking for dollars.

In just such a quest, Miss Patricia Adair of Adairville, Kentucky, sets out, and the novel follows her between Bluegrass Kentucky and Broadway. Godfrey Vandeford appears in the opening chapter's cast. Readers get a popular American novel of money, ambition, and a Kentucky heroine seeking her fortune in the wider world.
29897-runaway:
William Morrison wrote this tale of a schoolboy hero, with pictures by Ashman. Its epigraph says heroism is merely daring and ingenuity at the age of ten, and experience can come later. Plato, the boy hero, leaps to his feet when the dorm master calls, sliding a book under his pillow and seizing a textbook at random. He claims he was so absorbed in study that he missed the assembly bell.

The dorm master, frowning from the doorway, tells Plato to live up to his name and show some intelligence. Plato winces at his miserable name, which has dogged him since before he knew the first Plato was a philosopher. The book under his pillow holds a space tale of Rogue Rogan, a rocketing spaceship, and a day of retribution long feared. Morrison joins school life and space peril in one brisk tale.
30019-navy-day:
Harry Harrison wrote Navy Day, with pictures by Kelly Freas. Its headnote gives the Army a new theme song: anything you can do, we can do better, and they meant anything, including up-to-date hornpipes. General Wingrove looks at rows of faces without seeing them. Beyond the Congress of the United States and past a balmy June day, his vision reaches another day that is coming, when the Army will hold its destined place of authority.

He draws a deep breath and gives what may be the briefest speech ever made in Congress's hallowed halls. The General Staff of the United States Army asks Congress to do away with the Navy, called an archaic branch of the armed forces. Admiral Fitzjames climbs slowly to his feet, every line of his body denoting outraged dignity.
30357-select-poems-of-thomas-gray:
William J. Rolfe edits select poems of Thomas Gray, with notes and engravings, published by Harper and Brothers in New York in 1883, under an 1876 entry. Rolfe, head master of the high school at Cambridge, Massachusetts, argues in his preface that many editions of Gray in the last fifty years were none of them critically exact. Neither text nor notes passed his test. Some were elegant, and some showed considerable editorial labor. Since Mathias in 1814, he says, no editor had printed the Elegy's second line as Gray wrote it.

Gray's collected poems, he notes, reach their most accurate form in the editio princeps of 1768, printed under Gray's own supervision. The first edition of the Pindaric odes, The Progress of Poesy and The Bard, from Strawberry-Hill in 1757, was printed with care. Rolfe collated his text line by line with these early editions, adopting no later reading.
30361-the-stowaway:
Alvin Heiner's stowaway reaches the Moon by sneaking aboard, chasing glory yet meeting a destiny far unlike the one he imagined. Joe Spain, eyes feverish and voice holding intensity, tells a lunch group in the shade of Building B that he has got to get on that ship. He is going to make it. His mates answer with amusement, contempt, and curiosity, calling him plain nuts and asking what the Moon has that they have not got right here.

Joe stands to harangue the workers: he is a little guy, a working stiff, part of the great inarticulate masses. Laughter answers his big words, with a demand to talk English. Joe points to Building A across the desert, a building that needs two passes and a permit. Glory, for a little guy, starts with getting past that gate.
30680-all-day-wednesday:
Richard Olin writes All Day Wednesday, a science fiction story from Analog, March 1963, illustrated by George Schelling, opening with a claim that practically everybody would agree this is Utopia. Ernie turns the dial on his television at night, alone in his room, sipping a can of beer as the set brightens from dark to blue.

Jory looks out at him, tired and looking bad, and says hello, Ernie. Ernie turns to the next station and hears the same greeting, then the next, then the next, until five stations all show Jory saying hello. Olin turns a quiet evening of channel surfing into an eerie puzzle about sameness, media, and a world that calls itself perfect.
31011-the-tadpoles-of-bufo-cognatus-say:
Hobart M. Smith wrote this short paper on the tadpoles of Bufo cognatus, Say. It was published in the University of Kansas Publications, Museum of Natural History, volume 1, number 3, pages 93 to 96, with one figure, on August 15, 1946. The tadpoles had been described by Bragg in 1936 and 1937. Smith finds that Bragg's drawings and descriptions of the mouthparts, taken from dried, immature, or transforming individuals, do not agree among themselves.

They also clash with larvae later collected and still kept at the University of Kansas natural history museum. Smith had at hand two series, one collected July 2, 1938, a mile and a half east of Meade County State Park in Kansas. A second lot held many sizes from 14 to 31 millimeters, with several transforming specimens showing the pattern typical of the species. It is a correction to the earlier tadpole descriptions.
31027-walt-whitman-yesterday-today:
Henry Eduard Legler's 1916 study looks back at Walt Whitman from the vantage point of sixty years after Leaves of Grass first appeared. That thin 1855 volume held only twelve poems and carried no author's name on its title page. It startled the literary world with its free form and frank language, drawing a storm of abuse from reviewers.

Legler follows Whitman from that hostile debut toward later recognition, weighing the poems against the scorn they first met and the praise that slowly followed. Printed in a limited run of six hundred copies, the book offers a compact early portrait of America's most unruly poet and of how a nation's taste caught up with him.
31177-ritual-conformity-interpretations-:
Published by Parker and Company in Oxford and London in 1881, Ritual Conformity records the work of a conference held at All Saints, Margaret Street, in 1880 and 1881. Forty-eight meetings brought together clergy and students of ritual. They agreed that needless diversity in church practice was a real and growing evil among those upholding Catholic doctrine in the Church of England.

Their answer was a body of comments on the rubrics of the Book of Common Prayer, with cautions against practices that broke the law and usage of the church. The volume thus offers a practical program for Anglo-Catholic uniformity, and it remains a primary source for the ritual controversies that stirred Victorian Anglicanism.
31257-dainty-s-cruel-rivals-or-the-fatal:
Mrs. Alex. McVeigh Miller's dime novel, copyrighted in 1898 and published by the Arthur Westbrook Company of Cleveland as Hart Series number 88, follows Dainty through forty chapters of romance and calamity. It opens with Olive Peyton and her cousin Ela Craye rejoicing over an invitation. Dainty herself appears as a sweet girl graduate, the prettiest girl in the room, on the happiest day she had ever known.

Later chapters bring an old monk, a dream, love's rosy dawn, the trail of the serpent, the Ellsworth honor, grim fates, and a maddened lover. They go on to a ghost alarm, the night before the wedding, a madman's deed, unmasking, the darkest hour, and a new home. Melodramatic and breathless, the book is a classic of the cheap sensation fiction its readers loved.
31622-optimism-an-essay:
Helen Keller's essay Optimism was published at New York by T. Y. Crowell and Company in November 1903, printed by D. B. Updike at the Merrymount Press in Boston, and dedicated to her teacher. Its three parts are Optimism Within, Optimism Without, and the Practice of Optimism. Keller writes from a life lived without sight or hearing, and she argues that optimism is a matter of will and habit, not of circumstance.

The essay moves from inward cheer to outward conduct, and it closes with practice, the daily work of holding a hopeful temper. Keller's optimism is not easy comfort, but a discipline she defends with the authority of her own experience.
3178-the-gilded-age-a-tale-of-today:
Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner wrote this 1873 novel together, and it gave an age its name. Squire Hawkins and his Tennessee land open the story, as he decides to remove to Missouri. He meets and adopts the boy Clay, survives a steamboat explosion, and takes in the little girl Laura. Colonel Beriah Sellers, dreamer of fortunes, joins the family circle.

Trouble and darkness follow, with a proposed sale of the Tennessee land hanging over all. The novel satirizes speculation, railroads, and Washington jobbery, where everything glitters and little is gold. Gilded, not golden, became the verdict on the era. The book remains the classic portrait of American greed dressed up as progress.
31836-better-than-play:
Mabel Quiller-Couch's Better Than Play, published in London by the Religious Tract Society, opens on washing day at the Henders' cottage, where all is misery, bad temper, and steam. The air smells of soap-suds. The children hate washing day: Aunt Emma is always cross, they may not stay indoors, they must make no noise, and they may not wander away to play.

Chapters follow washing-day tempers, a little herb-bed, sage bushes and rose bushes, Aunt Maggie's suggestion, first customers, and a step forward to success. Readers get a wholesome children's story of work turned to enterprise, in which helping at home proves, as the title says, better than play.
31962-the-ethical-way:
Joseph Farrell's short story The Ethical Way was printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in March 1958. It opens with Jarth Rolan asking anxiously whether it is time, while pilot Lan Barda pushes him gently back into a seat. Their vehicle hovers at the permitted limit in Earth's upper air, waiting for a signal.

The people below have almost reached the critical point, and Jarth worries about going down into a radioactive atmosphere and whether any of them will live. Readers get a science-fiction story about observers bound by an ethical rule, watching a world on the edge of a decision they may not make for it.
31993-round-the-yule-log-christmas-in-no:
P. Chr. Asbjörnsen's Christmas book, translated by H. L. Broekstad and published in Boston with an 1895 copyright, frames Norwegian folk tales as stories told beside the fire at Christmas. Its narrator is a lieutenant spending a gloomy December in Christiania. He joins a household where children, their aunts, and old Mother Skau gather before the stove, asking for tales.

The tales he tells give the book its core. They include Buttercup and the dog Goldentooth. They also tell of brownies at Vager and Bure who steal hay from each other, and of the brownie at Hesselberg who teases a house dog. Another tale follows Peter Gynt facing trolls that invade a farm each Christmas Eve. Alongside the stories, the frame scenes show Norwegian Christmas customs, from porridge left for the brownie in the hay loft to talk by firelight.
32312-janice-day:
Helen Beecher Long's girls' novel, copyrighted in 1914, introduces Janice Day, a new-fashioned girl who comes to the small town of Poketown. She meets 'Rill Scattergood and her school, walks the road with Walky Dexter, and faces a time of trial involving Nelson Haley. Chapters follow tea and talks with her father, a rainy day, an afternoon of adventure, and a little girl who lost the echo.

Later the story turns to Christmas news, a fly-by-night visitor, a sugar camp, and the dedication of a new school. Janice grows through work, friendship, and fresh starts across two winters in Poketown. Long writes with warmth about country manners, school life, and a girl learning to stand on her own feet while winning over a wary town.
32371-the-bonadventure-a-random-journal-:
Edmund Blunden's journal, published in London in 1922, records a random Atlantic holiday taken for health. In the autumn of 1921 Blunden found himself in bad health, and the editors he worked for suggested a sea voyage. Though he could usually afford only modest ships, his editors' generosity and that of the shipowners sent him, to his friends' envy, bound for the River Plate.

Blunden calls the book a round trip, dedicated to H. W. M., and fills it with sea, ports, fellow passengers, and the slow change from illness to recovery. An epigraph from Isaac Watts on ships, sea monsters, and Leviathan sets the tone. The journal suits readers who enjoy travel writing, poetry, and a writer's plain account of rest at sea.
32433-how-to-see-a-play:
Richard Burton's guide, published in New York in 1914, teaches readers how to watch a play with understanding. Burton opens by calling the play a form of story telling, alongside the short story, the novel, the epic, and the ballad. Each form, he argues, tries to give human happenings unity and growth toward a definite end, through a clear connection of characters and events.

Eleven chapters carry the reader from story structure to acting, staging, and criticism, with notes for further study. Burton quotes Farquhar's remark that every critic likes a play because he likes it, warning readers against taste alone as a test. The book suits students, playgoers, and amateur actors who want to see more in a performance than plot alone.
3244-to-him-that-hath-a-tale-of-the-west:
Ralph Connor titles this western novel from a Gospel line: to him that hath shall be given. The game opens it, with tennis calls of forty-love, game, and set. The cost of sacrifice, a heathen quest, and Annette follow, with the rectory and a grievance committee. A foreman, free speech, and the day before lead toward the night of victory.

A new manager, light that is darkness, and a strike carry the story into gathering clouds and a storm. A gallant fight closes the arc. Connor writes of labor, capital, and conscience in a mining west, where a manager's choices decide livelihoods. The novel argues, through its plot, that power used well grows and power hoarded fails.
32541-one-way:
Miriam Allen deFord's tale, printed in Galaxy in March 1955, follows parents saying goodbye to their only child, Hal, chosen for the Lydna Project. The narrator and Lucy, married twenty-seven years, take a copter-taxi back to Homefield rather than let neighbours see the big skycar marked Lydna Project and drop in with curious interest. Some parents boast that sons and daughters were picked for Lydna, but the narrator sees only chance within limits, and love for an only child.

Lucy says nothing on the way back, and the narrator, remembering Hal at two looking up after a hard day at work, also falls silent. The tale's framing note says the narrator tried every way to save Hal and failed, but the women did not. DeFord builds a quiet, moving story of parental love, sacrifice, and women's resourcefulness under a cold official plan.
3258-a-laodicean-a-story-of-to-day:
Thomas Hardy builds this novel around Paula, heiress of Stancy Castle, and the men who seek her. George Somerset, an architect, leads the first book, with Dare and Havill in the second. De Stancy takes the third, and the later books mix Somerset, Dare, and De Stancy around Paula herself. The preface notes how the old order of country manors may change slowly or suddenly.

Paula is a Laodicean in love and faith alike: warm to nothing fully, torn between modern ideas and old loyalties. Castle restoration becomes the novel's image for that divided mind, as new work meets old stone. Readers who like Hardy with a lighter touch will enjoy it, though the ending still carries his familiar irony about choices made too late.
3264-dennison-grant-a-novel-of-to-day:
Robert Stead sets this prairie novel in motion with a harvest shout. Chuck at the Y D tonight, and a bed under the shingles, Transley calls to the procession. Linder, foreman and head teamster, straightens from a half load of new hay, tightens the lines, and makes a sound in his throat. Horses press into their collars, and each wagon takes up its place.

Dennison Grant himself stands at the center of the farming world that follows. Stead, a Canadian novelist of the wheat lands, writes work as it was done: teams, hay, and weather deciding the day. A man's standing, earned in the field rather than declared in the town, is Stead's prairie measure throughout.
32642-allan-ramsay:
Oliphant Smeaton traces the life of Allan Ramsay, the Scots poet who rose from wigmaker to bookseller in Edinburgh. Twelve chapters follow his family, his trade, his marriage, and his early verse. They also follow his place in the city's clubs and print shops.

The later chapters weigh his best-known work. That work includes his pastoral play The Gentle Shepherd, his editing of Scots songs, and his book of Scots proverbs. Smeaton closes with Ramsay's late years in a house on Castlehill, and judges him as a writer of pastoral verse, satire, and song.
32724-feet-of-clay:
Phillip Hoskins sends trouble-shooter Cassidy to Kash, a world of the Extrasol Traders, where manager Dillon has lost control. Kash, fourth world of a distant sun, is two-thirds Earth's size, with half Earth's gravity and no moon. Its people call both star and planet home of the Gods.

Traders mapped the world and set up an outpost, yet within months all broke loose. Natives look to priests and gods, and a sick or absent holy man shakes their trust. Cassidy, who knows aliens better than Dillon, must find why a good and kindly god now shows feet of clay, before trade and faith both fail.
33168-famous-singers-of-to-day-and-yeste:
Henry C. Lahee's Famous Singers of To-day and Yesterday, published in Boston in 1898 and illustrated, traces opera singing from 1600 to 1800. It goes through Pasta to Mario, Mario to Tietjens, and the prima donnas of the fifties, sixties, seventies, and eighties, before closing with tenors and baritones and contraltos and bassos. Illustrations show Calvé, Jenny Lind, Patti, Nordica, and Melba in their roles.

Lahee writes for music lovers who wanted lives and voices in one volume, with a chronological table and index to help them find their favorites. The book's sweep, from early opera to the stars of Lahee's own day, makes it a useful survey of a golden age of singing. For opera fans and historians, it preserves the reputations of singers whose voices survive only in description and in the memories of those who heard them.
33303-russian-life-to-day:
Herbert Bury's Russian Life To-Day, first printed in March 1915, sketches Russia's great spaces and daily life on the eve of revolution. Bury, Bishop for Northern and Central Europe, dedicates the book to his fellow countrymen at work in Siberia, and his frontispiece shows the Tsar himself. His chapters range from vast distances to town life, church, and the war's early strain.

The book's value lies in its on-the-spot view, written by a churchman who knew Russia well and wrote for English readers. Its tone is sympathetic and plain, noting both grandeur and hardship. For students of Russian history, it is a vivid snapshot of a world about to vanish, told by a witness who saw it whole.
33320-across-the-continent-by-the-lincol:
Effie Price Gladding's Across the Continent by the Lincoln Highway, copyrighted in 1915, tells of a motor journey across America on the new Lincoln Highway. Gladding, with photographs to illustrate the road, dedicates the book to lovers of the open road. Its pictures show the highway near Soda Springs, California, and other stops along the way.

The book captures a moment when motoring was still an adventure, with rough roads, small towns, and wide western spaces. Gladding writes as a keen, cheerful traveler, noting people and places with a tourist's eye. For readers of road history, it is a delightful record of early American motoring, when crossing a continent by car was still news.
33759-the-key-to-yesterday:
Charles Neville Buck writes a romance of art, racing, and memory in this 1910 Grosset and Dunlap novel, in twenty-one chapters. It opens at Churchill Downs, where a Derby crowd surges around the grandstand and two colts fight out the final furlongs, a blood-bay colt pressed by a black, foam-flecked muzzle. A tall stranger, lean-jawed and broad-shouldered, watches with an interest beyond that of the casual race-goer, his grey eyes keen yet tinged with a dreamer's wistfulness.

The story turns to Steele's praise of an artist whose career has been a march of successive triumphs, and to Duska, whose portrait stands at the novel's heart. From racetrack excitement, Buck builds a tale of love, art, and the past, with the key to yesterday unlocking old feeling. Readers of early twentieth-century romance will enjoy its sporting color and sentimental plot.
33915-mammals-taken-along-the-alaska-hig:
Rollin H. Baker wrote this 1951 survey of mammals along the Alaska Highway, in the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History series. The paper, pages 87 to 117 of volume five, lists collecting places from Circle and Fairbanks to Tok Junction, Anchorage, and Haines, with sites in Yukon Territory as well.

Baker records which mammals were taken at each place, giving field workers a route map of northern fauna. A figure in the text aids the account. The paper serves mammal students who work the highway country and want a first, careful list.
33939-sturdy-and-strong-or-how-george-an:
G. A. Henty wrote this boys' tale of George Andrews, published in New York by the Federal Book Company. A frontispiece shows Surly Joe with a child on either side, telling sea stories. Henty's preface sets the theme, saying the upward path in England lies open to those who brace themselves to climb it.

Luck, Henty argues, is mostly opportunity met with readiness and quickness to use it. George's way upward tests that claim through work and hardship. The book offers a sturdy Victorian tale of pluck, patience, and making one's way.
34000-rachel-ray:
Anthony Trollope wrote this novel in two volumes, published in London in 1863 by Chapman and Hall. Rachel Ray, a young woman of a Devon family, meets Luke Rowan, a young man from a brewery, and their courtship draws in mothers, clergy, and neighbors. Chapters follow Mrs. Tappitt's ball, Mr. Prong at home, and visits to Bragg's End.

Trollope watches how talk, money, and respectability press on a young couple. Rachel must weigh her own heart against her family's care. The novel endures as a warm, clear Trollope tale of provincial life and love.
34024-ruth-fielding-at-lighthouse-point-:
Alice B. Emerson wrote this girls' adventure tale, published in New York in 1913. Ruth Fielding, heroine of the Red Mill and Briarwood Hall, goes to Lighthouse Point, where a castaway girl named Nita enters the story. Chapters follow an initiation, trouble at the Red Mill, a signal gun, and a lifeboat launched to a girl in the rigging.

Nita's own story, a fishing mishap, and Tom Cameron to the rescue carry the later chapters. Emerson writes briskly for girls who like action with friendship. The book remains a lively entry in the Ruth Fielding series.
3468-poems-by-the-way:
William Morris gathers lyrics and short narrative poems in this collection, first printed in December 1891 and reprinted in 1892. Contents include From the Upland to the Sea, Of the Wooing of Hallbiorn the Strong, Echoes of Love's House, The Burghers' Battle, and The Hall and the Wood. The poems move between meadows, sea coasts, old halls, and the world of Norse legend.

Morris writes in a musical, old fashioned style, full of flowers, winds, and quiet longing. His speakers wander among bays and meads, sit in porches, and dream of a sun god's lonely home on a hill. The collection suits readers who enjoy late Victorian verse that looks back to medieval craft and story, rather than to city life.
3535-a-narrative-of-the-expedition-to-bo:
Watkin Tench, a marine officer, writes a first hand account of the First Fleet voyage that founded the settlement at Botany Bay in Australia. Tench promises to keep the nautical detail brief, for the sake of general readers, and to offer both amusement and information. The expedition had excited wide curiosity in Britain, with hopes and fears about what a penal colony might become.

Tench describes the voyage, the landing, and the first encounters with the new land and its peoples. His little tract became one of the earliest published accounts of Australia. Readers interested in exploration, convict history, and the start of Sydney will find a clear, lively eyewitness narrative.
3702-foul-play:
Charles Reade and Dion Boucicault write a sensation novel that opens in a London merchant's dining room in Russell Square. The room is large, with sickly green walls, heavy maroon curtains, and mahogany chairs. A turkey carpet an inch thick covers the floor, in a place that seems at first sight inaccessible to romance. A young clerk, at school till fifteen and in his father's office till twenty two, shows such aptitude that the merchant John Wardlaw plans to advance him.

From this staid beginning the story moves into crime, forgery, shipwreck, and adventure, as Reade and Boucicault pile twists upon twists. The novel suits readers who enjoy Victorian sensation fiction at its most melodramatic, where a respectable office hides a plot that will carry its hero across the world.
3780-the-king-s-highway:
George Payne Rainsford James wrote this historical romance around a lover who dares to hope above his station. The hero loves a duke's daughter. Yet he knows the duke is proud of family, wealth, rank, and daughter alike. The duke has already favored a match with the son of the Earl of Byerdale, a nobleman of vast influence near the sovereign's counsels. The lover's suit must therefore fight pride, power, and an arranged rival.

James fills the tale with courts, country houses, and the codes of an older England, where a duke's consent counts as a great condescension. The prose is full and formal, in the manner of the early historical novel. Readers who enjoy Scott style romance will find a story of love against rank, told with ceremony and suspense.
3827-the-days-before-yesterday:
Lord Frederick Hamilton, encouraged by the welcome for his earlier reminiscences, offers a second lumber room of memories in this volume. He warns that readers hoping for scandals will be disappointed, since the book holds everyday events rather than revelations. Chapters recall a childhood of crocodiles, grizzlies, and chimney sweeps, a live lion at a tea party, and Landseer the painter as a family friend.

Later pages visit Paris, where judges dine and a Frenchman named Ducros cries Slop basin as his one word of English praise for a fine dish. Disraeli, Lord John Russell, and the Earl of Aberdeen pass through the narrative. Readers who like Victorian high society recalled without malice will find a genial and well mannered memoir.
4044-what-the-animals-do-and-say:
A natural history book for young readers gathers stories of what animals do and say, from farmyards to far islands. A writer on the Faroe Islands describes crow courts, where crows gather as if summoned, some with drooping heads and others grave as judges.

If a crow is proved guilty, the flock deals with it, in a folk tale of animal justice. Other chapters follow beasts, birds, and fishes through habits that seem almost human. The book suits children curious about nature, offering short, vivid tales that mix fact, fancy, and old country lore.
4078-the-picture-of-dorian-gray:
Oscar Wilde's novel follows Dorian Gray, a beautiful young man whose portrait ages while he stays young. In a sampled chapter, Dorian reclines in Lord Henry's little library in Curzon Street, among olive-stained oak, cream friezes, and silk Persian rugs.

Lord Henry's witty, corrupting talk shapes Dorian's path, as beauty, pleasure, and sin trade places in his life. Wilde writes with epigrams and rich description, turning a Faustian bargain into a study of art and morals. Readers who enjoy brilliant, unsettling fiction will find a short classic that still provokes debate.
5090-i-will-repay:
Baroness Orczy's novel opens in Paris in 1783, when a boy is publicly humiliated and swears revenge on the man who shamed him. Years later, in the shadow of the French Revolution, that oath returns to shape the lives of both men, as old debts, honour, and love collide amid political terror.

Orczy, best known for tales of the Revolution, writes a story of vengeance pursued to its bitter end. Disguises, narrow escapes, and moral choices test her characters. Readers get a romantic historical adventure in which a childhood vow proves harder to keep, and harder to escape, than either man expected.
515-margret-howth-a-story-of-to-day:
Rebecca Harding Davis sets this Civil War-era novel in a mill town shadowed by battle. Margret Howth, a teacher's daughter, faces work, poverty, and a lover torn between duty and doubt. Davis opens by refusing grand war themes, choosing instead homely, narrow life on the border of the battlefield.

Margret's story tracks mills, schools, and sickrooms, where plain folk bear grief in silence. Davis writes with moral gravity, seeking hope in humble things. The novel stands as an early realist portrait of wartime home life, where the true world grows, slowly, from endurance.
5229-felix-o-day:
F. Hopkinson Smith's novel Felix O'Day opens on Broadway, the Great White Way, where coloured signs pencil the skyline in fire and rain turns the asphalt to liquid gold. Through that crowded thoroughfare moves Felix, an Irish-American figure of the New York theatre and street world, whose fortunes the novel follows.

Smith writes with affection for old New York, its crowds, its traffic, and its sudden poetry. The book offers a warm, episodic portrait of city life in the early twentieth century, told by a writer who loved Broadway and knew its people from the inside.
5257-the-broad-highway:
Jeffery Farnol's Broad Highway opens with its narrator eating fried bacon with a tinker on a summer morning, dreaming of a book about roads, by-roads, wayside inns, and country people. The story itself begins with an uncle's will, then sends the hero out on foot, where he meets a bagman, a pugilist named Tom Cragg, a one-legged soldier, and many others.

Farnol writes a rambling, cheerful romance of the English road, in the manner of old picaresque tales. Readers will find inns, fights, love affairs, and landscape in generous measure. It is told by a narrator who loves the highway and the company found upon it.
5629-dorothy-dale-a-girl-of-to-day:
Margaret Penrose wrote Dorothy Dale: A Girl of To-Day as the first book of the Dorothy Dale series, followed by Dorothy Dale at Glenwood School. Contents run from Dorothy herself and Dorothy at the office through a strange adventure, a clew, and Miles Burlock. A swing, what happened in the orchard, Squire Sanders at school, apple blossom magic, and a soldier's daughter follow.

Later chapters bring an unprovoked attack, a queer picnic, a secret, Dorothy in politics, Dorothy in danger, a surprise trip, and an eventful journey. Penrose writes a modern girl's school and home adventures with warmth. Young readers get a cheerful series opener, full of friends, mysteries, and pluck.
5632-five-little-peppers-midway:
Margaret Sidney wrote Five Little Peppers Midway as another book about the Pepper family, lovingly inscribed to her little Margaret, who is Phronsie Pepper to all who know her. Contents run from Phronsie's Pie and Cousin Eunice Chatterton through rehearsals, welcome home, the little brown house, and old times again, to Badgertown calls, a sudden blow, and the party separating.

Poor Polly, new work for Polly, Mamsie's wedding, and questions of where Phronsie is and whether she is well again carry the family story forward. Readers get a warm, old-fashioned family tale, full of pies, plays, and Pepper loyalty.
5673-the-young-musician-or-fighting-his-:
Horatio Alger's novel follows Philip, a poor boy with a fiddle, who faces the threat of the poorhouse and a set of neighbors allied against him. The chapter titles trace his path. A call from Nick Holden comes first, then an auction and a fuss about his fiddle. A stay in the poorhouse and bad tidings follow, until he escapes on a night adventure. Music is both his gift and his trouble, since it marks him out and gives him a way forward.

We meet a classic Alger hero: young, hardworking, and determined to earn an honest living rather than accept charity or defeat. The story moves through small-town scheming, kindness from unexpected friends, and the slow turn of fortune that rewards persistence. It is a plain, encouraging tale for young readers, and a clear example of Alger's belief that pluck and honest work can change a life.
5698-fanny-s-first-play:
Bernard Shaw's Fanny's First Play, first published in 1911, is a comedy that turns the theatre itself into its subject. A young woman writes a play, and her family and their friends gather to judge it, bringing their own pride, prejudice, and respectability into the stalls with them. Shaw uses the occasion to mock critics, parents, and polite society in turn, letting each voice expose itself.

The fun comes from the layers: a play within a play, and an audience on stage watching an audience. Readers meet sharp dialogue, brisk reversals, and Shaw's familiar habit of letting a clever character say the uncomfortable truth aloud. It is a lively entry point to Shaw's stagecraft, and it still amuses readers who enjoy argument dressed up as entertainment.
5893-two-little-women-on-a-holiday:
Two Little Women on a Holiday follows two girls through a holiday of plans, arrivals, and small social adventures. Chapters trace a wonderful plan, a favourable decision, the arrival, a merry quartette, going about, a matinee idol, and great preparations. A caller, fine feathers, a skating party, collections, a lost jewel, suspicions, a tea room, and Dolly's ride carry the holiday forward.

Here is a bright girls' story of friendship, shopping, theatre, and mild mystery, where a lost jewel tests trust. The tone is cheerful and orderly, with holiday freedom balanced by good manners. Young readers who enjoy series stories of girls on holiday will find familiar pleasures here, and adults will enjoy its light, old-fashioned picture of leisure.
5894-the-extra-day:
Blackwood's The Extra Day follows children into a world where wonder interrupts ordinary time. Chapters trace the material and fancy as the seed of wonder. They move through the death of a mere fact and fact edged with fancy. Then come the birth and growth of wonder, before imagination wakes and wonder hides. A priest of wonder, fact and wonder in clash, and Judy's and Tim's particular adventures follow, as time hesitates and Maria stirs.

The book gives a children's fantasy of philosophy, where a day outside time lets young heroes see the world afresh. Blackwood writes with lyric feeling, favoring mood and image over plot machinery. The book suits readers of classic children's fantasy, and adults who enjoy stories where wonder itself is the adventure, granted for one extra day.
598-heimskringla-or-the-chronicle-of-the:
Snorri Sturluson chronicles Norway's kings from about 850 to 1177 in this saga collection, written in Old Norse around 1225. Sixteen sagas run from Halfdan the Black and Harald Fairhair through Olaf Trygvason, Saint Olaf, Harald Hardrada, and Magnus Barefoot to later kings. Family trees, songs, and old tales ground the history.

Sturluson writes as poet and historian, mixing fact with legend in clear, stark prose. Scholars debate his accuracy, yet his work remains a prime source for the Viking Age. The book endures as a vast, gripping history of kings, battles, and faith in the North.
6002-little-miss-by-the-day:
Lucille Van Slyke chases an elusive figure she calls little Miss By-the-Day, a whimsical young person who slips out of towns, countries, and even rooms just before one arrives. The narrator feels cheated of something rightfully hers, as if a fascinating soul known perfectly well can never quite be met.

At first Miss By-the-Day sounds casual and commonplace, just a little seamstress, and the narrator lets her slip through her fingers. Chapters on a barred garden, a house in the woods, lost dreams, an unfinished song, and certain legal matters follow. Van Slyke turns a search for one girl into a meditation on near meetings.
6601-verses-and-rhymes-by-the-way:
Nora Pembroke offers verses and rhymes made along the way, with a nod to poor Mango's poems and to Burns on the lowly daisy. Her dedication speaks to a dear friend who stood near in dark days, and thanks a higher guide for a debt of love. The contents list a tale of Plantagenet, a legend of a Buckingham village, and poems on Ottawa and the lake.

Pembroke's verse is plain, pious, and home-like, with a taste for local names and quiet feeling. She writes for friends and neighbors, not for fame, and her rhymes carry that modest aim. Verses and Rhymes by the Way is a small, sincere book of Canadian verse from a life lived close to home.
6627-barriers-burned-away:
E. P. Roe wrote his first novel in sympathy with Chicago after its great fire, hoping its losses and fortitude might teach lessons once the news had died away. Flames, he says, can show with harsh light the need and worth of Christian faith. The book is dedicated to his mother's memory, and its preface speaks with plain, earnest feeling.

The story that follows turns on love, loss, and faith tested by fire and by the rebuilding of lives. Roe writes as a preacher-novelist, warm and direct, for readers who like a moral tale. Barriers Burned Away is a sincere, period romance of a city burned and a people remade.
6785-wallenstein-s-camp-a-play:
Schiller's Camp of Wallenstein, in James Churchill's translation, serves as an introduction to the great Wallenstein tragedy. Its vivid portrait of the general's army, the translator notes, gives the best clue to the spell of his gigantic power. Blind faith in his arms, belief in supernatural aid, wild indulgence, and scorn for all law save the camp's have swollen his soldiers with a sense of endless sway.

Oppression of peasants and plunder of the country feed that swagger, yet the camp speaks for itself in the play. A prologue passage on Schiller's view of the Camp closes the note. Wallenstein's Camp is a lively, rough prelude to one of Schiller's greatest dramas.
6790-demetrius-a-play:
Schiller's Demetrius opens at the Diet of Cracow, with the Polish senate hall in full view. On a raised platform under a canopy sits the king on his throne. Escutcheons of Poland and Lithuania hang at his sides. Ten royal officers stand by him. Bishops, palatines, and castellans sit below, and deputies stand in double line, all armed. The Archbishop of Gnesen, primate of the kingdom, sits near the front with a chaplain bearing a golden cross.

His opening speech hails a tempestuous Diet brought to a cordial close, with king and commons parting as friends. Into that calm steps a claimant who will shake the realm. Demetrius is a grand, unfinished drama of false princes and real power.
718-tono-bungay:
H. G. Wells wrote this novel about George Ponderevo, a young man drawn into the rise of his uncle Edward, a salesman of genius. Edward builds a fortune on Tono-Bungay, a patent tonic of little worth, sold with bold ads and grand claims. George, trained in science, helps build the firm even as he doubts its wares.

The novel follows the firm from shop to empire to collapse, and George from youth to disillusion. Wells uses the quack cure to satirise English business, class, and the hunger for quick wealth. It is a big, restless book, part life story and part social critique, and one of Wells's most personal novels.
7365-if-i-may:
A. A. Milne, later famous for children's books, first made his name with light essays for newspapers and magazines. If I May collects those early pieces, written in the years around the First World War. They range from art and writing to the small absurdities of daily life, and they carry the easy, talkative voice that made Milne a popular columnist.

One thread runs through the wartime essays: what use are artists to a nation at war, and what place should they claim when workers can halt the country by striking? Milne answers with humor rather than preaching, defending the artist's work while poking fun at his own trade. The book is a good entry point to Milne before Winnie-the-Pooh, witty without ever turning heavy.
7427-toasts-and-forms-of-public-address-:
William Pittenger wrote this manual for anyone suddenly called upon to speak. Its subtitle promises the right thing in the right way, and its contents deliver. There are after-dinner speeches, ancient and modern. There is advice on the value of a good story and how to introduce it. There are plain directions for making speeches, toasts, and responses. Holiday speeches for the Fourth of July, Memorial Day, and Christmas are included.

Beyond toasts, the book gives presentation addresses, addresses of welcome, and wedding and anniversary speeches, plus miscellaneous addresses for centennials and similar occasions. Pittenger had already written volumes for serious speaking; this one serves the convivial assembly. It remains a handy, old-fashioned guide to saying something graceful when the moment demands it.
763-the-round-up-a-romance-of-arizona-no:
John Murray and Marion Mills Miller novelized Edmund Day's melodrama The Round-Up into this romance of Arizona ranch life. Cowboys, cattle, and the desert form the stage, where love, loyalty, and old wrongs clash at round-up time. The stage play's bold scenes are retold in prose, with the same broad strokes and high feeling.

The novel keeps the melodrama's pace: chases, showdowns, and reconciliations follow fast. Its heroes are plain-spoken ranch folk, its villains clear-cut. The book preserves a popular stage hit in book form, and it gives modern readers a taste of the western romance as audiences first loved it, before the screen took it over.
7764-little-bear-at-work-and-at-play:
Frances Margaret Fox's Little Bear at Work and at Play gathers short tales for young readers, first printed in Youth's Companion and Christian Observer. Little Bear brags, refuses work, learns to swim, finds a lost otter baby, visits school, gets his wish, and hosts a surprise party.

Mother Skunk helps him, three bears come to breakfast, and Grandpa Tortoise shakes his hand in Warner Carr's pictures. Dedicated to the first girls of Martha Cook Dormitory at Ann Arbor, the book teaches work, kindness, and good manners through animal play, in short, gentle stories.
78706-such-a-happy-day:
Catharine Shaw wrote this tale for the young, one of a set of her books for them. Its three parts are named for the day in full: a happy day, a happy spell past noon, and a happy eve. The tale opens at dawn in a home. A small boy, Cyril, greets his sire with a glad Good day. His face is as fresh and cool as a fruit of the vine, the sire jokes, though his cheeks are red like fruit of the tree, not green.

Cyril has been out with his mother. They have been out to pick blooms, but he will not say what for. He loves a hid thing, and begs his sire not to guess. The mother comes in at the glass door with her pail of blooms in hand, and lets the boy speak.
7895-a-terrible-temptation-a-story-of-to:
Charles Reade's A Terrible Temptation opens in a Portman Square morning room. A gentleman leans on a mantelpiece and talks to a young lady at her work, his eyes full of loving admiration while she bends her fair head with modest, demure air. She suspects she is admired and will not look.

Miss Arabella Bruce, with dark red hair, white neck, dove-like eyes, and blooming oval face, is the beauty at the center. The gentleman, sunburned and bright-eyed, smiles well but scowls with a power of hating. Through love, money, and temptation, Reade builds a sensational novel of today.
7984-the-old-santa-fe-trail-the-story-of:
Colonel Henry Inman, late assistant quartermaster of the United States Army, wrote this history of the Santa Fe Trail with a preface by W. F. Buffalo Bill Cody. The trail ran from Missouri across the plains to Santa Fe, carrying traders, soldiers. And settlers through country that Cody's preface compares to the steppes of Russia and the interior of Africa for grandeur and solitude. Inman tells of caravans, Indian encounters, forts, and the hardships of the road.

The book captures the trail while its travellers were still living, preserving stories that would otherwise have faded. It mixes adventure with the practical detail of freighting and frontier soldiering. For readers of Western history, it remains a first-hand-flavoured account of one of America's great highways before the railroad replaced it.
7987-the-fair-maid-of-perth-or-st-valent:
Sir Walter Scott set this novel in medieval Perth, around Catherine Glover, the Fair Maid of the title, and the craftsmen, nobles, and clan chiefs whose quarrels engulf her. St Valentine's Day gives the story its opening festival, and the action builds through civic pride, court intrigue, and the famous clan combat on the North Inch of Perth. Scott's introductory pages begin with Edinburgh's quarters before turning to Perth itself.

The novel mixes romance with Scottish history, giving the town's guilds and the wild Highland clans equal colour. Catherine's steadiness anchors a plot full of disguise, rivalry, and violence. For readers of the Waverley novels, it is one of Scott's most atmospheric Scottish tales, and a good portrait of a medieval burgh under pressure.
882-sketches-by-boz-illustrative-of-ever:
Charles Dickens, as Boz, wrote these sketches of everyday life and everyday people when he was a very young man. Published one by one, then gathered, they catch London streets, shops, omnibuses, and lodgings, with illustrations by George Cruikshank and Phiz. The people are clerks, cabmen, and shabby-genteel families.

Dickens's eye for small detail and his ear for speech already mark the future novelist. The sketches are light, funny, and often touching, and they preserve a London that was vanishing even as he wrote. The volume is the best place to meet the young Dickens, before the great novels made him famous.
9850-the-lyric-an-essay:
John Drinkwater's 1922 essay asks a simple question with no simple answer: what is lyric poetry? He begins with poetry itself, arguing that it puts the best words in the best order, then narrows to the short, songlike poem.

Chapters test his ideas against Paradise Lost, sort lyric forms, and weigh why songs and short poems stay popular with readers. Drinkwater writes for ordinary readers, not scholars, and uses plain examples throughout. The essay remains a friendly guide for anyone who loves poems but wants to understand what makes a lyric work.
a-bicycle-of-cathay: Frank Stockton tells a comic novel that begins with a doctor's daughter and a bad twist of fate. Its chapters bring in a duke's dressing gown, a country inn, a runaway, and a large and lively family. The story moves through advice, mishaps, and romance with the light touch Stockton was known for. Readers meet a string of odd characters whose plans keep crossing in unexpected ways.
a-daughter-of-the-dons-a-story-of-new-me: William MacLeod Raine tells a story of New Mexico today centered on a daughter of the dons. Don Manuel introduces himself first, and two land grants set the plot in motion. Chapters visit the Yuste hacienda, follow fisherman's luck, and tame an outlaw. Raine writes a western romance of old Spanish families, new fortunes, and desert adventure.
a-daughter-of-to-day: Sara Jeannette Duncan tells of a daughter of today through Miss Kimpsey and Mrs. Leslie Bell. The novel opens with Kimpsey waiting, tired and thoughtful, for Bell to come downstairs. Rapid footsteps overhead suggest hasteful preparation for the meeting. Duncan writes a modern story of women, manners, and the choices of a new generation.
a-laodicean-a-story-of-to-day:
Thomas Hardy calls his novel a story of to-day and divides it into six books named for the people who rule each stretch: George Somerset, Dare and Havill, De Stancy, and Paula. His preface treats the changing of the old order in country houses, and notes the book was finished by dictation through a five months' illness. Paula Power, a rich young heiress of no firm faith, is the Laodicean of the title.

Paula owns a castle, a telegraph, and a Baptist conscience at war with her taste for the medieval. Somerset the architect, the De Stancys, father and son, and the scheming Dare fight for her hand and fortune. Hardy sets new money and new machines against old names.
a-millionaire-of-yesterday:
E. Phillips Oppenheim opens in a filthy West African trading post, where Trent and his older partner Monty wait, ragged and sick, for their chance. The two men are digging for a fortune the hard way. Years later, one of them returns to England rich, with a past that must stay buried.

Forty-two chapters follow blackmail, society drawing rooms, and a woman who knows more than she should. Oppenheim, a master of the popular thriller of his day, keeps secrets stacked on secrets and pays them off in turns. The tale moves between the fever coast and London polish, and its smooth plotting carried his name around the world.
a-narrative-of-the-expedition-to-botany-:
Watkin Tench, an officer of marines, offers his little tract to the public, as his introduction says, to amuse and inform about the expedition to Botany Bay. He sailed with the fleet sent to found a colony in New South Wales, a scheme some foresaw as beneficial and others called big with folly and ruin. Tench declines to judge before the trial is fair.

Fourteen chapters cover the voyage out, the landings, and the first state of the settlement at Sydney Cove. He describes the country, the convicts and officers, and the Aboriginal people with a clear, humane eye. His narrative was among the first books of Australia, and it stays fresh for its plain good sense.
a-terrible-temptation-a-story-of-to-day:
A Terrible Temptation, subtitled A Story of To-Day, is an 1871 novel by Charles Reade. Reade was a leading Victorian novelist, famous for turning close research into dramatic stories of modern life. The subtitle is his signal: unlike his historical romances, this tale is set in the England of his own day, among its present manners and pressures.

As the title promises, the story turns on a temptation and the damage it threatens to those who face it. Reade builds his fiction on strong situations and moral stakes, and this novel applies that method to contemporary society. It stands in his output as his pointed look at the temptations of modern life, written for the readers who were living it.
a-walk-from-london-to-john-o-groat-s-wit: Elihu Burritt walks from London to John O'Groat's in this volume, opening with motives to the walk and the iron horse against his rider. Railway track and turnpike road have their sceneries compared. The first day brings rural footpaths, Tiptree Farm, and Alderman Mechi's operations in steam power, under-draining, deep tillage, and irrigation. Birds and their song, old houses, hedges, harvest aspects, country inns, and a three-thousand-acre farm follow by the way.
a-wasted-day:
Richard Harding Davis opens in the office of Arnold Thorndike, called the wisest man in Wall Street. A letter arrives from a probation officer about Spear, a young stenographer who once took Thorndike's letters on the train. Spear has been convicted of theft and faces sentence on Tuesday.

Learning what Thorndike does with that letter fills the rest of the tale. Davis contrasts the great man's busy, guarded day with the one errand that might save a foolish young clerk. The story is slight in plot but warm in feeling, and it questions what a successful man's time is really for. Davis writes the office scenes with a reporter's quick eye.
abraham-lincoln-a-play: John Drinkwater turns Abraham Lincoln into a play of 1919, with a foreword by Arnold Bennett and a gift note to Lord Charnwood. The author's note says his aim is that of the play-maker, not the chronicler, and he thanks Charnwood's fine life of Lincoln for its facts. He has freely squeezed events and bent invention to their course. The made-up Burnet Hook joins Lincoln's cabinet to stand for certain forces of the time.
an-essay-toward-a-history-of-shakespeare: Martin Bronn Ruud writes an essay toward a history of Shakespeare in Norway, tracing how the poet's work reached and took root in a northern land. With a prefatory note by the author, the study follows translations, performances, and criticism. It shows Shakespeare's afterlife far from England, in a culture making his plays its own.
barriers-burned-away:
Edward Payson Roe's Barriers Burned Away is a novel prompted by the great Chicago fire, which Roe visited among its smouldering ruins. Roe says the sufferers' losses and fortitude taught lessons that deserved to outlast the newspaper echoes, and that even destructive flames could throw Christian faith into sharper light.

The fire itself fills only a small share of the story; the wider story follows its characters through love, pride and the social barriers that burn away under trial. Roe, dedicating the book to his mother's memory, calls it the first child of his imagination, and its early copyright dates run from 1872. Readers of sentimental Victorian fiction will find here a Chicago novel where disaster tests, rather than merely destroys, its people.
boys-and-girls-from-thackeray:
Kate Dickinson Sweetser made Boys and Girls from Thackeray in 1907, with pictures by George Alfred Williams. Sweetser retells scenes from Thackeray's novels for young readers, keeping his people and much of his voice. Henry Esmond's lonely boyhood at Castlewood opens the set.

Becky Sharp at school shows the great schemer as a girl. Cuff's fight with Figs brings the schoolyard of Vanity Fair to life. George Osborne and Rawdon Crawley, Clive and Ethel Newcome, and Arthur Pendennis follow in turn. Caroline, a Cinderella tale, closes the book. Sweetser trims the long novels to their young hearts. Children met Thackeray's world early, in pieces sized for them, before tackling the full novels later.
britain-at-bay:
Spenser Wilkinson published Britain at Bay at New York in 1909, a call for a national army. Wilkinson opens with Salisbury's 1900 charge that the British constitution fails as an instrument of war. A second warning, Asquith's on German battleship building, frames the present danger.

Force and right, arbitration, and the balance of power fill the early chapters. Wilkinson then argues that war has become national, so defence must be national too. Navy needs, England's military problem, and the cost of one army, not two, get plain counts. A chain of duty closes the case. Morning Post articles form the core. Edwardian readers met the conscription plea in full.
britannica-1911-alcott-louisa-may:
Alcott, Louisa May, an American author of 1832 to 1888, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Daughter of Amos Bronson Alcott, she was born at Germantown, Pennsylvania, on her father's birthday in November 1832. She began work early, teaching now and then and writing. Her first book, Flower Fables of 1854, gathered tales written for Emerson's daughter Ellen.

Six weeks as a nurse in the Union Hospital at Georgetown during the Civil War gave her Hospital Sketches, letters home that showed real power of observation. Moods, a novel of 1864, promised much despite an uncertain touch. Then she turned to rapid production of stories for girls, and one of them made her name permanently. Little Women established her family in comfort, and its public never tired of the volumes that followed in its line, from An Old-Fashioned Girl to Rose in Bloom.
britannica-1911-algoa-bay:
Port Elizabeth owes its start to Algoa Bay, a broad and shallow inlet on the South African coast. British settlers bound for the eastern part of Cape Colony first landed there in 1820 and built the town six miles north-east of Cape Recife. Its harbour takes shelter from every wind except the south-east, and sailors often use the bay's name for the town itself.

Cape Recife and Cape Padrone mark the bay's ends, 436 miles east of the Cape of Good Hope. Inside lies St Croix Island. Bartholomew Diaz landed there soon after 3 February 1488, his second landing in South Africa, and a cross he is believed to have raised gave the island its name.
britannica-1911-arbor-day:
Arbor Day is an American day for public tree planting. Nebraska first put it into successful operation. The year was 1872. J. Sterling Morton led the movement there. He was president of the state Board of Agriculture. Governor Furnas gave official sanction in 1874. A state law made it a legal holiday in 1885. Nebraska was the pioneer state throughout.

The movement spread rapidly nationwide. Nearly every state and territory adopted it. Some mark it as a legal holiday. Others mark it as a school holiday. Northern states usually choose April or early May. Southern states choose winter months instead. January, February, and December all appear. Localities within a state sometimes differ. New Zealand introduced a like practice. Egleston's history of Arbor Day is cited. Schauffler's later anthology closes the references.
britannica-1911-avaray:
Avaray is a French territorial title held by the Bésiade family, who moved from Béarn into the Orléanais in the 17th century and gained the Avaray estate there. Théophile de Bésiade, marquis d'Avaray, became grand bailiff of Orleans in 1667, an office later held by several descendants.

Claude Antoine de Bésiade sat for Orleans in the states-general of 1789 and proposed a Declaration of the Duties of Man beside the Rights of Man. He later became a lieutenant-general, a peer of France, and duc d'Avaray. His son Antoine Louis François won fame for devotion to the comte de Provence, the future Louis XVIII, aiding his flight and being called his liberator.
britannica-1911-ay:
Ay and Aye gathers two small words that look alike but sound and mean differently. Ay, said like the end of day, means always, and is kin to Greek aei, always, and Latin aevum, an age. The New English Dictionary prefers this spelling for the word of time.

Aye, said almost like eye, means yes. It is probably the same word at root, parted from the other by usage, though often confused with yea. The form ay serves for this sense too, but awkwardly, and poets once wrote it with a single letter I, as Michael Drayton did in 1593. The entry sorts spellings, sounds, and senses for both.
britannica-1911-azuay:
Azuay, sometimes written Assuay, is a province of Ecuador bordered by Cañar to the north, Oriente east, Loja south, and El Oro west. It was formerly called Cuenca and once formed part of a larger department of Azuay that also included Loja. Its capital is the city of Cuenca.

High and mountainous, the province runs through many climates. Its products vary with the height. Silver and quicksilver come from the ground. Wheat, Indian corn, and barley come from its fields. Cattle, wool, cinchona bark, and straw hats complete the list. That spread of goods from mines, farms, and herds in one mountain province is the entry's whole picture of Azuay.
britannica-1911-bay:
Bay is one spelling for five different words, set out in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The first bay is the sweet laurel, a tree whose leaves crowned poets of old, so that “bays” came to mean fame and reward.  The second bay is a wide opening in a coast line, where the sea cuts into the land. The third is a colour, a reddish brown used chiefly of horses, with shades such as light bay and bright bay, from a Latin word Varro used for horse colour.

Sound and space close the set. The fourth bay is the deep bark of dogs, from a French word for gaping. From the hounds' baying comes “at bay,” of a hunted beast turning to face them. The fifth is a building term: one division of an arcade, the space from pillar to pillar. A bay-window projects outward from a wall.
britannica-1911-baybay:
Baybay is a town of the province of Leyte, in the Philippine Islands, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the west coast of the island of Leyte, at the mouth of the Pagbañganan river. The town lies forty-five miles south-south-west of Tacloban, the provincial capital. Its people numbered 22,990 in the count of 1903, a large town by the measure of the island. The Cebu dialect of the Visayan language is spoken there.

Trade is the short entry's whole second half. A superior grade of hemp, the fibre used for rope and cloth, is exported from Baybay, and heads its list of goods. Other products named are rice, corn, copra, the dried flesh of the coconut used for oil, cacao, and sugar. Cattle and horses are also raised in the district and sold.
britannica-1911-bernay:
Bernay is a town of north-western France, capital of an arrondissement in the department of Eure, on the left bank of the Charentonne, 31 miles west-north-west of Evreux. The 1911 Britannica entry, giving a 1906 population of 5,973, praises its setting among green wooded hills and its quaint wooden houses and old churches.

The town grew around a Benedictine abbey founded by Judith of Brittany early in the 11th century; the abbey church now serves as a market. Bernay makes cotton and woollen goods, holds a Lenten horse fair called the Foire fleurie, and trades in grain. Its fortress was razed in 1589.
britannica-1911-biscay:
Biscay, in Spanish Vizcaya, is a maritime province of northern Spain. The Bay of Biscay bounds it north, Guipúzcoa east, Álava south, and Burgos and Santander west. Its area is 836 square miles, and its 1900 population was 311,361. It is one of the Basque Provinces of Spain. The name Biscay is at times used for the whole Basque country of three provinces. The coast from Ondarroa toward Castro Urdiales is bold, rugged, and deeply cut in places.

The Cantabrian chain crosses the province toward the south, making most of it mountainous. Narrow valleys and small plains break up that high ground. Oak, chestnut, and pine forests once covered the hills to their tops. Felling for fuel has stripped much of that cover since. The 1911 Britannica entry praises the people's schooling and enterprise at its close. Density in 1900, at 372.4 people per square mile, topped every other Spanish province.
britannica-1911-boulder-clay:
Boulder clay is the stiff clay, packed with stones, that glaciers leave behind. It forms in and beneath ice sheets. It is the classic deposit of the Ice Age in northern Europe and America. It is also called till or ground moraine. Names are given in German, French, and Swedish too. Most of it lies in no layers, though some kinds are thinly bedded.

Lumps of sand, gravel, or loam turn up inside it here and there. Its colour comes from the rocks the ice ground over. In Britain it is red over Triassic ground. It is black over coal rocks, and buff or grey over Silurian. Where the ice crossed chalk it can be white and chalky. Fresh dug, it is often bluish-grey. It weathers brown at the surface. The stones sit in the clay in no order.
britannica-1911-bruay: Bruay is a town of northern France in the department of Pas-de-Calais, set on the river Lawe 19 miles north-north-west of Arras by road. The hosted entry is a short gazetteer note: it gives the town's population as 16,169 in 1906, places it in a rich coal-mining district. Names brewing as a leading industry alongside the mining that defines the local economy.
britannica-1911-caraway:
Caraway is the fruit, or so-called seed, of a plant. The plant is Carum Carui, of the umbel family. This 1911 Britannica article describes it and its oil. The plant grows across northern and central Europe and Asia. It has finely cut leaves and heads of small white flowers. Its fruits are oval and laterally compressed. Each fruit splits into two curved parts called mericarps. Five pale ridges mark each of those parts.

Bruised caraway gives off a pleasant aromatic smell. Its taste is agreeable and spicy. The fruit yields 3 to 6 per cent of a volatile oil. Carvone and limonene are among its named contents. The oil is got by distillation for medicine and flavouring. It serves as a stimulant and settles the stomach. Whole caraway goes into cheese, cakes and bread. It also forms the basis of caraway comfits, a sweet.
britannica-1911-causeway:
Causeway is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a word for a path laid on a raised dam or mound across marshes or low ground. The term also covers old paved highways, such as the Roman military roads. In English dialect, “causey” still names a paved or cobbled footpath. The entry spends most of its short space on where the word comes from.

Properly, the word is “causey way,” built from causey, a mound or dam. That word came through the Norman French caucie, the ancestor of the modern chaussée. Behind it stands the late Latin via calciata, a road stamped firm by treading, from calcare, to tread. In a few lines the entry moves from marsh paths and Roman roads to the Latin root and its path through French into English. The physical sense and the word history stay tightly bound together.
britannica-1911-chimay:
Chimay is a town in the extreme south-east of the province of Hainaut, Belgium, dating from the 7th century and holding 3,383 people in 1904. People more often place it in the district between the Sambre and the Meuse, the entry notes. Its closeness to the French frontier brought many sieges upon it over the centuries. The last came in 1640, when Turenne ordered it ruined so that it could never stand another siege.

Fame rests chiefly on the castle and park of the same name, held first by the Cröy family and now by the princes of Caraman-Chimay. Of seven towers only one ruined tower remains, and a modern château in Tudor style dates from the 18th century. Madame Tallien, later princess de Chimay, held a small court here until her death in 1835. The chronicler John Froissart died and was buried at Chimay, and a statue honours him.
britannica-1911-colonsay:
Colonsay is an island of the Inner Hebrides in Argyllshire, Scotland, ten miles south of the Ross of Mull. It runs about seven and a half miles long and three miles broad. Its high point, Carnan Eoin, reaches 470 feet. Loch Fada lies near its middle, long but very narrow. Two more small lakes and a few streams dot the land.

Fine sandy shores break a much-cut coast. Kiloran, Kilchattan and Staosunaig are the chief bays. Cliffs on the north-west coast stand out as the best sight. Oronsay lies south across a strait that men can ford at low water. Church ruins, standing stones and carved crosses mark both isles. Their names honour Columba and Oran, said to have stopped there from Ireland. Boats link Scalasaig with Glasgow. A golf course at Kilchattan adds a modern touch.
britannica-1911-cooke-jay:
Jay Cooke (1821–1905) was an American financier born at Sandusky, Ohio, on 10 August 1821. His father was a pioneer Ohio lawyer and a Whig member of Congress. Trade was the boy's set path from the start. He trained in a trading house in Saint Louis and in a transport booking office in Philadelphia. At eighteen he entered a great private banking house in that city.

His gift for business showed at once. Three years later he held a share in the firm. Before he was thirty he was partner in its New York and Saint Louis branches as well. In 1858 he left and spent three years reviving dead Pennsylvania railways and canals. On 1 January 1861 he opened his own banking house in Philadelphia. War loans at par brought him quick, signal success. At one point his sales of bonds ran past the sum Congress had allowed, and Congress sanctioned the excess at once.
britannica-1911-fosse-way:
The Fosse Way, or Foss Way, is the early English name of a Roman road, or series of roads, in Britain. The English used it after Rome's fall, and almost all its line still serves as modern road or lane. It runs from Lincoln by Leicester and Bath to Exeter. From Lincoln it passes through Newark and Leicester, the Roman Ratae, to High Cross, where it crosses Watling Street at a point often called the centre of England.

From High Cross the road runs to Moreton-in-the-Marsh, Cirencester, Bath and Ilchester. It then crosses the hills near Chard, Axminster and Honiton and enters Exeter. Antiquaries have often carried it farther, to Totnes, but without warrant. The short piece is signed by F. J. Haverfield, the great student of Roman Britain.
britannica-1911-friday:
Friday is the sixth day of the week, from the Anglo-Saxon frige-dæg, the day of Frige or Frigg, goddess of love. It matches the Roman Dies Veneris, the French Vendredi, and the Italian Venerdi. The bad luck tied to the day is said to come from its link with the Crucifixion. The old Scandinavian peoples held it the luckiest day of all.

Both Western and Eastern Churches have kept Fridays as fast days in memory of the Passion. Christmas Day falling on a Friday is the one exception. The yearly day of the Passion itself is Good Friday. In Muslim tradition Friday is the Moslem Sabbath. Adam was created on that day, entered Paradise, and was cast out. It was also the day of his repentance and of his death. It will be the Day of Resurrection.
britannica-1911-galloway:
Galloway is a district in the south-west of Scotland, made up of the counties of Kirkcudbright and Wigtown. The 1911 Britannica entry notes that the Romans knew the area as Novantia. Until the end of the 12th century it also took in Carrick, now the southern part of Ayrshire.

The name has no civil use, the entry says, but it is well established in history and local speech. The Bruces were lords of Galloway, and the earldom of Galloway, created in 1623, is held by a branch of the Stewarts. Galloway also names a well-known native breed of black, hornless cattle. For fuller treatment, readers are sent to the entries on Kirkcudbrightshire and Wigtownshire.
britannica-1911-glace-bay:
Glace Bay is a city and port of entry in Cape Breton county, Nova Scotia, Canada, on the Atlantic Ocean, 14 miles east of Sydney. The 1911 Britannica entry ties it to Sydney by both steam and electric railway. Its growth is coal growth: the population runs from 2,000 in 1892 to 6,945 in 1901 and 13,000 in 1906.

The town is the centre of the Dominion Coal Company's properties, founded in 1893, which produce most of the coal of Nova Scotia. It has a fair harbour of its own. Still, the entry notes, most shipping is done from Sydney in summer and from Louisburg in winter. The notice is a brief port entry built on the coal figures and the fast-rising population.
britannica-1911-green-bay:
Green Bay is a city of Wisconsin, county-seat of Brown county, at the south end of Green Bay where the Fox river meets it, 114 miles north of Milwaukee. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its population as 25,236 in 1910, up from 9,069 in 1890. Four railways, an inter-urban line, and lake and river steamers serve it.

The city stands on high level ground on both sides of the river. It holds the Kellogg Public Library, the county court house, and the earliest Roman Catholic bishopric in the North-west. A point of pride is the Tank Cottage, said to be Wisconsin's oldest house, built in 1766 by the French-Canadian voyageur Joseph Roy. The Green Bay Historical Society bought and moved it in 1908. The entry continues into the city's trade and its French and British past.
britannica-1911-hogmanay:
Hogmanay is the name in Scotland and parts of northern England for New Year's Eve, and also for the cake given to children then. On the morning of the 31st of December, children go in small bands from door to door. They sing a short rhyme asking for white bread, not grey, and beg small gifts or alms. The gift usually takes the form of an oaten cake.

Where the word comes from has been much disputed. Cotgrave in 1611 tied it to the cries of country folk begging New Year gifts. He linked it, through Norman French forms, to the old French aguilanneuf, read as au gui-l'an-neuf: to the mistletoe, the New Year. A French origin for the word may hold, but his detailed derivation is now rejected by philologists. The French word itself stays obscure.
britannica-1911-holiday:
A holiday was originally a holy day, a festival set apart for religious observance in memory of a sacred event or person. From that root it came to mean any day on which ordinary work stops. In the plural it also names a regular period away from work, as at schools. Public holidays, whose observance the state prescribes, are the account's main subject.

In England, saints' days no longer close government offices as they did at the start of the 19th century. Against that loss, four Bank Holidays are set by statute as general holidays, and the sovereign may proclaim others. Practice across the British colonies varies: Canada generally observes eight public holidays, from New Year's Day and Good Friday to Dominion Day and Labour Day. The trend noted is toward shorter hours and more regular rest.
britannica-1911-knight-daniel-ridgway:
Daniel Ridgway Knight (1845– ) was an American artist, born at Philadelphia in 1845. He studied at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris under Gleyre. Later he worked in the private studio of Meissonier. After 1872 he lived in France, with a house and studio at Poissy on the Seine. His paintings of peasant women out of doors won him great popular success.

Honours came from both sides of the Atlantic. At the Paris Exposition Universelle of 1889 he received the silver medal. He also took the cross of the Legion of Honour. In 1893 Munich made him a knight of the Royal Order of St Michael of Bavaria. In the same year he won the gold medal of honour of the Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts. His son, Ashton Knight, is also known as a landscape painter.
britannica-1911-lady-day:
Lady Day was originally the name for every day in the church calendar marking an event in the life of the Virgin Mary. The name is now restricted to the feast of the Annunciation, kept on the 25th of March each year.

In medieval and later times Lady Day opened the legal year in England. In 1752 the year's start was moved to the 1st of January, but the 25th of March remains one of the Quarter Days. In some districts old Lady Day, the 6th of April, is still the date for paying rent.
brotherly-love-shewing-that-as-merely-hu:
Mrs. Sherwood and her daughter Mrs. Streeten wrote a tale for the young, printed in 1851. Its full title warns that brotherly love, as a mere human tie, may not always hold. The first tale inside bears a plainer name: The Brothers, or Be Not Wise in Your Own Conceit.

Fall leaves open the tale. Mr. and Mrs. Mortimer get a letter from Portsmouth that calls for a face-to-face reply. One day's delay is too much. Packs are made in haste. One hard point stays: what of Marten and his small brother Reuben, left at home for the first time? Their mother owns her worry out loud. Marten hears more than he should from the next room. Home bonds, pride, and trust form the ground the tales till.
by-ways-of-bombay:
S. M. Edwardes wrote sketches of Bombay's inner life, first run in the Times of India. A pen name, Etonensis, hid his name in the paper. Edwardes served years as a state officer in the city. The first book run sold out in a month, by his note of June 1912.

No claim of deep study is made. Folk met and things seen in his years of work form the stock. Streets, trades, and faiths off the main roads give the book its name and plan. A second run adds plates by M. V. D. Taraporevala Sons put out that run. First-hand sight is the book's whole plea: a police-side view of a great port town, told in short, plain takes. Men and women of the byways, not kings or firms, fill its pages.
byways-around-san-francisco-bay:
W. E. Hutchinson wrote and drew a book of walks round San Francisco Bay, dated 1915. His wife, his dear yet stern judge, gets the book. Poems dot the frame: a sunset piece at the Golden Gate opens it, and bay, fall, and fence poems sit in the run.

Brook and waterfall, mount and vale, and cañon walks fill the first trips. Wild-cat Cañon and fall days come next. Camp fire tales and trout work in the Berkeley hills fill the heart. Beach, Muir Woods, and Chinatown spread the net. A glass-bottom boat, bay fog, and Meiggs' Wharf give the shore side. Moonlight, Mount Tamalpais, and Bear Creek close the list. His own plates show the road to Strawberry Cañon, trout pools, and old trees that have stood the storms of ages, by one plate's line.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-all-saints-da:
All Saints' Day, a solemnity on 1 November, honours all the saints, known and unknown, and, in Urban IV's words, supplies deficiencies in the year's celebration of saints' feasts. Its vigil is popularly called Hallowe'en. In the early Church Christians marked the anniversary of a martyr's death at the place of martyrdom. As martyrs multiplied under Diocletian, a separate day for each became impossible, so the Church appointed one common day.

The first trace appears at Antioch on the Sunday after Pentecost. It appears in St. Ephrem the Syrian's sermon in 373 and St. John Chrysostom's seventy-fourth homily in 407. At first the feast honoured only martyrs and St. John the Baptist, though the Chaldean Calendar already lists confessors in 411. In the West, Boniface IV consecrated the Pantheon to the Virgin and all the martyrs in 609 or 610. Gregory III fixed the anniversary for 1 November, and Gregory IV extended it Church-wide.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-all-souls-day:
All Souls' Day, the commemoration of the faithful departed, falls on 2 November, or on 3 November if the second is a Sunday or a solemnity. The clergy recite the Office of the Dead, and all Masses are Requiem Masses. Its basis is the doctrine that souls not perfectly cleansed, or not fully atoned, are barred from the Beatific Vision. The faithful on earth can aid them with prayers, alms, and especially the Mass.

Early Christians entered the departed's names in the diptychs. By the sixth century Benedictine monasteries commemorated their dead at Whitsuntide. Spain kept such a day before Sexagesima or Pentecost in Isidore's time. Germany, Widukind of Corvey testifies, prayed for the dead on 1 October. St. Odilo of Cluny ordered the annual commemoration in his monasteries, whence it spread among Benedictines and Carthusians. Liège adopted it first, under Bishop Notger. Otricus introduced it into Milan for 15 October.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-see-o:
Bergen covered the provinces Nordre and Sondre Bergenhus and Sondmor in Romsdal.
