The discovery at Selo in 996 of the remains of Saint Sunniva and her companions moved King Olaf Trygveson to build a church. Only in 1068 did King Olaf Kyrre found a bishopric and monastery at Selo. Bernard the Saxon served as first bishop. He later moved to the city of Bergen and died as first bishop about 1090.

In 1152 Bergen became suffragan to the metropolitan see of Trondhjem, with a cathedral chapter. Bishop Paul, from 1156 to 1194, saw Christ Church Cathedral finished. It hosted a provincial council and the coronation of King Magnus Erlingson in 1164, the first coronation of a Norwegian king. Sunniva's relics moved to the cathedral in 1170. In 1247 Cardinal Wilhelm of Sabina crowned King Haakon Haakonsson under Bishop Arne. King Magnus built a royal chapel between 1275 and 1302 to house a relic of the Crown of Thorns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ash-wednesday:
Ash Wednesday, the Wednesday after Quinquagesima Sunday, opens the Lenten fast. Its Latin name, dies cinerum, day of ashes, found in the Roman Missal and in the earliest copies of the Gregorian Sacramentary, probably dates from the eighth century at least. On that day, by ancient custom, all the faithful are urged to approach the altar before Mass begins. There the priest, dipping his thumb in blessed ashes, marks each forehead, or for clerics the tonsure place, with the cross.

He says the words, Remember, man, that thou art dust and unto dust thou shalt return. The ashes come from burning palms blessed on the previous year's Palm Sunday. Four ancient prayers bless them, they are sprinkled with holy water and scented with incense, and the celebrant himself, bishop or cardinal, receives ashes in turn. The entry explains a rite that opens Lent with dust.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bombay:
Bombay's archdiocese stretches from Bombay Island and Salsette far north to Quetta, though 200 miles of Damaun diocese cut it from its center. About 18,000 Catholics live under the archbishop, served by German Jesuits, native secular priests, and sisters teaching and doing charitable work across 24 churches and 25 chapels.

Portuguese settlers and Franciscans planted the island's churches from 1534, and the work continued after England took Bombay in 1665. Goanese clergy were expelled in 1720, and a double jurisdiction dispute, the Goan schism, long troubled the mission. Carmelites held the vicariate until 1854, Capuchins briefly followed, and by 1858 the whole Bombay-Poona mission lay with the German Jesuits.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-branch-sunday: Branch Sunday was a medieval English name for Palm Sunday, born from the shortage of palms for its rites. English churches used boughs of yew, willow, or other home-grown trees, and the day took their names, as Yew Sunday, or the general term Branch Sunday. The custom shows how a feast kept its shape while local trees stood in for palms from far away.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cantate-sunda:
Cantate Sunday is the name for the fourth Sunday after Easter. It comes from the first words of the Mass introit that day, Cantate Domino novum canticum, meaning sing to the Lord a new song. Like Gaudete and Laetare Sundays in Advent and Lent, the name comes from the chant that opens the liturgy.

Names of this kind probably date from the twelfth century and were common in the Middle Ages. They were used to mark dates in everyday business as well as in church life. John of Salisbury, Bishop of Chartres, who died in 1182, counts among the earliest writers known to use the name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cesar-egasse-:
César-Egasse du Boulay, known as Bulæus, was a French historian born early in the seventeenth century at Saint-Ellier in Mayenne and dying on 16 October 1678. After teaching humanities at the College of Navarre he rose to high posts in the University of Paris, serving as its rector and historian.

His main work, the Historia Universitatis Parisiensis, runs from the university's supposed foundation by Charlemagne in 800 down to 1600. The university censured its first three volumes, published in 1665. The king's censors, however, found nothing blameworthy, and the last three volumes appeared in 1673. The history matters for its many original documents, though its value suffers from the author's weak judgment and criticism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cyprien-tangu:
A life sketch follows Cyprien Tanguay, a priest of Quebec born in 1819 and dead in 1902, who became the great keeper of French Canadian family records. Ordained in 1843, he spent twenty-two years in parish work, notably at Rimouski, where he helped found the future diocesan seminary. His love of family history flowered after his 1867 post with the Dominion Statistics Department.

He then spent his life gathering parish and church records across Quebec, the Maritimes, Ontario, and old French towns in the United States, visiting France twice for the same task. His great book of French Canadian families, issued from 1871 to 1890 in seven huge volumes, lets every French Canadian trace forebears to old France. Flawed in places, it stays highly reliable and nearly unique, and Leo XIII gave him a prelature in 1887.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel-murray:
A biographical entry presents Daniel Murray, Archbishop of Dublin, born near Arklow in 1768. Schooled at home and at Salamanca, he was ordained in 1790 and served as curate in Dublin and Arklow. In 1798 soldiers shot his parish priest in bed, and Murray fled to Dublin to escape the same fate.

Made coadjutor bishop in 1809 at Archbishop Troy's request, he succeeded to Dublin in 1823, after a year as president of Maynooth College. An uncompromising foe of the veto and a firm backer of the Catholic Association, he backed Stanley's national education scheme and tolerated the Queen's Colleges, against Archbishop MacHale. He declined a Privy Council seat and died respected even by opponents.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-denis-jamay:
A life of Denis Jamay, a Franciscan Recollect who led the first missionary band to Canada. Chosen as provincial commissary in 1615, he sailed with Champlain, reached Tadoussac in May, and met native peoples at Sault Saint Louis. On 24 June 1615, at Rivière des Prairies, he said the first Mass of the new mission.

He sailed home in 1616 to press the colony's needs before the king and the Rouen Associates. Chosen commissary again in 1620, he returned with Champlain, urged Quebec settlers to obey the viceroy, and blessed the first regular Recollect convent, dedicated to Our Lady of the Angels. He went back to France in 1621 and died there in 1625.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-du-coudray:
Du Coudray was a French soldier born at Reims on 8 September 1738 who died at Philadelphia on 11 September 1777. Trained for the army, he shone as an engineer and served as adjutant-general of artillery, counted among the best military experts of France. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how in 1776 he volunteered to aid the American colonists against England. Silas Deane and Benjamin Franklin promised him a major-general's commission with command of the artillery.

That promise angered officers already in the army when he landed in May 1777 with twenty-nine officers and twelve artillery sergeants. Several threatened to resign, so a compromise made him inspector-general in August with major-general's rank. His grave is now unknown, the entry notes, closing a short American career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmund-and-jo:
Edmund Hay was a Scottish Jesuit and envoy to Mary Queen of Scots, born about 1540 and dead at Rome in 1591. In 1562 he went with Father Nicolas de Gouda on a mission from Pope Pius IV to Mary. Mary was then newly back in Scotland. Hay acted as go-between at their secret meeting at Holyrood. He also led a band of young Scots back to join the Society.

After study at Rome he served as confessor to the archduchesses at Innsbruck and later as rector of Clermont College in Paris, reporting to Rome on Scotland and its queen. The entry pairs him with his kinsman John Hay, a noted scholar and teacher who died at Pont-a-Mousson in 1608. Together they show Scots Catholics working from exile for a queen and a church under siege.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-family-of-har:
The Harlay were a French family of parliamentarians and bishops. Achille de Harlay, born in 1536, became first president of the Parlement of Paris. He stood against the League and endured imprisonment in the Bastille. His long career spanned the Wars of Religion and their troubled aftermath.

Achille de Sancy, born in 1581, served as ambassador to Constantinople. He later became an Oratorian and bishop of St-Malo in 1631. Scholars in 1904 named him editor of Richelieu's Memoires. Francois de Harlay, archbishop of Rouen, reformed the abbey of Jumieges and founded an academy at Gaillon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-lecl:
Francois Leclerc du Tremblay, better known as Pere Joseph, was born at Paris on 4 November 1577 and died at Rueil on 18 December 1638. He was a Capuchin friar who became Cardinal Richelieu's grey eminence. Through his kinsman the Constable de Montmorency he appeared at court at eighteen as Baron de Maffliers and served in Henry IV's armies against Spain. On 2 February 1599 he became a Capuchin novice and was provincial of Touraine in 1613. In 1616 he helped negotiate Loudun between Marie de Medicis and Conde's malcontents, giving Richelieu his first conference with Conde.

 As Richelieu's confidant he built French Capuchin missions in the East, ten by 1633, sending missionaries to Egypt, Abyssinia, and Morocco, though the last two ventures failed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-galloway:
Galloway, a diocese in southwest Scotland, claims the oldest church foundation in the country. It spans Dumfries, Kirkcudbright, Wigtown, and most of Ayr, some 3,347 square miles, with 373,670 people of whom Catholics form a small share. Its founder, Saint Ninian, a Briton schooled at Rome, set his see at Whithorn in 397 and named his church for Saint Martin of Tours.

Bede calls it Candida Casa, the White House, for its unusual stone build. The bishop list broke three times for about three hundred years each, and after the last Catholic bishop died in 1558 the see lay empty for 320 years. Leo XIII restored it in 1878 under John McLachlan, who swiftly gave the scattered, mostly laboring Catholics churches, schools, presbyteries, and clergy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaudete-sunda:
Gaudete Sunday, the third Sunday of Advent, takes its name from the Mass Introit's first word, Rejoice. Advent began as a forty-day fast after Saint Martin's feast, called Saint Martin's Lent, then shrank to four weeks by the ninth century and softened from fast to abstinence by the twelfth. Gregory the Great first ordered its Office, and Rome's Gregorian book gave Masses for its Sundays.

Like Mid-Lent's Laetare Sunday, Gaudete breaks a penitential season midway with signs of joy. Organ and flowers return, rose vestments replace purple, deacon and subdeacon resume dalmatic and tunicle, and cardinals wear rose. Its station falls at the Vatican basilica, and a new Invitatory hails not the Lord who is to come but the Lord now nigh at hand.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-day:
George Day, Bishop of Chichester, held the Catholic line through Henry, Edward, and Mary. Born in Shropshire about 1501 and graduated at Cambridge, he became Master of Saint John's in 1537 and provost of King's College in 1538. Consecrated bishop in 1543 by Cranmer, he defended altar doctrine in the Lords and voted against communion under both kinds and the new Prayer Book.

Day's preaching so stirred his diocese that in 1550 the Council sent Cox to counter it, then hauled Day in for refusing to tear down altars. He answered that he would rather suffer bodily than corrupt his soul, and for that contempt he sat in the Fleet and lost his see in 1551. Mary restored him at once as bishop and almoner, and Cardinal Pole confirmed him in 1555. He died in August 1556.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-hay:
George Hay, a Scottish bishop and writer born at Edinburgh in 1729, led the Lowland Catholics for nearly forty years. Bound for medicine, he tended the wounded after Prestonpans at sixteen, followed Charles Edward's army, and, after Culloden, spent twelve months in London custody. There a Catholic bookseller opened the faith to him, and he was received in December 1749.

Barred by penal laws from a medical degree, Hay took ship as a surgeon, met Bishop Challoner in London, and instead studied eight years at Rome's Scots College. Ordained in 1758, he became coadjutor in 1769 and bore the vicariate's whole burden. He printed Scotland's first English Catholic Bible and his Sincere, Devout, and Pious Christian of 1781 to 1786, still a standard work. He died in 1811.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-pray:
George Pray, an abbot, canon, and librarian born in 1723, wrote Hungary's early history from its sources. His Tyrolese family settled him at Pozsony, and he entered the Society of Jesus in 1745, studying at Vienna and Nagy-Szombat. Ordained in 1754, he taught across Hungary and at Vienna's Theresianum, tutoring the Salm princesses and lecturing on political science and moral theology.

At the Jesuits' suppression in 1773, Maria Theresa made Pray imperial historiographer at four hundred florins a year. He ran Buda's university library from 1777, surrendering his manuscripts and documents to it in 1784 for a life annuity. He became canon of Grosswardein in 1790 and abbot of Tormowa. Pray first drew notice to Hungary's oldest coherent text, the Funeral Oration of about 1199, called the Pray Codex after him. His Annals of Hungarian kings fill five volumes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-good-friday:
Good Friday is the day in Holy Week on which the Church keeps the anniversary of the Crucifixion of Jesus Christ. In the Roman Missal it is called Feria VI in Parasceve, in the Greek liturgy the Holy and Great Friday, and in German Charfreitag, Sorrowful Friday. It is one of the two oldest feasts in the calendar. A Catholic Encyclopedia article calls its office the most peculiar, composite, and dramatic in the liturgy.

Parasceve, meaning preparation, first named the sixth day's preparation for the Sabbath. By metonymy it then named the day itself. Irenaeus and Tertullian called the day the Pasch, though later writers distinguished the Pascha of death from the Pascha of resurrection. The origin of Good is unclear: some derive it from God's Friday, others from the German Gute Freitag, and the Anglo-Saxons sometimes called it Long Friday.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-saturday:
Holy Saturday, once called Great Saturday, the Angelic Night, and the Vigil of Easter, closes Lent and opens paschal time. It is no longer a day of pure joy like Maundy Thursday, but one where joy and sadness mix. By a notable exception, the early church allowed fasting on this Saturday alone, and the fast was severe: from Irenaeus onward, an absolute fast held for the forty hours before Easter.

The Easter vigil itself shifted strangely over time. In the first six or seven centuries ceremonies ran through the whole night, so the Alleluia met the dawn of Resurrection day. In the eighth century they moved to Saturday afternoon, and later, by a singular anachronism, to Saturday morning. The entry follows those changes in hours, fasting, and rite.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-martiana:
Jean Martianay, a French Maurist Benedictine born in 1647 at Saint-Sever and dead in Paris in 1717, gave his life to the Bible. His order's annals praise his Greek and Hebrew learning. He spent over thirty years searching French libraries, above all for Jerome's works.

Martianay begged every Benedictine abbey to aid a full critical edition of Jerome, and, save for the Hieronymian Vulgate done with Pouget, he finished the vast task alone. He taught Scripture at Arles, Bordeaux, and Carcassonne. He wrote on inspiration against Richard Simon, defended the Hebrew text and Vulgate chronology, and treated the canon's history and French Bible versions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-barclay:
John Barclay was a Latin novelist and satirist whose Argenis became one of the most read political novels of its age. Born at Pont-a-Mousson in 1582, son of the jurist William Barclay, he was schooled by the Jesuits and published a commentary on Statius at nineteen. He tried his fortune in London under James I, published his Satyricon in Paris, and wrote poems and an account of the Gunpowder Plot.

His 1609 edition of his father's work denying the pope's temporal power over princes drew Bellarmine and others into a long controversy, sharpened by his 1611 Apology attacking the Jesuits. Invited to Rome by Paul V in 1616, he was pensioned by the pope, published a plea to sectaries in 1617, and finished Argenis in July 1621, dying the next month. Contemporaries admired his honesty and rare courtesy, and his friend Thorie wrote his elegy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-o-kane-m:
John O'Kane Murray was an Irish-American physician and popular historian of American Catholicism. Born in County Antrim in 1847, he came with his parents to New York in 1856 and studied at Saint John's College, Fordham. He took his medical degree in New York and practiced in Brooklyn until 1880. He spent his last five years fighting the tuberculosis that killed him at Chicago in 1885.

A constant contributor to the Catholic press, he compiled books that found wide readership and always exerted a good influence. They were a Popular History of the Catholic Church in the United States in 1876 and Poets and Poetry of Ireland in 1877. The list continues with Catholic Heroes and Heroines in 1878, Little Lives of Great Saints in 1879, Catholic Pioneers of America in 1881, and Lessons in English Literature in 1883. He also revised Kearney's General History and had begun the same work on Lingard's England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jubilate-sund:
Jubilate Sunday is the third Sunday after Easter in the Catholic liturgy. Its name comes from the first word of the Mass Introit, Jubilate Deo omnis terra, shout joyfully to God, all the earth, from Psalm 65. With the two Sundays that follow, it carries on the Church's song of joy in the Resurrection through Paschaltide.

During Eastertide, Alleluia joins every antiphon, responsory, and versicle of Office and Mass. The Jubilate Introit invites all to joy. The Epistle urges the faithful, above all penitents and the newly baptized, to obey lawful powers and live as worthy disciples of the risen Christ. The Gospel counsels patience under life's trials for the sake of heaven.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-judica-sunday:
Judica Sunday is the fifth Sunday of Lent, better known as Passion Sunday. Its name comes from the Introit's opening words, Judica me, Deus, judge me, O God, from Psalm 42. In Germany it is called Black Sunday from the veiling of crosses and statues, once done at the Gospel words Jesus hid himself.

On this day the Judica psalm drops from the start of Mass until Easter, and the Gloria is omitted to mark the shame of Christ's Passion, when his glory seemed laid aside. The whole Office and Mass turn solemn, preparing for Holy Week. Rome once kept the day's station at the Vatican Basilica.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-laetare-sunda:
Laetare Sunday, the fourth or middle Sunday of Lent, takes its name from the Mass introit Laetare Jerusalem, Rejoice, O Jerusalem. Early Lent began after Quinquagesima with only thirty-six fast days, until four days were added to make forty.

Strictly the Thursday before is Lent's midpoint, once marked as such, but signs of joy meant to hearten penitents moved to the Sunday. Flowers deck the altar, the organ sounds at Mass and Vespers, rose vestments replace purple, and deacon and subdeacon wear dalmatics rather than folded chasubles. Rome's station stood at St. Croce in Gerusalemme, the Golden Rose was blessed then, and the day also passed as Refreshment Sunday, Mid-Lent, and Mothering Sunday.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lettice-mary-:
Lettice Mary Tredway, called Lady Tredway (1595-1677), was Sir Walter Tredway's daughter. In July 1616 she entered the novitiate at Sin, near Douai, of the Lateran Canonesses Regular of Notre-Dame-de-Beaulieu. In October 1617 she made solemn profession. In 1631 she and Father Carre planned a house for English canonesses only at Douai.

 In 1634 it was settled to open this English convent at Paris, with Dr. Smith, Bishop of Chalcedon, exiled in Paris, helped so generously he counts as co-founder. He blessed her as abbess, and Notre-Dame-de-Sion was firmly set up in the Rue des Fosses in 1639. They also practically founded the Seminary of St. Gregory for the English Mission.  She stayed abbess till 1675, when infirmity forced her to resign.  For forty-one years she laboured bravely for her convent, and the community, forced to leave France, now stands at Ealing in England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-low-sunday:
Low Sunday is the first Sunday after Easter, named, it seems, for its contrast with the great feast just past. As the octave day of Easter it still belongs to that feast, though in a lower degree.

Its liturgical name, Dominica in albis depositis, recalls the newly baptized, who on this day first laid aside their white robes, a custom Augustine already mentions. Writers also call it Pascha clausum, the close of Easter week, and Quasimodo Sunday, from its Mass introit, Quasi modo geniti infantes, a name still common in France and Germany.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ludger-duvern:
Ludger Duvernay was a French-Canadian journalist and patriot, born at Vercheres in 1799 and dead in 1852. A printer by trade, he founded papers at Three Rivers and Quebec, then La Minerve at Montreal in 1827 with Morin, a leading voice of French Canada.

Jailed in 1832 for protesting the Legislative Council with Tracey, he won a medal for public devotion. His lasting deed was founding the Society of St. John the Baptist in 1834, choosing the Precursor as patron, the maple leaf as emblem, and the motto Our language, our institutions, and our laws. Exiled for the 1837 rebellions, he returned to revive La Minerve under responsible government.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maria-cosway:
Maria Cosway was a miniature painter, born at Florence in 1759 and dead at Lodi in 1838. Her maiden name was Hadfield, her father an Englishman. She drew with great talent young, and at nineteen joined Florence's Academy of Fine Arts, where Visitation nuns had schooled her. Her father died in 1778, and Angelica Kauffman brought her to England.

There she married Richard Cosway, a leading miniature painter, in London in 1781. She showed at the Academy until 1801, though her mythological oils won less praise than her miniatures and copies of her husband's work. Her London Sunday concerts drew notice from Horace Walpole. At Cardinal Fesch's urging she opened a girls' school at Lyons, closed by war in 1811, then founded one at Lodi in 1812. She bought its buildings, joined its community to the Dames Inglesi, and gave her life and fortune to the school. Emperor Francis I made her a baroness in 1834.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maundy-thursd:
Maundy Thursday, also called Holy Thursday, solemnly marks the founding of the Eucharist and stands as the oldest rite peculiar to Holy Week. In early Rome the day gathered extra ceremonies: the blessing of the holy oils and the welcome back of penitents. Both were practical steps ahead of Easter, when candidates finished their preparation. The day's central Mass, the Missa chrismalis, blessed oils for the year ahead.

Custom varied by place: Rome kept everything in daylight, while Africa held the Eucharist after the evening meal to mirror the Last Supper more closely. A Carthage canon excused the faithful from fasting before Communion that day, since bathing and fasting were deemed at odds. Augustine notes that some churches offered the oblation twice, morning and evening. The entry thus opens a window on how the early Church shaped its holiest week.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-melleray:
Melleray, in Brittany's Loire-Inferieure and the Diocese of Nantes near Chateaubriand, was founded about 1134. Foulques, Abbot of Pontron in Anjou, sent monks from Loroux, a daughter of Citeaux, to plant a monastery in Brittany. They loved the solitude of a spot near Old Melleray, shown by Rivallon, pastor of Auverne, and given by owner Alain de Moisdon. Guitern, first abbot, raised the monastery in 1145, but the church was finished only in 1183 under Geffroy, the fourth abbot.

Built for about twelve religious, Melleray stayed regular until wealth and commendatory abbots loosened discipline in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Etienne de Breze in 1544 was the first commendatory abbot. Decline lasted until late in the seventeenth century, when Dom Jouard restored St. Bernard's rule and the buildings. Suppressed in 1791, its few religious scattered, yet Melleray lived on through Trappists sheltered at Val Sainte in Switzerland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-melo-uruguay:
Melo, a planned diocese in Uruguay, was decided in 1897 as one of two sees suffragan to Montevideo, but political causes have so far blocked all appointments. Talks to renew diplomatic ties between the Republic and the Holy See are under way. Since state recognition of the new dioceses is a condition of resumption, approval will probably come shortly. The diocese is to take in Uruguay's north-east.

Its bounds will cover, in whole or part, Cerro Largo, Rivera, Tacuarembo, and Treinta y Tres. The area runs some 19,600 square miles. Barely 145,000 people lived there in 1906, practically all Catholic. The land is very fertile, yet farming is slight, since most people, largely Brazilians, breed cattle. Melo town, founded in 1796, is Cerro Largo's capital with about 7,000 souls, near the Tacuari River some 315 miles north of Montevideo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-natal-day:
A natal day, from Latin natalis and natalicium, is what we call a birthday, the anniversary of the day a man was born. Greek genesia and genethlios served the same use. In both tongues the primitive sense widened even before Christianity. Latin natalis sometimes meant little more than anniversary, and covered the emperor's accession day as well as his birthday.

Games held on an emperor's birthday in life often continued after his deification on that anniversary, as if he still lived. Greek genesia often marked the annual commemoration of a dead person by sacrifices and rites, held on his birthday rather than his death day. When Smyrna's Christians about 150 described gathering Polycarp's bones, they spoke of meeting in gladness on his natal day. From that usage grew the church's feast of a martyr's heavenly birthday, his death day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-new-year-s-da:
New Year's Day opens with the word year, etymologically the same as hour, signifying a going or movement, while in Semitic tongues year means repetition of the sun's course. Since the year's circle has no necessary starting point, nations and epochs chose widely different New Year dates. Spring's opening was a natural beginning, and the Bible links the year's start closely with seasons.

The ancient Roman year began in March, but Julius Caesar, correcting the calendar in 46 BC, made January the first month. Christian nations universally adopted that custom, though September through December, the seventh through tenth months, recall March's start. Christian writers and councils condemned the Saturnalia's heathen orgies at year's beginning, and Tertullian rebuked Christians treating strenae gifts as mere friendly tokens. The entry follows later customs and church observance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-norway:
Norway, the western half of the Scandinavian peninsula, rises in high plateaus cut by deep fjords along the Atlantic. Mountains like Snähätten and Galdhöppigen tower over valleys, lakes like Mjøsen spread inland, and islands offshore feed shipping and fishing, with twenty million cod a year from Lofoten alone.

Oats and barley, not wheat, make the daily bread, cattle and sheep number in the millions, and Lapps herd over a hundred thousand reindeer in the north. The entry moves from land and livelihood to church history, missions, and the Catholic life of a Lutheran kingdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-our-lady-of-a:
Our Lady of Ambronay is a sanctuary of the Blessed Virgin at Ambronay in France, counted one of the two candles of devotion to Our Lady in the Diocese of Belley. Recluses founded the first church in the seventh century. Saracens destroyed it, and Saint Barnard rebuilt it about 803, together with the famed monastery of the same name.

Mid-thirteenth-century rebuilding gave the church a grander scale. It still stands, despite the ravages of 1793, as a grand diocesan landmark. Its windows, sacristy, altar, and spiral stair draw notice, and the facade of one nave dates from the ninth century. Pilgrims have long sought the shrine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-palm-sunday:
Palm Sunday, the sixth and last Sunday of Lent, opens Holy Week and ranks so high that no commemoration of any kind is allowed in its Mass. In common law it starts the Easter duty season. The Roman Missal sets its station at Saint John Lateran, where the pope led the rites before September 1870. Greeks keep the day with great solemnity, calling it the Sunday of the branches, or Lazarus Sunday, for Lazarus's raising the day before.

Latin books name it Sunday in Palms, or Hosanna Sunday, from the crowd's cry in the procession. Since every great feast recalled the resurrection and bore the name Pascha, it also won names like flowery Easter, and Florida took its name from this day in 1512. Blessing flowers woven among palms gave it the name Flower Sunday, known in England, Germany, and Slav lands alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paraguay:
Paraguay is a landlocked republic of South America, free from Spain and independent since 1811. Its name is debated: some read it as river of the Payagua tribe, from Payagua plus the Guarani word for water, while others prefer crowned river, from palm-crown plus water. The country spans about 196,000 square miles in South America's heart, bounded by Brazil, Argentina, and Bolivia.

The Paraguay River splits it into the Oriental region, Paraguay proper, and the Occidental Chaco. Its people, 805,000 by the 1908 census, mix Indians, white Europeans, few Blacks, and their offspring, with Spanish-Indian stock dominant, and nearly 700,000 are Catholics. Later pages trace its missions, wars, church provinces, and the Jesuit reductions that shaped its early Catholic life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-passion-sunda:
Passion Sunday, the fifth Sunday of Lent, ranks first class and bars any feast, whatever its rank, while allowing commemorations of feasts not transferred. The Missal calls it Sunday of the Passion, the Breviary Sunday of the Passion, and Durandus and other writers call it simply Passion, or Passion of the Lord. It also bears the name Judica Sunday, from its introit's first word.

Other names mark its place: Isti sunt, from Matins' first response; Octava mediana, as eighth day after Laetare, or middle of Lent; and Repus, short for repositus, hidden, from veiling the crosses. Slavs call it painful, sorrowful, deaf, quiet, deadly, or black Sunday, a name also found in Germany as Black Sunday. After it the Greek Church urges sharper penance, holding up penitent Mary of Egypt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrick-murra:
Patrick Murray was an Irish theologian born at Clones in County Monaghan on 18 November 1811 and dead at Maynooth College on 15 November 1882. Schooled at Clones, he entered Maynooth on 25 August 1829, the year of Catholic emancipation, among its first emancipated class. He passed with high distinction and was elected a Dunboyne senior student in June 1835.

Toward the Dunboyne course's end he took a Dublin curacy in Francis Street, winning fame as a zealous worker and eloquent preacher. After competitive examinations he became Maynooth professor of English and French in 1838, then professor of theology in 1841. The rest of his life went to theological science, and in 1879 he became prefect of the Dunboyne house. His books include Essays Chiefly Theological, De Ecclesia Christi, De Gratia, and a treatise on marriage impediments.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-guilla:
Pierre Guillaume Frédéric Le Play was a French economist and social reformer, born at La Rivière in Calvados on 11 April 1806. Raised by a poor widowed mother, he studied at Havre College, then science at Paris's Polytechnic and School of Mines. He became secretary of the Annales des mines and professor of metallurgy at the School of Mines in 1840.

Each year he travelled six months, questioning traders, workmen, owners, and peasants across Europe. From 1833 to 1855 he invented and perfected his method of studying families and societies; from 1855 to 1882 he expounded his doctrine. His Ouvriers européens, whose second edition of 1877 to 1879 forms a compendium of Europe's social history, argues that prosperous nations rest on the Decalogue and public worship. Testamentary freedom, employers' patronage, freedom of instruction, and decentralization matter too. Napoleon III made him commissary-general of the 1867 Universal Exposition. He died at Paris in 1882.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reductions-of:
The Jesuit Reductions of Paraguay rank among the most singular and beautiful creations of Catholic missionary work. This long encyclopedia entry says they have done more than any other factor to fix Paraguay's name in history, drawing admiration and criticism. Their founding and plan make sense only against Spanish colonial conditions in the La Plata region.

That country, discovered in 1515 by Juan Díaz de Solís, was conquered only slowly, in bloody and at first disastrous battles with warlike, liberty-loving tribes. By 1590 Spaniards had founded ten cities and forty colonies, subduing the natives by force. Later pages test legends of Jesuit wealth against hard figures, showing claims of vast yerba harvests and 300,000 Indian workers as pure fancy against the real numbers. The 1787 expulsion inventories and the traveller Von der Steinen, who called the expulsion a blow from which the natives never recovered, close the account.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sainte-anne-d:
Sainte Anne d'Auray, a village three miles from Auray in Brittany, is famed for its shrine and pilgrimages, called pardons, in honour of Saint Anne. When the Bretons first became Christian they dedicated a chapel to her, destroyed near the end of the seventh century, yet the village kept the name Keranna, village of Anne. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia traces a devotion revived by visions.

In 1624 and 1625 Anne is said to have appeared several times to the villager Yves Nicolazic, bidding him rebuild the ancient chapel. Witnesses spoke so widely that the bishop of Vannes inquired, heard Nicolazic and many others, and allowed the building. Pilgrims have streamed there ever since, and the entry shows how a peasant's visions remade a whole countryside's religious map.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-john-char:
John Charles Day, jurist born near Bath in 1826, died at Newbury on 13 June 1908. He was schooled at Rome and Fribourg, then with the Benedictines at Downside, who prepared him to graduate with honors at London University and to shine at the Bar. Called to the Middle Temple in 1849, he took silk in 1872, became a Bencher in 1873. He rose to the Queen's Bench in 1882 with a knighthood, resigned in 1901, and became a Privy Councillor in 1902.

His first ten years at the Bar were a constant struggle, until his book on Common Law Procedure Acts brought fame and fortune. As a judge his severe sentences, above all for crimes of violence, made him the terror of evildoers, who nicknamed him Day of Reckoning and Judgment Day. He was also a noted art connoisseur, owning one of England's best Barbizon collections. He served on the Parnell Special Commission.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sunday:
Sunday, the Day of the Sun, takes its name from Egyptian astrology, and this entry follows the day from planet lore to Christian worship. Seven planets each ruled an hour of the day, and the planet ruling the first hour gave the day its name. Rome took the seven-day week from Egypt in the first and second centuries, and Teutonic peoples renamed the days for their own gods, turning dies Solis into Sunday.

For Christians the first day of the week, the day of resurrection, gradually replaced the Jewish Sabbath as the day of public worship. Acts, Corinthians, and Revelation show first-day gatherings for the Eucharist, the Didache commands Lord's Day assembly, and Justin first calls the day Sunday while describing early worship. Later sections cover rest laws for workmen in modern Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thanksgiving-:
Thanksgiving Day is a civil holiday observed yearly in the United States on the last Thursday in November, now the fourth Thursday. The president proclaims it a day of national thanksgiving and prayer, and state governors concur, suspending public business. The custom began in 1621, when Governor Bradford of Plymouth appointed a day of praise and prayer after the first harvest, spreading through New England colonies.

The first national observance came when Washington, at Congress's request, recommended Thursday, 26 November 1789, as a day of public thanksgiving and prayer. It acknowledged God's favours and besought pardon, religion, virtue, and prosperity. New York first noticed the day officially in 1817, and by 1859 twenty-eight states and two territories observed it. Lincoln's 1863 proclamation named the last Thursday of November, followed by Johnson in 1867 and Grant in 1870, with no change since. Catholic recognition by special features came only recently and was not yet general in 1911.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trinity-sunda:
The first Sunday after Pentecost, instituted to honour the Most Holy Trinity. Early Christians set aside no special day or Office for the Trinity. As Arianism spread, the Fathers prepared an Office with canticles, responses, a Preface and hymns for recital on Sundays.

Alexander II refused a petition for a special feast, saying the Roman Church daily honoured the Trinity, though he did not forbid it where it already existed. John XXII ordered the feast for the whole Church on the first Sunday after Pentecost, using a new Office by the Franciscan John Peckham, later Archbishop of Canterbury. Pius X raised it to a primary feast of the first class in 1911.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-uruguay:
Uruguay, the Oriental Republic, is the smallest independent state in South America, stretching from latitude 30 to 35 degrees south and longitude 53 to 58 degrees west. It lies south of Brazil's Rio Grande do Sul and east of the River Uruguay, hence its old Spanish name Banda Oriental. Its bounds run along the Uruguay river in the west, the Río de la Plata for 425 miles in the south, the Atlantic for 200 miles, and Lago Mirim toward Brazil.

The northern boundary, 450 miles long, was settled by treaty with Brazil on 15 May 1852. The entry describes the country's geography, its people, its government, and its church history, from Spanish colonial days through independence and civil war to the modern republic. It closes with the church's dioceses, clergy, and schools, a full portrait of a small nation between two great neighbours.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vaux-de-cerna:
Vaux-de-Cernay was a famed Cistercian abbey in the Diocese of Versailles, in the old Isle-de-France. In 1118 Simon de Neauffle and his wife Eve gave land to the monks of Savigny for a monastery honouring the Mother of God and St John the Baptist. Blessed Vital, Abbot of Savigny, accepted the gift and sent monks under Arnaud, their first abbot. Nobles soon added further gifts to the young community.

Once settled, the abbey drew many postulants, allowing the founding of Breuil-Benoît in 1137 in the Diocese of Évreux. In 1148 Vaux-de-Cernay, with the whole Savigny congregation, joined the Cistercian Order. The entry follows its abbots, its famous preacher Guy, its part in the Albigensian crusade, and its later fortunes to suppression in the Revolution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-william-w:
William Way, alias May or Flower, was a priest executed at Kingston-on-Thames in September 1588. Born in the Exeter diocese, in Devon or Cornwall, he received tonsure at Reims in 1584 and was ordained at Laon in 1586. He set out for England that December and by June 1587 was committed to the Clink prison.

Indicted at Newgate in September 1588 merely for being a priest, he refused trial by a secular judge. The Bishop of London was summoned, but Way would acknowledge neither him as bishop nor the queen as head of the Church, and was condemned at once. Much given to fasting and austerity, he had wept when others were tried before him, fearing he had offended God, and rejoiced when his own turn came. He was hanged, disembowelled, and quartered.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vicomte-de-fa:
Frédéric Alfred Pierre, Vicomte de Falloux du Coudray, was a French statesman who lived from 1811 to 1885. Two women shaped him most, his mother, who had been at Louis XVI's court, and Madame Swetchine, whose life and letters he later published. His first books marked him as a man of unbending principle.

Within a decade this staunch monarchist served under President Louis Bonaparte and ranked among the Liberal Catholics, taking advantage of opportunities as his practical maxim. Elected deputy for Segré in 1846 on a legitimist platform and to the Constituent Assembly in 1848 for Maine-et-Loire. He helped Catholic members elect Buchez president. As mouthpiece of the committee investigating the national workshops, he proposed their abolition, a measure followed by the bloody June insurrection.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-barcl:
William Barclay was a Scottish lawyer who defended the rights of kings in books read across Europe. Born in 1546, he died at Angers in France in 1608. Of Aberdeenshire stock, he studied at Aberdeen, then at Paris and Bourges among Catholic Scots youth in France. In 1578 the Duke of Lorraine gave him the civil law chair at the new University of Pont-à-Mousson, as law dean and councillor of state.

De Regno et Regali Potestate of 1600 answered Buchanan and others on royal power, and Locke later weighed its doctrines at length. After twenty-five years he quit his chair in 1603 and sought favour from James I in England. He spurned a rich post tied to renouncing his faith and went back to France. Angers then gave him its vacant law chair, and his posthumous De Potestate Papae of 1609 drew a reply from Bellarmine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-court:
William Courtenay was Archbishop of Canterbury from 1381 until his death in 1396, a firm foe of the Lollards. Born near Exeter about 1342, son of Hugh Courtenay, Earl of Devon, he studied at Oxford, took a doctorate in civil law, and won election as university chancellor in 1367. After prebends at Exeter, Wells, and York, he became Bishop of Hereford in 1370 and of London in 1375.

Courtenay backed the Prince of Wales and Bishop Wykeham against John of Gaunt's anti-clerical drive, and pressed Parliament and councils against Wyclif's followers. He cited Wyclif at Saint Paul's, where Gaunt's presence broke the court into confusion, and later councils condemned Lollard views. As archbishop he also held the kingdom's chancellorship briefly in 1382 before resigning it after three months.
chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-435-volu:
Seven hundred cows at a Glasgow distillery, fed on grain refuse and milking for the city, show economy at work in the opening pages of number 435, dated May 1, 1852. Chambers's Edinburgh Journal follows the draff to the dairy and the dung to an added farm, then faults the wasted liquid manure, under a heading about forced benefits.

Monsieur Jerome and the Russian princess carry the fiction, and memoirs of Lord Jeffrey the literary interest. A moonlight ride, the gold-fever in Australia, and burgomaster law in Prussia range widely. Traces of Danes and Norwegians in England, children kept in prisons, and Jupiter as an evening star close the number. Gratuitous services get the last word.
chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-436-volu:
Concert advertisements from April to August fill a newspaper column. The musical season leads number 436, dated May 8, 1852. Quartet parties sit beside philharmonic giants. Every taste from ballads to madrigals finds a club. Music, the piece shows, had become London's spring industry.

The tallow-tree of China promises vegetable fat from a seed. A tollman's story, Cardinal Mezzofanti the great linguist, and curiosities of posthumous charity follow. Lord Rosse's discoveries turn eyes to the telescope, while South-African reptiles keep other eyes on the ground. Labour standing on golden feet, extreme minuteness under the microscope, and a set of verses complete the mixture.
chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-437-volu:
London's crossing-sweepers, once men of capital who died rich and left legacies, now scrape a poorer living: number 437, dated May 15, 1852, opens with their fallen trade. Chambers's Edinburgh Journal remembers when a foot of mud filled every channel and a good crossing was a fortune, and measures what paving took away.

Insect wings get close scientific attention, and rustication in a French village gives the travel piece. Phantoms of the Far East carry the marvellous, while a decimal system of weights and measures argues reform. Two short tales, The Little Gray Gossip and The Wet Shroud, close the fiction side. The number moves from street mud to fairy tale in sixteen pages.
chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-438-volu:
Babies do not truly laugh, argues the philosophy of laughter in number 438, dated May 22, 1852. A child's laugh expresses triumph or scorn. The light-hearted laugh of children is a fond mistake. Chambers's Edinburgh Journal watches nursery sports, grave as housekeeping, to prove how late real amusement arrives.

A tale called The Counter-Stroke and an attack on the taxes on knowledge follow in earnest. The vegetation of Europe is surveyed, and a half-pennyworth of navigation shows how far small money goes at sea. A London newspaper of 1667 and a scene in Boston look backward and outward. Mrs. Newton Crosland's Tongue of Fire ends the number in a devotional key.
chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-439-volu:
Reasoning itself is on trial in number 439, dated May 29, 1852. Its heading is Therefore and Because. A quoted view holds that women feel a truth while men calculate it. The essay calls that pretty account too easy. Chambers's Edinburgh Journal argues for one reasoning mind, examined with common care, in its lead piece.

David's last picture turns to art and age. Summer lodgings begin the season's practical worries, and paper-money and banking in China explain a distant system in plain terms. Things talked of in London, a meditation in expectation of death signed Constantia, and a piece simply headed Water follow. A lottery of death and a man for the world close the month of May.
demetrius-a-play:
Friedrich Schiller's Demetrius is an unfinished historical play about the pretender who claimed the Russian throne. It opens in the great senate hall at Cracow. The Polish Diet sits in state beneath the escutcheons of Poland and Lithuania, with bishops, palatines, castellans and armed deputies in their places.

The Archbishop of Gnesen declares the tempestuous Diet closed in peace, the nobles consenting to disarm while the king pledges redress of just complaints. Into this settlement steps Demetrius, whose claim threatens to reopen war and ambition. Schiller's fragment breaks off before the story resolves, but its opening scenes show his late mastery of political drama. Readers of Schiller will value Demetrius as a powerful torso, not a finished play.
dennison-grant-a-novel-of-to-day:
Robert Stead set his novel Dennison Grant in the ranching foothills of western Canada, calling it a novel of to-day. Contractor Transley opens the story, moving his haying outfit to the Y D ranch after losing other work. Transley is able, restless, and hungry for money and power. Dennison Grant works as foreman on the neighboring Landson ranch.

Grant holds views far from Transley's creed of getting ahead. He talks with a ranch visitor about reorganizing society and sharing wealth more fairly. Work, accidents, and courtship bring the two men's worlds together. Stead uses hay fields, roundups, and valley ranches as the stage for a clash between raw ambition and a gentler social ideal, told in the plain speech of the foothills country.
doe-osti-2997919-multi-gigawatt-electric:
Solar Synergies' final technical report on award DE-EE0011021, led by Marvin Keshner, covers an October 2023 to May 2025 project on a new kind of power line. The design buries the conductors: fat aluminum beams run close together inside a concrete tunnel about 11 feet high and 11 feet wide, instead of thin wires on tall towers. Bigger conductor cross-section means more power with less loss.

For the same cost per mile, the 230 kilovolt alternating current version carries 1.2 gigawatts, about 4.5 times a conventional double-circuit line of the same voltage. Beam cross-section is 12.5 times that of two one-inch wires, and losses over 200 miles fall to 1.8 percent against 5 percent. Beams hang from strings of four standard ceramic insulators rated 34.5 kilovolts each. A full concrete tunnel was out of scope for this phase, and a tent cover was rejected over snow load worries.
doe-osti-3023347-ground-effects-of-the-2:
Yue Chen, Kyoung Ho Kim, Steven K Morley, and Jesse R Woodroffe of Los Alamos National Laboratory analyze what the May 2024 Mother's Day superstorm did at ground level. Their report is LA-UR-26-21645, issued March 16, 2026. Geomagnetic storms drive currents in power lines and pipelines, called geomagnetically induced currents. This storm was among the strongest in decades, so its ground record is a useful stress test.

The team combined observations from many sources and checked timing against interplanetary shock fronts that arrived and passed during the event. Large current swings lined up with the intervals of sharp geomagnetic index changes. A location comparison pulls in a monitored device in the United States, New Zealand readings adapted from a Transpower report, and simulated current levels for United Kingdom sites.
doe-osti-3028534-electrify-monterey-bay:
Central Coast Energy Services ran Electrify Monterey Bay under Weatherization Assistance Program award DE-EE0010267, an enhancement and innovation grant, with Julie Garcia and Laura Diaz directing the project. The program brought weatherization and electrification upgrades to households around Monterey Bay, on California's central coast. Its reporting stresses who was reached, not just how many homes were treated.

Demographic tables count the people served: 207 household members in all. Seniors over sixty numbered 63, people with disabilities 41, homes with children 85, and Native American households 4. The authors argue that aiming at these groups steers program money toward residents most exposed to extreme temperatures, rising energy costs, and housing conditions that can harm health. The upgrades also bought comfort and safer living conditions alongside energy savings.
doe-osti-3366238-science-amp-technology-:
The April/May 2026 issue of Science & Technology Review, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory's magazine, honors the lab's 2025 R&D 100 Award winners. Four Livermore technologies took awards, bringing the laboratory's total to 186. Feature articles explain each winner for a general audience: monolithic telescopes, a flexible imaging diffraction diagnostic for laser experiments, an in-air drop encapsulation apparatus, and a metaoptics nanolithography platform.

One story shows the device making microcapsules with living cells inside that survived storage, in under a second from nozzle to dry capsule. Other features cover a brain-on-a-chip milestone and fiber-optic cable that measures ground motion. The magazine, published eight times a year, translates weapons-lab research into plain accounts for Congress, partners, and the public.
doe-osti-3488008-scalable-high-throughpu:
Stanford closes award DE-EE0010227 with a final report on open-air spray-plasma making of solid-state lithium batteries. Reinhold H. Dauskardt led the project. The project ran from October 1, 2022 to September 30, 2025. Open-air, high-throughput coating could cut battery factory costs.

One design coats a nanocrystalline LCO cathode layer on platinum-coated silicon. LLZO electrolyte then fills pores to form a dense joined structure. Full cells with plasma-cured electrolyte were cycled to prove the build works. Battery makers gain a spray route that skips costly vacuum chambers for solid-state cells entirely.
dorothy-dale-a-girl-of-to-day:
Dorothy Dale, a Girl of To-Day, by Margaret Penrose, opens a girls' series built around a lively heroine and her friend Tavia. Penrose gives Dorothy a public honor in the first chapter: she will be Daughter of the Regiment, and the day begins with fog, flags, and a rush not to be late. The series list promises school stories to follow, starting with Dorothy Dale at Glenwood School.

Twenty seven chapters carry Dorothy through a strange adventure, a clew, and a soldier's daughter, then into schoolyard trouble with Squire Sanders. Later headings promise apple blossom magic, an unprovoked attack, a secret, a queer picnic, and Dorothy in politics, where the girls have it their way. Danger, a surprise trip, and an emergency case test her courage before the close. The book sells energy and nerve as a modern girl's equipment.
dotty-dimple-at-play:
Sophie May wrote Dotty Dimple at Play in 1868 for the youngest readers, and she gave the book to the blind children of the asylum at Indianapolis, whom the first chapter visits. Dotty Parlin is a small, merry girl, and her cousin Katie, called Flyaway, steals most scenes with her baby talk and bold ways.

The chapters are games and scrapes: playing ship, a spoiled dinner, playing truant, playing prisoner, and playing thief. A train ride to Indianapolis opens the book, with Katie thrilled to ride in the cars. Thanksgiving Day and Grandma's old times slow the pace, and a crystal wedding closes it. May, who also wrote the Little Prudy books, keeps each fault small and each lesson kind. The talk is full of child speech, spelled as it sounds, which was the book's charm for its first readers.
dotty-dimple-s-flyaway:
Sophie May centers her 1871 Dotty Dimple volume on Katie Clifford, the small cousin everyone calls Flyaway because she is so light the wind might take her. Her father jokes that a cent in her pocket keeps her from flying off. Dotty Dimple shares the stage, older and steadier, but Katie's runs and schemes drive the book.

Chapter heads tell the pattern: running away to church, running away to heaven, a railroad savage, and the rag-bag. Katie knows all news byfore, as she says, and pets and scolds follow her everywhere. A bedtime quarrel shows her temper at full stretch, hunting for words fierce enough to make Dotty quail. May writes small children with close love and sharp ears. The book stands as a portrait of a willful little girl in a big, fond family that bends around her.
early-kings-of-norway:
Thomas Carlyle wrote Early Kings of Norway from the Icelandic sagas, crediting Iceland's long-winter writing habit and excellent penmanship for whatever history of the Norse kings survives. The Sterling Edition text gathers his 1875 essay with footnotes as endnotes. Carlyle follows Harald Fairhair's unification and the jarls of Orkney and Lade.

The narrative reaches Saint Olaf's stormy sainthood, Magnus, and the sea-kings' tragedies of crime and heroism, pausing even for Edmund Ironside's murder and Knut's sole kingship of England. Carlyle's prose heaves like the northern seas, and his hero-worship finds perfect material in the saga kings. Readers wanting Snorri in concentrated, thunderous English abridgement have used this essay ever since.
english-dialects-from-the-eighth-century:
Walter W. Skeat, founder of the English Dialect Society, surveys English Dialects from the Eighth Century to the Present Day in this Cambridge book of 1911, reprinted 1912. Early chapters set out the four old dialects and the meaning of Anglo-Saxon. Specimens follow, region by region, with Northumbria traced to 1300 and beyond.

Skeat quotes old documents, like the proclamation older than the first three Edwards, rich in native words later displaced. He notes fultume for assistance and holde for faithful before French words drove them out. Foreign elements from Norman and Italian get their own chapter. The East Midland and other modern dialects close the survey. Skeat writes for readers who want the map of English speech drawn by its best mapmaker.
euripides-alcestis-murray:
Euripides staged Alcestis in Athens in 438 BCE, his earliest surviving play. Gilbert Murray translated the Greek tragedy into English verse. King Admetus may escape death if another person dies in his place.

His wife Alcestis alone accepts the bargain, and the household mourns her deeply. Heracles arrives as a guest, learns the truth, and wrestles Death for her. The play blends grief, gratitude, and an almost comic rescue. It was performed in the slot usually given to a satyr play. Murray's graceful verse keeps its strange, gentle mood intact for English readers.
euripides-electra-murray:
Euripides wrote his Electra around 413 BCE, retelling a story Sophocles also staged. Gilbert Murray translated the tragedy into English verse. Electra lives in exile, married off to a poor farmer, while her mother rules with Aegisthus.

Her brother Orestes returns in secret, and recognition slowly dawns between them. Together they plan the killing of their mother Clytemnestra and her lover. Euripides makes the revenge feel squalid rather than heroic, questioning its justice. Peasant decency contrasts sharply with royal crime throughout. Murray's version brings out the play's bitterness and pity in equal measure.
euripides-hippolytus-bacchae-murray:
Gilbert Murray translated two of Euripides' darkest tragedies in this pairing. Hippolytus dates to 428 BCE, while The Bacchae was produced after the poet's death. Both plays show gods punishing humans who refuse them honor.

Hippolytus spurns Aphrodite, and his stepmother Phaedra's desire destroys them both. In The Bacchae, Dionysus returns to Thebes and drives its women into frenzy. King Pentheus, who denies the god, is torn apart by his own mother. Euripides treats divine power as beautiful and terrifying at once. Murray's verse versions long introduced English readers to these unsettling masterpieces.
euripides-iphigenia-tauris-murray:
Euripides wrote Iphigenia in Tauris around 414 BCE, late in the Trojan War cycle. Gilbert Murray translated the play into English verse. Iphigenia, thought sacrificed by her father, actually serves Artemis in a distant land.

As priestess she must prepare captured strangers for sacrifice on the altar. Two Greeks arrive, and one proves to be her brother Orestes. Brother and sister plot an escape with the goddess's statue in hand. Unlike most tragedies, the play ends in rescue and reunion. Murray renders its suspense and tenderness with unusual charm. Athena herself arrives to bless the escape at the close.
euripides-medea-murray:
Euripides staged Medea in Athens in 431 BCE, at the start of a long war. Gilbert Murray translated the tragedy into English verse. Jason has abandoned Medea, his foreign wife, to marry a Corinthian princess.

Medea pleads, schemes, and finally takes a revenge that still shocks audiences. She kills the princess, the king, and her own two children. Euripides gives her arguments so strong that Jason looks small beside her. The play asks what a wronged outsider owes to law or mercy. Murray's translation carried its power to generations of English readers.
euripides-rhesus-murray:
Rhesus is a short tragedy of a night raid during the Trojan War. Gilbert Murray translated the play, which tradition assigns to Euripides. Modern scholars often doubt that Euripides actually wrote it.

Thracian king Rhesus arrives to aid Troy and camps outside the city walls. Odysseus and Diomedes slip through the dark and kill him in his sleep. A charioteer survives to accuse Hector of betrayal and treachery. The action stays tight, nocturnal, and full of confused alarms. Even as a lesser work, it shows how Greek dramatists mined the Iliad for fresh scenes.
euripides-trojan-women-murray:
Euripides produced The Trojan Women in 415 BCE, while Athens was fighting its own brutal war. Gilbert Murray translated the tragedy into English verse. Troy has fallen, and its royal women wait to be handed to Greek masters.

Hecuba, the widowed queen, watches every remaining hope stripped away. Cassandra is dragged off, Andromache loses her small son to murder, and Helen pleads for her life. Almost nothing happens except suffering, speech by speech. That stillness is the point, and the accusation. Murray's version became famous as an anti-war statement in its own right.
extracts-from-the-diary-of-william-bray:
William Bray was a Surrey lawyer and antiquary, a man who studied old records and local history, and his diary runs from 1756 to 1800. Bray, born at Shere in 1736, worked as an attorney, served the Society of Antiquaries as treasurer, and lived to ninety-six. These extracts, printed for his descendants, add his later memoranda to the daily entries.

Entries record calls, card games, law business, planting, and trips around Surrey and London. Bray also completed a three-volume history of Surrey and edited the memoirs of John Evelyn, work the opening memoir describes. The pleasure here is ordinary eighteenth-century life noted down day by day, plainly and without fuss.
famous-violinists-of-to-day-and-yesterda:
Lahee's Famous Violinists of To-day and Yesterday surveys celebrated players across the instrument's history. Henry C. Lahee first issued the book in Boston in 1899. This copy is the tenth impression, dated January 1916. An Ole Bull portrait fronts the volume.

In his preface Lahee promises a bird's-eye view, not deep lives of a few. He follows the same plan as his earlier Famous Singers. Performers before the public win places over famed teachers. Chapters run in birth order rather than by schools, he explains. A school plan led only to confusion in drafting, he admits. A chronological table rests on the best authorities he could find. The book suits readers who want the violin's great names in sequence.
fanny-s-first-play:
Fanny's First Play, by Bernard Shaw and dated 1911, is a comedy about a young woman's secret debut as a playwright. Shaw calls the piece a potboiler in his preface, then uses the preface to attack mere morality: the habit, he says, of doing what others do simply because others do it. Right and wrong, honor and disgrace, once guided conduct; now custom does the work, and the young suffer for it.

The play frames Fanny's work as a private performance judged by critics who do not know the author. Around that device Shaw builds his satire of the theater world, respectable families, and the fear of disgrace that rules both. Parents and children trade places as judges. The text here keeps Shaw's own spelling habits, a small rebellion he practiced in print as faithfully as his characters practice theirs on stage.
fbi-vault-9-11-commission-report-9-11-fb:
A letter dated May 24, 2004, from the Federal Bureau of Investigation to a congressional committee chairman opens this file. The chairman had asked, after a March 2004 letter from Director Mueller, for answers on how intelligence is shared and what the bureau had changed. The file holds the bureau's full set of replies.

The sampled pages turn to the training of intelligence analysts. They tell of new funds from Congress for that training, a plan to build a cadre of skilled analysts, and a train-the-trainer path to spread the skills. Other pages deal with the bureau's evaluation strategy. The file reads as a formal defense of reforms, given to Congress while the lessons of September 11 were still being weighed.
fbi-vault-9-11-commission-report-9-11-in: One interview report stands alone in this file from the Federal Bureau of Investigation records on the September 11 attacks. Agents spoke with Abdulhakim Ali Hashem Murad as he was flown from Manila to New York. A sealed court charge in New York accused him of a plot to destroy United States aircraft. Agents read him his rights in English and in Arabic. He signed the waiver forms in both tongues and agreed to speak in English. The report covers the flight and the rights process, not what he said.

Samir Abdoun is the man spoken to in this Federal Bureau of Investigation interview record dated May 15, 2002. The talk took place at the United States Attorney's office in San Diego, California. Bureau agents, immigration staff, and prosecutor Michael Wheat took part. Abdoun came with a lawyer and gave his account of his own will. The rest of the file, as freed, is redaction blocks and case codes. What Abdoun said cannot be read from these pages, and no account of it is offered here.

An Atlanta cable dated May 18, 2004, reports interview work in this Federal Bureau of Investigation file on Mohdar Mohamed Abdullah. The case name links him to the San Diego circle around two of the hijackers. Agents gathered his prison history in Atlanta and word from a man who had been held with him.

That man had shared the immigration detention site in San Diego with Mohdar. He called him childish, said he talked too much, and could give no firm case in point. He said Mohdar wished to marry an American woman, though he did not know why. He also said Mohdar had handed some immigration papers to another man in the cells. The cable is a character sketch built from jail talk, and it reads as such.

Phoenix prepared this Federal Bureau of Investigation summary on Rayed Mohammed Abdullah, dated May 5, 2002. It states the base for the case and then walks the reader through the hijackers' last weeks. Much of the sampled text is a record of how plane tickets were bought.

Khalid Al-Mihdhar and his seatmate paid cash for their tickets on September 5, 2001, at the American Airlines counter at the Baltimore airport. On August 27, 2001, Nawaf and Salem Al Hazmi bought theirs through a travel website, with a debit card in Nawaf's name. On August 31, Hani Hanjour's card was refused at a New Jersey travel shop when the fare topped its limit, so he paid cash. The pages close on his flight training in New Jersey and Maryland.

San Diego reported an interview with Charles Sabah Toma on May 18, 2004, in this Federal Bureau of Investigation file. The talk fed the case of Mohdar Mohamed Abdullah, a man tied to the San Diego hijackers. Toma had fresh facts on how the hijackers got false papers.

Toma said Mohdar helped the men get false identity cards from a seller he did not name. On his account, Mohdar drove them to Los Angeles, to spots near McArthur Park and Huntington Park. There Mohdar bought about four or five false California driving identity cards and gave them to the hijackers. Toma also spoke of the men's San Diego flat and their move out of it. The cable kept the case's San Diego thread alive three years after the attacks.
fbi-vault-9-11-commission-report-9-11-th:
Daily threat pages from the bureau's web system fill this Federal Bureau of Investigation file for May 2001. The pages come from the Usama Bin Laden and Radical Fundamentalist unit's threat update. A note to readers warns that the text is raw reporting, for news value only, and that no case should start from it without headquarters' leave.

The update for May 7, 2001, lists fresh threats and events not in past editions. One item reports word of a fundamentalist threat aimed at London, New York, and Boston. The sampled pages also track a traveler named Chisti, who reached New York on an Air France flight, bound for San Francisco. Sections on Iranian and Hezbollah threats report no new items at all.
felix-o-day:
F. Hopkinson Smith's Felix O'Day opens on Broadway in the rain, the Great White Way splashed with liquid jewels. Playhouses blaze, crowds surge, and street urchins clutch gallery money. Against this glitter the novel sets its hero, glimpsed some ten years before the main action. Felix O'Day is an Irish gentleman ruined and exiled by a family disgrace.

In New York he works humbly in an antique shop, hiding his name and his past. A stolen miniature, a young girl's ruin, and his own wife's betrayal knot the plot. Smith, engineer, painter, and raconteur, loved the city's clerks and curio dealers. His Felix keeps a gentleman's honour in a shopkeeper's apron. The novel is his most popular fiction, a romance of redemption among Broadway's lights, where the moth found in the mud at dawn is answered by one man's quiet restitution.
five-little-peppers-midway:
Five Little Peppers Midway continues the Pepper family stories by Margaret Sidney, who dedicates the book to her own little Margaret, known to readers as Phronsie. Sidney returns to the little brown house and its five children, now older, busier, and pulled toward new houses and new duties. The contents open with Phronsie's pie and a visit from Cousin Eunice Chatterton.

Chapter titles map the family's season of change. A rehearsal and a play bring Badgertown callers, then a sudden blow separates the party. Polly takes up new work, news arrives, and Mamsie's wedding crowns the middle of the book. Phronsie vanishes and is found, in the best Pepper tradition of alarm ending in relief. The girls get Polly back for the close. Work, marriage, and sibling loyalty carry these domestic chapters.
foul-play:
Charles Reade and Dion Boucicault joined forces on Foul Play, a sensation novel that opens in a London merchant's dining room. Merchant Wardlaw rules his Russell Square house with iron routine and full dress at dinner. His son Arthur, clerk turned Oxford student, seems set to inherit firm and habits. Tutor Robert Penfold, who owes the family gratitude, guards the young man's studies.

Forgery and a lost ship drive the plot once the opening breaks. Helen Rolleston, a general's daughter, draws the loves of men whose secrets tie back to the Wardlaw firm. James Seaton, a broken man hiding from his past, watches her from the garden shadows. False charges, an insurance mystery, and a hunt for the forger keep the pace. Reade's research habits show in legal and shipping detail. Readers who like sensation fiction, with crime, courtship, and ruined names at stake, get a plate here.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BeckRay_Beck_Ra:
More than three years after the assassination, the FBI's Dallas office still carried an open subject line: Assassination of President John F. Kennedy. This memorandum, dated February 23, 1967, went to SAC Gordon Shanklin, the special agent in charge at Dallas, under file 89-43.

The sender's name is garbled in the scan, a reminder of the condition of much of the released paper. Dallas was where the crime happened, and its office held the local file that every new lead, letter, and claim still entered. The single memo is preserved as a page of that file's long afterlife.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BertrandClayDoc:
Clay Bertrand was the name Jim Garrison's investigation chased through New Orleans: the alleged alias of Clay Shaw, the businessman Garrison put on trial for conspiring to kill President Kennedy. These research notes, dated November 23, 1971, come from a researcher's work on that matter after the trial had ended.

The notes record that Ed Planer confirmed Jesse Core appeared in preserved Johann Rush footage, film connected with Dealey Plaza on the day of the assassination. They also record meetings with Garrison himself. Research notes like these are the workshop floor of assassination scholarship: half-checked leads, names, and film references kept for later use.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MarcusRay_Marcu:
Raymond Marcus published 'Truth vs. Political Truth' as a collection of essays, and this is volume one, dated August 2001. Marcus writes about media elites and how they shape public opinion. His central subject is the assassination of John F. Kennedy and the way it has been covered.

Marcus was a longtime researcher who argued that the press protected the official account. The essays measure news coverage against the evidence as he read it. For readers, the volume offers one researcher's case that political convenience, not proof, settled the story in print. It appeared nearly forty years after Dallas, in a debate that had by then moved from commissions to talk shows and the early internet.
gower-latin-works-macaulay:
George Macaulay's Complete Works of John Gower gathered the poet's writings in four volumes at the turn of the century. Volume Three, from 1902, prints Gower's Latin works with notes. Gower wrote in three tongues, and Latin was his language of public warning.

The chief work here is the Vox Clamantis, the Voice of One Crying, on the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 and the sins of every rank. The Cronica Tripertita treats the fall of Richard II. Shorter Latin poems fill out the volume. Macaulay's editing let English readers meet the stern moralist behind the gentle love poet of the Confessio.
happy-and-gay-marching-away: Happy and Gay Marching Away is a tiny American picture book for the youngest children, a few leaves of verse and alphabet. It opens with the alphabet in capitals. A rhymed introduction presents Tot, Tom, and Toby, with dogs, cats, horses, and goats to see. The reader is asked to turn the leaves gently, so as not to hurt the creatures in the pictures. A first tale tells how a wicked boy took a wild bird from its nest. It was made to teach letters and kindness at once.
heimskringla-or-the-chronicle-of-the-kin:
Snorri Sturluson, the Icelandic poet and historian, wrote Heimskringla around 1225, a cycle of sagas covering Norway's kings from about 850 to 1177. This English text opens with the sagas of Halfdan the Black and Harald Fairhair, then Hakon the Good and Olaf Trygvason. Snorri worked from skaldic verse, the praise poems he quotes as evidence.

The long middle reaches the saga of Saint Olaf, the largest in the book, and continues through Magnus the Good, Harald Hardrade, and later kings. Battles, sea voyages, and councils fill the pages, told in Snorri's terse, ironic style. Heimskringla remains the chief narrative source for early Norwegian history and a summit of medieval Icelandic prose.
her-own-way:
Clyde Fitch wrote this play in four acts, published in 1907. Georgiana, a young woman of strong feeling, loves a man who has gone off to war. Sam Coast, a rich suitor, presses her to marry him instead. She tells him plainly that her heart is not free.

The acts turn on visits, letters, and sharp talk between rivals. Georgiana holds her ground while friends and kin weigh in. Fitch mixes light social scenes with real risk, since her love may not come home. Readers get a stage piece about choice, pride, and faith kept under strain.
hetty-gray:
Rosa Mulholland, later Lady Gilbert, wrote this children's novel. Its second title calls Hetty Gray nobody's bairn, or child. Hetty is a small orphan found in the village of Wavertree. Kind folk take her in, but her place is never sure.

Chapters follow Hetty through new homes, lessons, and small trials. She rebels, errs, and holds fast to those she loves. A late turn asks who Hetty truly is and where she belongs. The tale is warm and moral in tone, shaped for young readers who like a brave, lone child at the center.
how-to-live-on-24-hours-a-day:
Arnold Bennett addressed the office worker's secret poverty in How to Live on 24 Hours a Day: not money, but time. Bennett argues that the day holds a daily miracle of unspent hours outside work, and that most men fritter them as careless spenders fritter income. His program asks for a modest start: an hour or so of serious reading, reflection, and interest in the arts, protected like a budget.

Chapters cover controlling the mind, the reflective mood, and dangers to avoid, all in Bennett's brisk, funny, elder-brother voice. He scolds, encourages, and sets homework. The little book became the classic of self-improvement literature, and its central claim still stings: you already have the time; you are spending it on nothing.
i-will-repay:
Baroness Orczy's I Will Repay continues the world of the Scarlet Pimpernel in revolutionary Paris. A prologue in 1783 shows a card-table quarrel over the notorious Adèle de Montchéri. The young Vicomte de Marny hurls insults and cards at Paul Déroulède, the rich newcomer. A duel follows, and the boy falls.

De Marny's sister Anne Marie nurses the family's vow: I will repay. Ten years later the Revolution gives her the weapon she needs. Déroulède, now a popular deputy, shelters a persecuted girl in his house. Anne Marie enters his service to destroy him, and loves him instead. Orczy weaves denunciation, prison, and rescue into her melodrama. The Pimpernel himself moves at the edges. Honour and revenge fight for one woman's soul across the Terror.
if-i-may:
A. A. Milne's If I May gathers essays reprinted from The Sphere, The Outlook, The Daily News, The Sunday Express and Vanity Fair, with alterations and additions. Milne, already known for Not That It Matters, writes here before his fame as the creator of Winnie-the-Pooh.

Contents include The Case for the Artist, A London Garden, The Game of Kings, Fixtures and Fittings, Experts, The Robinson Tradition, Getting Things Done, and Christmas Games. Later essays treat the mathematical mind, going out to dinner, the etiquette of escape, and children's plays. Readers who enjoy light, witty essays will find Milne at his most companionable.
ivanoff-a-play:
Anton Chekhov's Ivanoff appears here in an early English translation credited to Anton Checkov. Its cast list is precise. Nicholas Ivanoff serves on the Council of Peasant Affairs. His wife Anna, born Sarah Abramson, is dying of consumption. His uncle Count Shabelski and the Lebedieffs complete the household, and Sasha Lebedieff loves him. Dr Lvoff, young and righteous, watches Ivanoff's debts and depression with disgust.

The stage fills with knick-knacks, revolvers, vodka, and salted herrings as Ivanoff's estate and marriage collapse together. Borkin, his manager, schemes while Sasha offers rescue through love. Chekhov's first full-length play already shows his method: no villains, much talk, and a gun that finally speaks. Its ending still divides audiences between pity and judgment.
keeping-fit-all-the-way:
Keeping Fit All the Way is Walter Camp's book on how to obtain and maintain health, strength, and efficiency. Camp, the famous Yale football coach, wrote it for general readers in 1919. A front photograph shows Camp himself beside ex-President Taft and Colonel Ullman. The three are named pioneers of senior service, the book's program for older men.

Part Two presents the Daily Dozen, Camp's short set of daily exercises. The exercises were devised for busy men who had no time for long training. Camp argues that fitness is a duty, not a hobby, in work and war alike. The book closes with the American Citizen's Creed. It remains the classic statement of Camp's daily-dozen plan.
laugh-and-play:
